subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING ELIGIBILITY OF MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT TO SERVE IN AIR FORCE

speechtext:
Right Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 102, to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act.﻿JUNE 12, 1941
Long Adjournment
He said: I should like to ask the leave of the house to introduce a bill which I think will receive general approval. A couple of days ago the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) drew my attention to section 12 of the Senate and House of Commons Act which provides that service in the naval or military forces shall not render a member ineligible to sit in parliament. When that section was enacted there was no air force, and there is a possibility that some doubt might arise if the word "air" were not added to the section. There are members of the present house who are serving in the air force. This amendment merely adds the word "air" to section 12, and adds another section that the act shall be deemed to have come into force on the tenth day of September, 1939.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.
Mr. LAPOINTE (Quebec East) moved the second reading of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, we approve the resolution moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), holding, as we do, the view that the house should not prorogue but adjourn. We have been of the opinion that an adjournment should not exceed' ninety days, but in this particular case, with the harvest season running at least into the end of October, I think the date selected by the Prime Minister is a wise one. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not rise to oppose the motion but I believe that before parliament adjourns the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) should inform the house what is Canada's foreign policy, whether it is that there shall be no further commitments and that parliament will decide in all these matters in the future as in the past. So far parliament has not been consulted at all. The executive does it. Private, secret agreements, notes and appeasements, have been made without parliament knowing anything about them. I think the Prime Minister should also tell us whether he proposes to continue the same appeasement policy respecting 500,000 bushels of grain to Japan and north China, because if Britain cannot appease them, how can Canada, as

has been demonstrated in the last three years with respect to Japanese action towards Britain at Shanghai and Hong Kong?
Second^, the Prime Minister has consulted some members of the House of Commons on Japan, secretly, unknown to other members of the house. All of it is known to our allies. In the recess of parliament no secret meetings of this kind should be held because we have a duty to the mother country and the other dominions, and the situation at the present time is too dangerous for these secret meetings and failure to give the house the facts.
Lastly, the Prime Minister should be in a position before the adjournment to inform the house as to the loss of Canadian merchant shipping off the coasts of Ireland, of men, food and munitions, part of which is reflected in our tax rate. Yesterday the United States was refused the use of these same empire bases off Ireland, and wre have not heard a word here as to what our policy is.
There should also be some stand taken immediately by this government as to the Vichy movement against the allies and our recognition of it here.
I should like to know whether the Prime Minister is prepared to make a statement on these three matters before the house closes. I support the motion, because in an emergency the members can be called together very quickly, but how can we and the people of this country know what is going on unless parliament .is given all this information? What is the use of looking for recruits and victory loans if the people are not informed of our foreign and defence policy? We should have an informed public opinion. We might as well meet in secret for all the information that has been given to the country throughout the whole of the sittings in the reports to the house or with regard to the unreported business.
Mr. JEAN-FRANCOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): Mr. Speaker I should' like to offer a suggestion. The members of parliament were greatly inconvenienced last fall because the preparation of the revised edition of Hansard and the publication of the statutes for last session was proceeded with only after prorogation. As the first part of the session is now almost concluded, I wonder whether the government would not be disposed to give instructions so that the statute book will be published at the earliest opportunity on account of the important legislation that has been passed, and so that revised Hansard will also be published at the earliest opportunity?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN TO NOVEMBER 3-ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would say first of all to my hon. friend from Broadview (Mr. Church) that I hope he will not regard me as an appeaser. I seek to be a conciliator where that is likely to prove helpful. There is a great difference between the two. Perhaps, in the latter capacity, I may be pardoned if I do not provoke a discussion on the floor of this house with regard to some of the questions to which he has made reference. There is the responsibility of inviting discussion of certain matters; there is equally the responsibility of seeking to avoid discussion. If I thought it would help the position of the allied nations in the war at the present time to have a discussion here with respect to Japanese matters, bases in Ireland, and other questions which my hon. friend has mentioned, I would not have waited until this time to invite such discussion. But, where there are the strongest reasons for believing that no good purpose would be served by any such discussion, I prefer to take the responsibility of not inviting it. All the matters to which my hon. friend has referred have been carefully considered by my colleagues and myself, and. we have taken in these matters the course which we believed to be in the interests of the war effort of the entire British commonwealth.
As to my hon. friend's reference to myself and conversations with certain private members, he evidently refers to the meeting I had in my office with hon. members from the province of British Columbia. I believe it is not only the right thing, but very much the duty of one who understands the situation affecting constituencies of a particular province, to seek to make known to those in the parts affected matters of which they would wish to have full knowledge. But that does not imply that one is seeking to impart to others information, which one would not be prepared to impart to all. I could not have said what I said to hon. members from British Columbia in a statement to the entire house at that time; had I said at that time publicly in the house what I said yesterday, I believe the understanding of it by hon. members would have been quite different, and the intent of it on their part and by others might have been viewed quite differently from the way in which it was. I do not think I have anything further to add on that subject.
My hon. friend the leader of.the opposition (Mr. Hanson) asked me a day or two ago about the Canada-United States permanent joint defence board agreement, as to whether that was not in the nature of an agreement which should have been submitted to parliament. I did not catch at the time the full significance of my hon. friend's remarks, and I therefore said I would like before replying to give the matter a little further thought.
As my hon. friend knows, that agreement is an agreement for the study of certain matters affecting defence, by representatives of the two governments, and such recommendations as are made under that agreement, are made by the representatives of the two countries to their respective governments. The study relates to sea, land and air problems.. In the broad sense it has to do with the defence of the north half of the western hemisphere. There are no commitments made by the permanent joint board of defence. The board's representations are made to the respective governments by their respective representatives on the board. The governments then take up with their own departments and themselves decide as to the particular course to be taken. There is no commitment of the country in advance to any obligation. For that reason it has not been thought necessary to put the agreement before parliament for approval.

speechtext:
I desire to ask the Prime
Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) a question, based upon the correspondence exchanged between himself and the premier of Ontario with respect to matters of taxation, and upon the recent request of Mr. Hepburn that the Prime Minister call a conference of all the provinces to consider the whole subject of the financial relations as between the dominion and the provinces. The reply of the Prime Minister was to the effect that, if requested so to do by all the provinces he would call such a conference. May I ask the Prime Minister if he will give further consideration to the proposal? I
The War-Canada's, Problems

would also ask the Prime Minister if he will, of his own motion, call such a conference, to be held at an early day, at which would be considered not only matters of finance and taxation but also the altered constitutional powers resulting from the invasion of the provincial field by the dominion under the provisions of the war measures and mobilization acts, and because of the necessities of war.
I have recently read a survey of public opinion as reflected) in the press and I am impressed with the almost unanimity of public opinion favouring such a conference, based on the theory of the promotion of national unity.
The Prime Minister may have felt that after what happened in January last and what has occurred since he could not, without loss of dignity, call the provinces together in conference without a unanimous request from the provinces. May I suggest-

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL OF ONTARIO PREMIER FOR CONFERENCE OF PROVINCES ON CANADA'S PROBLEMS
speechtext:
Thank
you, Mr. Speaker. May I suggest to the Prime Minister that I feel sure that there would be no loss of position if he, upon high consideration of national unity, and in a sincere and honest effort to unite this country in a supreme war effort, were to call a conference for the purposes suggested. It would be an exhibition of magnanimity and would, I believe, be applauded by all the thinking people of Canada.
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING
(Prime Minister):	Mr. Speaker, perhaps I
might refer at the outset to the concluding remarks of my hon. friend, in which he has suggested that there would be no loss of dignity on my part were I to call a conference, no loss of position if I were to do so, and that it would be an exhibition of magnanimity on my part and be applauded by all the thinking people of Canada if I were to call another dominion-provincial conference at this time.
I think my hon. friend will agree that I have never been one to stand on my dignity, nor

have I much regard for those who do. With respect to magnanimity, I think I have given ample evidence to the country that I am not afraid to assume that particular attitude in public. I have, to the best of my ability at all times, with respect to public affairs, sought to be as magnanimous as it would be possible to be not only towards my political opponents but towards any who may differ from me in opinion on any matter. As respects my hon. friend's remarks in that particular, I believe I need not say more.
But the leader of the opposition asks, would the Prime Minister of his own motion call such a conference, to be held at an early day, at which would be considered not only matters of finance and taxation but also the altered constitutional powers resulting from the invasion of the provincial field by the dominion under the provisions of the war measures and mobilization acts, and because of the necessities of war. Well, hon. members will recall that the conference which was held in January was, among other reasons, precisely for the purpose of considering the whole question of finance and taxation and the matter of the altered constitutional powers which might be necessitated by certain courses of action. But when the conference was held, one argument which was put forth for not continuing the conference-the argument which I heard most vigorously asserted-was that this was not a time-a time of war-to be considering constitutional questions; that ministers, particularly federal ministers should not be wasting their time discussing questions of finance, taxation and the like, but should be attending to their duties as ministers of the crown responsible for the war effort of Canada. We were told we had powers of taxation and it was for us not to talk about them but to exercise them as we thought the country's war needs required. That was the ground on which, broadly speaking, the last conference found it impossible to proceed. That ground was taken, not by myself nor by any member of the dominion government but by one or more of the provinces, and unless some of the provinces have had a [DOT] very material change of mind on that score I fail to see how another conference called at this time would not raise precisely the same arguments.

speechtext:
Yes, it might be a change of heart, but some hearts change too often. I do not speak with any expert knowledge of changes of heart in domestic affairs, but I can say something about them in relation to public matters.

The War-Canada's, Problems
I am obliged to my hon. friend for bringing up this subject at this time because it may help me to clear what appears to be either an intentional or an unintentional misrepresentation of the reply which I have made to the Premier of Ontario with respect to the calling of a conference. My hon. friend says he has reviewed the press in regard to the matter. I have not found the unanimity of opinion that he has with regard to the wisdom of having another conference called. Very different views have been expressed in the publications I have read. What I have noticed, however, is that some of the journals of the country are stating that I had refused to have another conference held. What I said has been construed as representing an arbitrary stand; that I was unwilling to have another conference called.
May I read the concluding paragraph of the communication which I sent to the Premier of Ontario:
If, however, the premiers of the several provinces should unite in a request for another dominion-provincial conference, the dominion government will be prepared to give immediate consideration to any such request.
The words "immediate consideration" were used advisedly. They were not intended to imply that we would not call such a conference, but rather that, before deciding upon any question of this kind, it would be necessary to do so in the light of the circumstances as they might exist at the time. It might be wholly inadvisable, under conditions that cannot be foreseen at the moment, to call a conference at any one particular time. That is all that is meant about giving the matter consideration-considering the nature of the replies that might be received from the several provinces, and what it would be wisest to do in the circumstances existing at the time.
Let me make it perfectly clear that if the premiers of the provinces of Canada unite in a request for a conference that conference will be called. I have no hesitation whatever in saying if I receive from the different premiers of Canada communications to the effect that they believe it would be in the national interest, and in the interest of Canada's war effort at this time, to have a conference called that I will undertake to see that such a conference is speedily called. But without receiving such assurances from the premiers of the different provinces, I am afraid that in calling a second conference I should be open to exactly the same course of chastisement and criticism that was followed at the last conference.
My hon. friend, and rightly so, places his question on the ground of high considerations
of national unity. It is precisely on that ground that I would view the whole question of the wisdom of holding another conference. If I believed that another conference called at this moment would help to further Canada's war effort by giving to the nation an exhibition of national unity on the part of all, particularly with respect to questions of taxation, constitutional problems and the like, I would be the first to have a conference called immeT diately. The conditions that should govern are I believe those which I have stated in the telegram which I sent to the Premier of Ontario, as contained in the following paragraph:
Having in mind the circumstances which occasioned the failure of the conference of five months ago, our government is of the opinion that unless there were general agreement on the part of all the provinces upon the desirability of holding another dominion-provincial conference, such a conference called at this time might only serve to accentuate the differences raised at the last conference. Were such to be the case, it would certainly prove prejudicial rather than helpful to Canada's war effort.
I do not think that anyone can deny the accuracy of that statement. Let me make the position perfectly clear. The premiers of all the provinces will have full knowledge of this correspondence. They will see in the press this afternoon and to-morrow the statement which I am making at the present time. I do not wish any of them to wait to be asked what their views are. I invite them now, if they wish to have a dominion-provincial conference called at Ottawa, to write and so notify me and indicate in their letters the agenda they wish to have considered at the conference; and if I receive requests from all the provinces to have a conference called, and agenda are supplied to show what they would wish to have considered at the conference, I will take the matter up with my colleagues immediately to see if we cannot so arrange the agenda as to meet the wishes of all, and have a conference called at the earliest possible moment.

speechtext:
I should like to direct a question to the new Minister of National War Services. I had given notice to the Prime Minister of my intention to refer to this matter yesterday in the house and asked if he was prepared to make an announcement of the appointment of a new minister. He anticipated my question by making an announcement, therefore I did not put the question. I am sorry I have not had the

Supply-Finance
opportunity of sending the question to the new minister; therefore I shall give him plenty of time to do what I am going to ask of him.
My question is based on a statement made in this house on June 4 by the then Minister of National War Services that he had not authorized a recent press dispatch appearing in the New York Daily News which said that Canadian householders were unwilling to come within the scope of a British plan for voluntary creamless days in the United States, so that increased food supplies might be available for Britain. Will the minister give this his immediate attention and try to offset the unfortunate effect of what appears to have been a slip by the department over which he now presides? Secondly, will he try to bring about a creamless day in Canada also, and in this way make additional food supplies available for Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This is an important item, and I promised that at some stage I would make reply to some questions which were asked by the leader of the opposition.
In his speech on June 2, on the motion for second reading of Bill No. 87, to amend the Income War Tax Act, the leader of the opposition asked that certain aspects of the proposed arrangement with the provinces be clarified, and I undertook to answer his questions when I had an appropriate opportunity of doing so. The first question dealt with the amount which would be payable to the province of Alberta in the event that province should choose option B. I quote from page 3386 of Hansard, where the leader of the opposition said:
What is to be the attitude of this government with regard to that province, having regard to the fact that for several years the government of Alberta has repudiated its solemn obligation to pay in full the interest upon its bonds, much to the loss of its credit and also potentially affecting the credit of other provinces? Is this government, in dealing with Alberta, to pay only to that province the actual amount of bond interest paid by that province, and thus recognize its default and thereby in effect condone its action? Or will it insist upon an arrangement being made by that province whereby the Alberta government will respect ts responsibilities?
Before I answer the question directly I should like to refer briefly to the proposal to the provinces which I described in detail in my budget speech. In that speech I dealt with the great difficulties with which we were confronted in our search for the necessary revenues with which to prosecute the war, because of the varying levels of taxation in the different provinces; and I said we had come to the conclusion finally that we should introduce taxes at rates which would be possible if the provinces were out of the personal income and corporation tax fields. At the same time we proposed to make an annual payment each year for the duration of the 
war to provinces which would temporarily vacate those two tax fields. It was difficult to decide upon a satisfactory formula for arriving at the amount of those annual payments to the provinces; indeed the one we decided upon would not do as a basis if a permanent arrangement were contemplated. But after very careful study we came to the conclusion that it was as good a formula as any that could be found for this particular and temporary purpose. It has the merit- when coupled with the proposal to discontinue the present annual grants to Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, and when the proposal to pay fiscal needs subsidies to provinces which can show they require them is taken into account-of providing an annual payment which will leave all the provinces in substantially the position they were in, from the revenue point of view, in 1941.
The formula is to pay either: (a) the revenues which the province and its municipalities actually obtained from personal income and corporation taxes during the fiscal year 'ending nearest to December 31, 1940; or (b) the cost of the net debt service actually paid by the province during the fiscal year ending nearest, to December 31, 1940, not including contributions to sinking funds, less the revenue obtained from succession duties dhring that period. In simple terms, the annual payments to the provinces are based upon either the cash actually received from taxes in 1940, or the cash actually paid out in interest. The formula is not based on the taxes which should have been collected or the interest which should have been paid. It is based upon the amount of the actual cash receipts or the cash disbursements.
Now the question is asked whether in the case of Alberta the formula should be changed so that the dominion would pay either the taxes actually collected, under option (a); or, under option (b), the interest which would have been paid if Alberta had paid its bond interest in full. According to preliminary estimates made by the Alberta treasury department, which were presented for purposes of discussion only and are subject to checking and revision, the annual payment to Alberta under the present formula, if it accepts the dominion's offer, would be approximately $4,000,000 under option (a), or $3,200,000 under option (b). If option (b) were changed and, based upon the interest at full rates, irrespective of whether such interest was paid or not, then the amount payable under that option

Supply-Finance
would be approximately $5,750,000. Under the present formula, therefore, Alberta would receive $4,000,000 under option (a), or approximately $800,000 more than it would receive under option (b). If option (b) were changed, however, and were based on the full amount of the bond interest, then the amount paid under this option would be increased to $5,750,000, which is $1,750,000 more than the amount which will be paid to Alberta under the present formula. I take it that no one would suggest that the dominion should pay an additional $1,750,000 to Alberta unless Alberta undertook to pay its bond interest in full. Otherwise, for no good reason, the dominion would be making a present to Alberta of a very large sum of money, which would be quite unjustifiable.
I must assume, therefore, that the suggestions which have been made that the annual payment to Alberta should be based upon the full amount of its bond interest are predicated upon an agreement by the Alberta government to pay its bond interest in full, but I have heard no suggestion on the part of the Alberta government that it would be prepared to pay this interest in full.
The privy council said it should do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I believe that is so. It
may be willing to do so, but I have not heard of it; and in the absence of any declaration to the effect that Alberta is prepared to pay its bond interest in full it seems to me the present formula is fair and reasonable, in that Alberta is dealt with in exactly the same way as all the other provinces. I do not see how, by the widest stretch of the imagination, this can be construed as condoning the attitude of the Alberta government in defaulting on its bond interest. To me such a construction does not make sense. Surely the dominion has given ample evidence of its attitude toward the repudiation of contractual obligations and of its desire, indeed of its anxiety, to find a constructive solution of the financial difficulties which have faced a number of the provinces as a result of depression.
While, therefore, I do not propose to change the formula for determining the amount which will be payable to Alberta if it accepts the dominion's proposal, this does not mean that the door is shut for all time, or that this government will not reconsider the matter if the situation changes. For example, if the Alberta government were to work out some refunding plan with its bondholders, and then ask the dominion to reconsider the basis on which the annual
payment is to be computed, we should be prepared to sit down and discuss the question, or any other reasonable proposal that might be presented.
Perhaps the minister does not wish to be interrupted at this stage.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We should be prepared to sit down and discuss the question or any other reasonable proposal that might be presented. I cannot give any commitment further than that. I cannot see that any good purpose would be served by trying to cross this bridge before we come to it.
In case these remarks should be interpreted by bond speculators to mean more than they do mean, I should add, perhaps, that if in the future any such arrangement should be worked out, and the dominion were a party to it in any way, undoubtedly it would be necessary to impose a capital gains tax or take other practicable steps to ensure that speculators were not allowed to reap profits out of appreciation in bond values arising as a result of the discussion or negotiation of such a programme or its consummation.

By implication, not expressly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In order to clear up any possible misunderstanding about this so-called summary, I should like to state that it is described in its heading as "a preliminary memorandum upon some of the points to be covered in the agreements with the provinces, if the offer outlined in Mr. Ilsley's budget speech on April 29, 1941, is accepted." This preliminary memorandum covers the points raised by the leader of the opposition and one or two others which I shall not read as they have no bearing upon this particular subject.
On May 16 an officer of my department wrote a letter to the Honourable J. J. Hayes Doone, provincial secretary treasurer of the province of New Brunswick, enclosing a copy of the preliminary memorandum referred to. As the letter comments on the question under discussion, I propose to read it. It is as follows:
Dear Mr. Doone:
Following our discussion the other day, you asked me to let you have a general outline of the basis on which the personal income and corporation taxes imposed by any of the provinces which accept the offer outlined in Mr. Ilsley's budget speech of April 29th last, will be discontinued. No final decision has been reached upon this matter, but I enclose a copy of a preliminary memorandum which may serve as a working guide for the time being, on the understanding that it is not binding upon the dominion in any way. You will see that this memorandum covers a number of the points which we have discussed, but that these are limited to the questions which will apply to all provinces which accept the offer. Other questions which apply particularly to your province, such as the arrangements which might have to be made with your municipalities if you accept the dominion's offer, are not dealt with in the memorandum, and presumably will have to be the subject of further discussion.
If there is any further information you would like from me in the meantime, please be sure to let me know.
Yours very truly,
W. L. Gordon.
It will be seen therefore that the problem of the New Brunswick municipalities was not overlooked. As the leader of the opposition himself stated, the municipalities are the creation of the province and their jurisdiction to impose income tax is derived from the province. The agreements which we are making will be with the provinces and not with their municipalities. The question is, should we stipulate in the agreements which we make with the provinces that they must deal fairly with their own municipalities, or should we leave this to the good judgment of the provincial governments concerned? I appreciate that in the opinion of the leader of the opposition it is desirable to include a definite stipulation respecting the position of the municipalities in any agreements which we make with the provinces. I think, however, that before arriving at a final conclusion I should prefer to discuss this further with the representatives of the government of the province of New Brunswick, who will be as anxious as the leader of the opposition to protect the position of their municipalities. On Tuesday, June 3, the leader of the opposition asked that a statement be placed on the record showing the net amount which would be payable to each of the provinces under option (a) and under option (b) of the proposal. The leader of the opposition also asked for information respecting the estimate of $90,000,000 which I gave in my budget speech as the net increase in the dominion's revenues from the changes in the personal income and corporation taxes, less the payments to the provinces. Hon. members will recall that the increased rates of graduated income tax, not including the national defence tax, were estimated to produce an additional $75,000,000 of revenue in a full year. The increase in the minimum rate of excess profits tax is estimated to produce $80,000,000, or a total of $155,000,000. If we add to this approximately $2,000,000 as representing the difference between the present special grants to the provinces which are to be cancelled and the fiscal need subsidies which will be paid in future, and $12,000,000 in special taxes to be imposed on banks, insurance companies, railway companies and other groups which might otherwise benefit from the discontinuance of existing provincial taxes, we get a total of $169,000,000. If we deduct from this the annual payments to the provinces which I have estimated at $80,000,000, we are left with a net increase in dominion revenues of $89,000,000. At the time I delivered my budget speech this estimate was placed at $90,000,000.
As I mentioned when the supplementary estimates were tabled, the total amount to be paid to the provinces in the present fiscal year will be much less than $80,000,000 plus whatever fiscal need subsidies may be necessary. From this total, whatever it may be, there will be deducted the amount of the taxes which the provinces are themselves collecting at the present time upon the taxpayers' incomes in 1940 or based upon the taxpayers' operations or status in 1940, and also their collections of arrears which pertain to 1939 and earlier periods. It is difficult to estimate the amount of such taxes which the provinces will collect this year, but it will be substantial, and the amount of the
dominion's payments will be reduced correspondingly. All things considered I think it is safe to say that the net payments to all provinces this year will not exceed $45,000,000, the amount called for in the estimate. If any of the provinces do not accept the proposal, the amount will be reduced.

Mr. Chairman, anxious as I am to facilitate the business of the house I must ask the committee to bear with me for just a few minutes to discuss this, one of the most important matters that will come before us. I regret that we have not more time for its consideration.
The minister's statement has the advantage of clarity, if in some respects it has not the distinction of finality. I want to deal with the second topic referred to, namely, the position of the municipalities in New Brunswick. I think I correctly stated their position when I dealt with the subject before. They are the creatures of the province, and this government cannot deal directly with them. But they are the same set of taxpayers who are paying to the dominion and to the provinces, and we have some obligation to protect them in any financial changes that are contemplated.
The only purpose I have in alluding to the position of the municipalities is twofold. The statement of the Minister of Finance did not make it clear that the municipalities would be protected. My hon. friend, I have no doubt, proceeded on the assumption to which he referred in his statement, that, the municipalities being the creature of the provinces, the provinces would be concerned in protecting them. This is an assumption which of course may be quite true. But I was fearful that at one time it might not be given all the consideration which it deserves. I do believe, however, that discussion of the matter in this house, calling the attention of the house and of the minister to the position, will have the effect I desire, namely, the protection of the municipalities.
If the minister cannot see his way clear to stipulate that the position of the municipalities be protected, I must say that I disagree with him. I think he can do it. He has the power and authority to make it a condition that the position of the municipalities shall be protected, and I think he should do so. If he does not do so, and they are not protected, there will of course be a tremendous reaction, in New Brunswick at all events. I am not going to say more than that. I am going to ask the minister to protect the municipalities if he feels that it is his duty, as it is undoubtedly within his power to do so.

Supply-Finance

There is just one collateral point that has not been touched upon by the minister. Municipal income taxation, as I understand it, is to be frozen at some level. I do not know whether it would be possible to make the proposal elastic enough so that there might be an increase, or, on the other hand, a decrease, in the amount of the allowance to the provinces by reason of anticipated increase or decrease in the revenue of the municipalities from this source of taxation. I do know that with a rising national income there is a rising revenue from this source for all the municipalities, including the larger ones, and I must say including the smaller ones because it has come to my knowledge that certain municipalities, what I may term rural municipalities, until recently have not properly, shall I say, explored this avenue for revenue. It is only within the last year or two that certain municipalities have been invoking the law which was set up in their favour for that purpose. I am informed by my colleague the member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield), who is the warden of his own county, that the freezing of this source of revenue to the municipalities at the 1940 figure, say, will work a distinct detriment to that municipality, because they are just beginning really to enforce the law, and the 1941 taxation returns from that source, if I understood him correctly, will be substantially in excess of the revenues for 1940. I know this is quite a difficult point to deal with and that there must be some finality. How it can be measured in the future other than on the basis of a given year is not quite clear to me. I shall not discuss the point further; I think I have performed my duty by referring to it. I ask the minister to do what he can to see that the position of the municipalities in New Brunswick is safeguarded and that, if possible, it be stipulated in the agreement itself. If we have it in the bond, then of course we shall be sure. If we haven't it in the bond, anything may happen.
The position of Alberta is, I admit at once, a very difficult one, not only for the minister but also for us here in this house. I am obliged to the minister for the statement of his position, as to its clarity, although I am somewhat disappointed in the attitude which he has taken. The minister waved the big stick over those who are speculating or are said to be speculating or who, he intimated, might be speculating in Alberta bonds in the hope that they would make a killing if the government required the Alberta government to pay its bond interest in full. Let me say at once that I am not concerned with these individuals who are speculating in Alberta bonds. If there be such I am not aware of

them, and I have had no communication with them. I need not tell the minister that I am not myself an Alberta bondholder. That is one thing I have escaped-not many, but that is one. I am not a bit concerned about the position of the bond speculator. I do not think, however, that the volume of Alberta bonds in the hands of speculators can be very large. My understanding is that the greater part of these bonds are held by financial and municipal institutions;' that a substantial proportion of the holdings of Alberta bonds is in the hands of our municipalities and other governmental bodies in the form of sinking-fund investments, and that it is a very serious matter to them. The great bulk of the investment of Alberta bonds is in the hands of institutions such as insurance companies which gather together the savings of the people in small lots, and the position of which, as a result of the default, the deliberate default, of the Alberta government, has been impaired.
In addition to that, I suggest to the minister-probably his department knows it better than I can state it to him-that a substantial quantity of these bonds is held by foreign investors of the type to which I have alluded, namely, the association of insurance companies in the United States of America. I have had some communications from one or two of them; I can say to the minister that their holdings are substantial and that they were acquired not for speculative purposes but for the purpose of safe, sound investment, on the theory that in the belief that a Canadian province would never default in the payment of its solemn obligation, or that, if it were compelled to do so, this federal government, the government of Canada, would come to its assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I interrupt a moment? I want to make it clear that I was not stating that the bonds generally are held by speculators.

No, I do not think the minister did say that; but he waved the big stick against those who are in that category, and he raised the bogy of the speculator-we had it once before in this chamber-and a demagogic appeal was made not to save the bondholders. I know that that is a popular attitude to take in certain quarters, and I am not constituting myself in any degree a champion of the speculator. But I am one of those old-fashioned1 persons who have always believed in the sanctity of contract. The issue of a bond by a province and the sale of that bond to a bona fide investor is a form of contract and the contract should be carried out.

Supply-Finance
May I point out what gave rise to this position. In 1935 a new government was bom in Alberta. In 1936 that government passed a series of statutes which, I believe, were intended to impair, or at least had the effect of greatly impairing, the financial position of the province. Among other measures, the provincial legislature in 1937 passed what is known as the Provincial Guaranteed Securities Interest Act, chapter 12 of the Statutes of Alberta, 1937, which act purported to reduce by one-half the interest on certain securities guaranteed by the province of Alberta; and the Provincial Securities Interest Act, chapter 13 of the same year-one statute following the other-which purported to reduce the interest payable on securities issued by the province to, in general, half the agreed rates. Those are the two statutes to which I refer: first, the direct obligations of the province, and second, the guaranteed obligations of the province.
The federal government, so far as my research has led me, did not intervene to disallow those statutes. It left the bondholders to fight their own battles, although, as was ultimately shown, the passing of these acts was a clear invasion of the federal authority and jurisdiction. The matter was tried first before Mr. Justice Ewing; then it went to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Alberta, these proceedings being carried on in 1937, 1938 and 1939, and finally got to the privy council, but private interests had to bear the burden of demonstrating the invalidity of these statutes. The privy council decided that the underlying principle of both these statutes was in pith and substance dealing with the matter of interest within the meaning of head 19 of section 91 of the British North America Act, 1867, a subject matter within the exclusive legislative competence of the dominion parliament, and that the acts were therefore ultra vires of the province. The case is reported in 1940 Appeal Cases, 513, and I would refer to the judgment of the Lord Chancellor, Viscount Caldecote, at pages 531 and 535, where in substance that was the conclusion reached. I am not going to inflict a reading of the judgment upon the committee. It establshes beyond peradventure the illegality and unconstitutional position of the province of Alberta, and that position has never been corrected by the province. It has been, in my view, a defiance of the laws of Canada; I do not think there can be any gainsaying that statement. I should like to go just one step further and say it does not reflect any credit on the government of Alberta to defy the law of this country. The figures of their budgets have amply demonstrated that, with the increased income they have had as a
result of new sources of revenue and the invasion of certain fields of taxation, they could, for the most part, if not all the time, have paid this bond interest, and the people of Alberta would not have been reduced to the position where they cannot hold their heads up in common with other citizens of this country. Their province, and their province alone, has defaulted-I believe, much against the will of the best elements in Alberta.
This dominion government-I do not speak of it at all in its party sense-would, I am sure, have been quite as willing to help Alberta fulfil its obligations to its bonded creditors as it was to help other provinces, which I shall not name, which did endeavour to keep their contracts with the investing public. I remember very well one occasion upon which the former government assisted the province of Alberta, after the change of government, I believe. But when the incoming Minister of Finance found that these statutes had been passed he was amply justified in taking the stand that he did-that he could not properly assist the province of Alberta because it would not fulfil its obligations.
What is the position to-day? A war has intervened. Alberta has made default in the payment of its bond interest. It has been obliged to make default in payment of certain principal issues that have fallen due, and without any relief from the dominion, on the basis entirely of the theory I have suggested, namely, that the dominion could not and would not condone the action of that province. War has come, but in the meantime Alberta, as I said a moment ago, has increased its revenues and has entered into new fields of financial operations; and if one is to believe what one hears-I do not wish to guarantee the truth of the observation which I am about to make-Alberta has entered new fields of financial endeavour which have cost many hundreds of thousands of dollars and which may not redound to the benefit of the people of the province.
I am not in a position to express an opinion on that last phrase, but that is the position that has been stated to me. It makes it abundantly clear, however, that Alberta as at present constituted, desires to be generous, if I may say so, before it is just. That is the only thing I will say in that regard.
_ Coming down to the proposals, the necessity for increased revenues for the prosecution of the war is before us. No one knows better than the Premier of Alberta the necessity of an all-out effort in connection with this war, and that means money to his province as well as to anyone else. I have read some of his protestations in that regard. I do
Supply-Finance

not question for a moment his bona tides with respect to participation; that is not the point at issue now. The Minister of Finance, however, in his budget proposals announced, in fact he intimated beforehand, that it would be necessary for the federal authorities to invade certain taxation fields of the provinces, and I think we all generally understood what was suggested. But in his budget speech on April 29 he was very definite and gave the reasons for his proposals, and as is well known, this House of Commons has unanimously concurred in the proposals in that regard. Now we are down to the point where it is intended to implement the position by voting the sum of 845,000,000 which the minister says it is anticipated will be required if the provinces enter into arrangements with the dominion to vacate the fields indicated, giving up their sources of revenue for the duration of the war.
Under the proposals the provinces are given the choice between two alternatives. I will not go over them; I have already alluded to them two or three times. The minister himself, in his observations to-day, again stated what they were, and I believe every one in the house and in the country who has given any study to the matter understands them. What I do suggest is that alternative (b), namely, the cost of net debt service actually paid by the province during the fiscal year nearest to December 31, 1940, not including contributions to sinking funds, less revenue obtained from succession duties during that period, and the wording of the estimate itself, clearly constitutes a recognition of the status quo with regard to the province of Alberta-and I have already indicated what that status is. It is a status of default.
The minister says that by no stretch of the imagination can it be declared that the wording of the estimate in the way it is drawn up, and the position he has taken, could1 be considered condonation of the position taken by Alberta. Well, that is pretty strong language. Assuming that is true, then it is a poor reflection upon the intelligence of a good many people in the country who have studied the situation. What can it be but condonation of the attitude of the Alberta government?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is condonation? Is it not approval?

Answering the minister's interjection, I would say there are all kinds of approval. There is express approval by words and there is approval by action, and this comes within the second category. This is approval by action.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not agree.
And not only is there approval, but it constitutes a discrimination.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a different point.
That is another point, I agree.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not agree that this implies or expresses any approval.

I know the minister does not want to agree to it. That is the point. He does not want to be driven into the position of making any admissions. That was the whole tenor of his prepared argument here to-day. But I want to tell him that the investing public believes that it is condonation, and it will be a distinct blow to the credit of this Dominion of Canada-absolutely. He has it in his power to-day to say to Alberta, "If you accept a certain proposal here you must accept it on the condition that you fulfil your legal obligations to the people who have advanced you money." When is a bond not a bond? That is a question that has arisen in the public mind.
When it is an Alberta bond.

I was not going to answer the question quite so broadly. The people are beginning to be fearful by reason of repudiation. That is a harsh word to use. It is conditional repudiation. That is what the position of Alberta is, and the government, by granting fiscal aid to the province in consideration of the vacating of certain fields of taxation, and by limiting the amount under (b), which is to be paid, to the amount of net debt service actually paid by the province, is putting the seal of its approval on that partial repudiation.
That is the position I take. I know that the government does not want to hear about it. I know that the Deputy Minister of Finance does not want to hear about this sort of thing. It is not a pleasant thing to say, that by implication or inference the federal Department of Finance is recognizing the position taken by the province of Alberta. It is not a pleasant thing to contemplate, but $45,000,000 for a part year and $80,000,000 for a full year is to be paid out to the provinces on certain considerations, and a substantial portion is to go to Alberta provided that accommodation or agreement is reached.
The taxpayers of this country who invested in Alberta bonds, the institutions which gathered the savings of the people of this country and in good faith invested them in Alberta bonds, have a right to assume that

Supply-Finance
by no word or action, express or implied, will the federal government do anything to perpetuate a situation which the highest court in this land has declared to be illegal. I cannot state the position any better than that. I can argue the matter further and give illustrations which might clarify the view I take, and perhaps I should take a few minutes to do that. Reams have been written about this position in days gone by. Let me put this first position to the minister-I put two or three the other day, but this I think is the strongest I.can take, and it is qua the taxpayer of Alberta, not the investing public.
It is clear that the result of alternative (b) is to discriminate between the taxpayer of Alberta and the taxpayer of the other provinces. That is the second point to which I alluded and which the minister and I agreed was not the same as the question of condonation. Let us compare the position of the taxpayer of Alberta and the taxpayer of Saskatchewan. To illustrate it as pointedly as possible, let us assume they live in adjoining towns with the provincial boundary between them. Each will now have to pay this new dominion tax, the increased levies of every kind as a result of the budget now passed. Each is offered under alternative (b) a consideration, a quid pro quo. This quid pro quo in the case of the Saskatchewan taxpayer is substantially double what it is in the case of the Alberta taxpayer. That is a relative term, of course.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In what way?

Let me
proceed; I think I can demonstrate it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The payment to some provinces of course will be greater than the payment to others.

The payments to Saskatchewan, which will pay its bond interest in full, are larger and therefore more effective on the Saskatchewan taxpayer than the payments to Alberta, .where they pay only half the interest. It may be exaggeration to say it is double, I have not figured out the ratio, but the principle is there. No amount of argument that this discrimination is justified by the action of the Alberta government can obscure the fact that it is a discrimination. In other words the Alberta taxpayer is being discriminated against in relation to his brother across the line. One is receiving more money on the same account than the other.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, no.
The interest is not extinguished in the case of the Alberta taxpayer. It is held in abeyance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If we were to pay Alberta
$1,750,000, all the taxpayers in Canada would pay more, to begin with.

Yes, I
agree with that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what the hon. gentleman is advocating, that we ask all the taxpayers of Canada to pay $1,750,000 more for the benefit of the Alberta bondholders-

That is
not an answer to my argument.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Let me follow this through -provided the thing is practicable at all. But we have had no intimation from Alberta that they would pass this on. As a government they would be $800,000 worse off if they were to do that, and there is not the slightest intimation that they would do anything of the kind. Surely there should be some suggestion from that government before we take $1,750,000 of the money of the taxpayers of Canada and attempt to force it on them for the benefit of the holders of Alberta bonds. In saying that, we have not condoned anything. I express in the strongest way our disapproval of the repudiation by the Alberta government; I am quite prepared to do that and I do it, but no approval is implied here. The hon. gentleman is repeating the arguments of the committee representing the Alberta bondholders and making a suggestion made by that committee. For those gentlemen I have the highest respect; I know they are sincere and I think the leader of the opposition is sincere. But having given this matter the most careful consideration I can I do not think that when we are making an offer to the whole of the provinces we should go back of this: we will pay you on the basis of cash received in taxes, or on the basis of cash paid. We do not go into the moral history of these people; we do not by that act express approval or disapproval. I am willing to express disapproval here and now of that repudiation, but that is not implied in the offer we have made to Alberta.

When the minister rose I thought he was insisting on controverting the argument I was putting forward. But instead he rose to make a speech and got quite hot about it. I do not see any necessity for heat. I can discuss this matter as calmly as anyone.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has
been attacking the deputy minister and the department-
Supply-Finance
No, I did not attack the deputy minister, I said the deputy minister would not want to hear even a suggestion of condonation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And there is none.

Well I
am suggesting that there is. I have the right to suggest it if it appeals to my reason, and it does. The minister evidently does not want to hear any more argument about this thing. I have stated the position, that this is condonation and discrimination. I am not going to labour the matter. The minister has made it abundantly clear that he is not going to do anything about it, so lhat I am wasting my eloquence on the desert air. I have been trying to prove a position, but if the minister takes the flat-footed, inflexible position that he usually takes, what is the use? The minister will I think learn from time to time that there are other points of view besides his own. Usually he is courteous in hearing them; I have not much complaint on that score. But I suggest that there was nothing in what I said to-day to cause him to take the attitude he did and to impute to those who hold other views that in effect they are talking nonsense. Because that is what his original declaration that by no flight of the imagination could it be considered that there was condonation spelled to me. That is a poor compliment to my intelligence at least. Perhaps the minister did not intend it that way; I am willing to think he did not. But I do impress upon him that there is more than one point of view in this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I realize that.

And that
the credit of Canada will suffer. Suppose the United States neutrality law should be lifted and this country should find itself in the position of having to go to the United States to borrow money. That is a possibility if the war goes on long enough. One of the first things the minister will be met with is this very question of the Alberta bonds. It is one of the things he would have been met [DOT] with if he had persisted in the 15 per cent tax on interest on provincial government bonds held by people outside the jurisdiction. The minister very properly, I think, went back from that position. I hope he did it not because of pressure from Mr. Hepburn, but because as a matter of national policy it was desirable to maintain the credit of the provinces, that that credit should not be impaired by federal taxation. I know the minister has heard some of these arguments before. Knowing the inflexibility of the minister's mind I have no hope that anything I may say will

be strong enough to induce him to change his position, but I am going to tell him that the whole financial world is watching this operation and the actions of the government. It is unfortunate that this discussion arose right in the midst of the victory loan campaign. I certainly hope it will have no bad effect; it is not intended to have such an effect, and if I had thought it would I never would have raised the question. As a matter of fact it should not have any effect on the loan situation to-day because these are two entirely different positions, and I have no doubt there will be no such effect.
I do say to the minister, however, that I think the government might very well have given consideration to the Alberta position to the extent of saying, "We will offer you not only the net debt service you have actually paid; if you will do your part we will offer you a sum sufficient to pay your debt service in full from now on, disregarding the past." I would not go any farther than that at the moment. Certainly we would not pay their arrears; and with respect to the principal obligations that have matured and are in default, certainly we should not offer to pay those at the moment. A matter such as this should be threshed out by the finance department with the province of Alberta and if possible they should be made to see that in war time the position adopted by the province is detrimental to this country's credit, and that position should be reversed.
Now, having regard to the heat with which the minister rebuked me, shall I say-no, I do not think he intended to rebuke me, but the heat with which he controverted and interrupted me-I do not think I will say anything more, because I am afraid it would be useless. But I do ask the minister and the department to review the whole position between now and when we meet again in November, in order to see if something cannot be done to remedy the situation. In the meantime I lay down the principle that if the present policy is pursued, on the one hand it is condonation and on the other it is discrimination.

I want to say to the minister first that I was very glad to hear him make the statement that if the Alberta government had approached the dominion government, and if an arrangement had been made under which the full debt service would have been paid to that province, no speculator would have been allowed to benefit by any appreciation of the bonds, and a capital gains tax would have been instituted. It is a reiteration of the position the minister took during the dominion-provincial conference in January, though apparently that was overlooked

Supply-Finance
by many of the critics of the conference who tried to make people believe that those of us who thought it better to straighten out difficulties as between the dominion and the provinces by conference before the end of the war, in order that we might continue the war and prepare for the aftermath, were friendly to the bondholders.
This morning we have listened for nearly an hour to the leader of the opposition making a plea for consideration of the bondholders and the creditors of the province of Alberta. I hold no brief for the government of that province, as I think everyone knows, but I do say that at the time Alberta found it necessary to reduce the interest on its bonded indebtedness the people of that province, like the people of Saskatchewan, were suffering one of the greatest financial and economic depressions that any people had ever been called upon to suffer. The necessities of the situation compelled the province, and I think perhaps ought to have compelled the neighbouring province of Saskatchewan, to do something in regard to the interest on its bonded indebtedness. I do not say that the right plan was adopted. I believe it would have been much better if the provinces of western Canada, in the situation with which they were faced, had entered into negotiations with a view to relieving themselves of a part of this burden. But let me say this also in defence of the province which did take a step in that direction, that the creditors during the years before the step was taken did not offer at any time to consider such proposals or to attend any such conference.
If the hon. member will allow me a word, is it not usual for a debtor to seek out his creditor, and is it not the duty of the debtor to do so if he wishes to make a compromise?

And if I may ask a question, was not a thorough investigation made by the Bank of Canada as to the ability of the province of Alberta to pay its debts? Was it not found in that investigation that the one province which of all the western provinces needed relief least was Alberta? Was it not found by the Bank of Canada that they could pay their interest?

Well, probably the hon. gentleman is right in a part of his contention. No doubt there were provinces on the prairies that required relief even more than Alberta, but that does not say Alberta did not require relief also. I was and still am critical of Saskatchewan in that it did not seek some relief at that time, because the failure to do
so placed a burden upon the people of Saskatchewan from which they have not as yet recovered.
I have in my hand a graph taken from the report of the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations, appendix 4, indicating quite clearly what happened. Taking 1926 as the base of 100 in dividends and interest payments, in 1930 these went up to just over 120 as compared with the 1926 level and then in 1933 dropped down to the lowest point, which was 78 as compared with 100 in 1926. But when you look at the condition of the people of the agricultural provinces, what do you find? Taking 1926 as the base of 100 we find that by 1932 they had reached the unprecedented depth of only 18 as compared with the 1926 level. And then my hon. friend the leader of the opposition speaks of the sacredness of a contract! I say that a contract ought to be sacred, but that human life, human happiness and human welfare are even more sacred.

Did not the Sirois report also recommend payment of the back interest; and did not Mr. Graham Towers, who made a survey of the whole position, say that Alberta could pay?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at three o'clock.

Just before one o'clock the leader of the opposition asked me if I knew that the Bank of Canada and the Rowell-Sirois reports had stated that Alberta could meet her full indebtedness. I have not looked up the Bank of Canada report in that connection, but if my memory is correct the only statement that could be interpreted in that way is one to the effect that Alberta's debt was not out of line with the debt of other provinces. I find the following at page 239 of volume I of the Rowell-Sirois report:
National interest has been centred on Alberta's arbitrary reduction of debt charges. These have consistently been the highest of any province in Canada and it is perhaps not surprising that they were singled out for attack. Provincial net debt charges in 1930 were $4*3 million annually, and in 1937 at full interest rates would have been (after adjustment for interest received) $5-4 million; actually they were $3-6 million. Only 22 per cent of the provincial funded debt is payable in Canadian currency only, and more than one-half the debt bearing 4i per cent coupon rates or higher does not mature until after 1950. It is consequently evident that the provincial debt at its original coupon rates was in a technically rigid and vulnerable position, and only small reductions in carrying charges would have been possible through orderly refunding.

However much we may dislike the idea of repudiation or forcible reduction, the Rowell-Sirois commission recognized that something more than was generally suggested had to be done about the matter. Although I am not defending the action of the Alberta government in making an arbitrary reduction, faced with the acute situation to be found on- the prairies at that time, I believe that they were justified in bringing about a reduction in the carrying charges of their debt. This morning I said that my criticism of the government of Saskatchewan was that it had dome nothing of a similar kind to relieve the 'terrible situation that existed. I am glad that in this suggestion of the Minister of Finance some removal of the debt burden will occur for that province. I should like to justify what I have said by quoting again from the Rowell-Sirois report at page 237:
Expenditures on education and public "welfare (excluding relief) were cut between 1930 and 1937 by one-quarter. Education was particularly hard hit-joint provincial-municipal expenditures on education were reduced 40 per cent and rural municipal expenditures were cut by two-thirds. In the long run, when the personnel affected can find alternative employment, these reductions must produce serious deterioration in standards, and, as we have observed elsewhere, this concerns not only Saskatchewan but the whole country. The reduction in public welfare expenditures at a time when needs were increasing on a gigantic scale is the cold statistical reflection of a tremendous amount of human misery. It is not a surprising, although a tragic, commentary that the pressure on mental institutions became particularly acute and beds are lacking for one-third of the serious eases. It is true that expenditures on a per capita basis are not materially below the Canadian average, hut in relation to the needs (and in relation to the previous standards which were maintained) they were inadequate.
What happened in Alberta was that the government, faced with the choice of maintaining certain social services-they were dropped to some extent-or maintaining contractual obligations on the bonded indebtedness, chose the former rather than the latter. When we discuss these matters in this house we should try to see both sides of the question. The minister, in making the statement that he did this morning was explicit when he said that even if some agreement were reached with Alberta, the speculators in provincial bonds would not be allowed to benefit. This will do much to relieve the minds of many people who have believed, quite honestly but without proper foundation, that the Rowell-Sirois report was drawn up from the point of view of bondholders rather than from the point of view of the welfare of the provinces.
I should like to repeat what I said yesterday, that if we are to maintain the morale of our people we must give them some assurance

that this parliament will endeavour to relieve distress now and, when the war is over, lay a foundation for something better than we have known. It seems to me to be useless to make speeches in this house decrying the attempts, however feeble or wrong they may be, that are made in that direction. The thing to do is to try to straighten out these difficulties and lay some foundation so that we may build more properly in the future. In the long discussion that has taken place I think there has been-I see the leader of the opposition is in his seat and I am going to make this criticism-a feeling on the part of some of us that the interests of the bondholders and the *financial elements in this country were being too well looked after, and that not enough attention was being given to the interests of the human family. I hope we can get the difficulties straightened out so that in the future we may be able to build for something better than we have known in the past.

In his tirade against Alberta the leader of the opposition probably overdid himself a little, and perhaps he merited a measure of attention on that account. May I proceed to give him that attention?
I gathered from what he said that he thought that the trouble in Alberta with respect to the cutting down of interest rates, default on maturities, et cetera, began with the election of a Social Credit government in 1935. It really is too bad that before the hon. member made such a reckless statement he did not more accurately inform himself concerning the history of Alberta. Considering,, however, the fact that he is rather new to his job and has a great many tasks thrust upon him, perhaps we must forgive him, but I believe it is my duty to point out to him certain facts so as to help him from falling into such errors again.
I am going to read some quotations from the Bank of Canada report on the financial position of the western provinces, but before I begin this rather tedious task may I observe, Mr. Chairman, that it is a great pity that people do not know more about the province of Alberta, and it is purely in the interests of giving general information to the people throughout Canada that I am imposing upon the committee this somewhat lengthy discussion this afternoon. May I now read from the Bank of Canada report, at page 4, concerning Alberta:
The policies pursued from the time the province was created (1905) until the year 1922, had a profound effect on the financial position of the government of Alberta. The roots of many of Alberta's present problems were

Supply-Finance
developed during this period. Only the exceptionally rapid economic progress of the time can account for the fact that extravagant governmental expenditures, direct and indirect, were allowed to proceed on such a scale and to last so long as they did.
Almost immediately after the formation of the province, ambitious telephone and railway policies were launched. Poor judgment, loose administration and over-expansion were to make both utility ventures costly.
May I draw to the attention of the leader of the opposition the fact that any government which takes power in Alberta has to assume responsibility for the results of those policies, regardless of the name that government may bear; the behaviour of that government therefore is going to be in large measure controlled by those policies and their effects going on through the years?
May I now read another passage from the same Bank of Canada report, at pages 34 and 35. While I am finding this passage may I pause to congratulate the governor of the Bank of Canada on what I consider to be one of the finest services he ever did for the dominion when he went out and made an impartial investigation into the province of Alberta. When from coast to coast there was misrepresentation, misunderstanding, ignorance and foolhardy passion concerning the province of Alberta, this young man went out there and calmly and judiciously investigated conditions in the province and set down the facts as he saw them in this report. I quote from page 34:
In appraising the present financial situation of the province of Alberta, we found that special emphasis must be placed on the events of the years 1905-22. In 1922, after Alberta had been in existence for 17 years, the province's debt (including guarantees, subsequently implemented) was approximately $95 millions. This debt was over twice as large as that of Saskatchewan in the same year, and 50 per cent larger than that of the much older province of Manitoba. Substantially more than half of the Alberta total represented accumulated losses and deficits, and so-called assets which, in fact, were proving a constant drain.
That was under a Liberal administration, too?

Yes. One could
remark about a Liberal administration but I do not wish to interject politics into this.
Oh, no.

Not at all, and I am talking, and no member knows what is in my mind except myself. I continue the quotation:
After making full allowance for the rapid economic development of the new province, and the legitimate cost of facilities provided by the government to aid and stimulate this development, it remains the case-in our opinion- that the 1905-22 period was characterized by 14873-245
waste, loose administration, and incurrence of debt to an extent which could not be justified even when allowance is made for the optimistic spirit of the times.
During the fiscal years 1923-30-on the whole a period of prosperity for all three prairie provinces-the Alberta government did not take the opportunity to improve its financial position; in fact, a deterioration would have taken place had it not been for the fact that the province was successful in selling its railways to the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National Railways in 1928 and 1929. In doing so, the province realized a substantial loss, but was fortunate in getting out of a venture which had cost, on the average, $3 millions per annum in cash advances and carrying charges during the twenties. The province was left with a residual liability of $244 millions, involving interest charges of approximately $11 millions a year. The advantageous sale of the railways enabled the province to regain its 1922 position in respect to net debt. As we had previously noted, the 1922 position was such a poor one that the necessity for an improvement should have been recognized at that time. The opportunity afforded by the years of prosperity was allowed to pass, and in only one year during this period would Alberta have had a real surplus on current account if allowance is made for the items which were capitalized instead of being charged to ordinary expenditure, where they belonged.
May I pause to point out that there again is the story of a series of events for which the Social Credit administration could by no honourable and fair-minded man be held accountable? The report goes on:
During the six fiscal years 1931-36, the net outstanding liabilities of the province increased by some $52 millions. Of this increase, approximately $16 millions was accounted for by deficits on current account.
May I stop there a minute? You notice that the report says "deficits on current account". Is the new administration coming into power in 1935 supposed to be able to run the province without a deficit of any kind? That is the question. And if it is to run the province without a deficit, then where is the safety-valve going to be? I continue the quotation:
Of this increase, approximately $16 millions was accounted for by deficits on current account, $13 millions by expenditures on fixed assets such as roads, bridges, buildings, irrigation, et cetera, and $19 millions by relief and relief works (including relief expenditures capitalized as public works). About half of the net increase took place during the first two years of the period, when capital expenditures were being continued on a substantial scale, and no marked retrenchment in ordinary expenditures was taking place. Moreover, debt charges were substantially increased during these two years, partly because of new borrowings to finance the capital expenditures and current deficits, and partly because of the large amount of refunding which had to be done under unfavourable market conditions.
