May I now read another passage from this same Bank of Canada report, this time at page 36:
Of the 1931-36 period as a whole, it may be said that delay in effecting the adjustments made necessary by the depression was responsible for a substantial increase in debt and debt charges. When measures of retrenchment were applied they were severe, but, even so, it was not possible to balance the budget on current account, much less provide for the province's share of relief costs.
Again, I read from page 25:
By the summer of 1935 Alberta had largely exhausted its liquid and realizable assets-
May I pause there to draw the attention of hon. members to this fact?
By the summer of 1935 Alberta had largely exhausted its liquid and realizable assets in order to meet its chronic cash deficiencies, and when a run on the savings certificates took place in August, 1935, the necessary funds were not available.
That run took place before the Social Credit government was elected and some time before the Social Credit government took office.
Now, if the leader of the opposition is going to be entirely fair, as I know he wishes to be, he will make allowance for facts such as I have outlined.
May I turn for just a few moments to the question of savings certificates, which was referred to in the last part of the excerpt that I just read. The savings certificates were, in a way, somewhat like our dominion savings certificates. For a good many years people in Alberta had been encouraged to lend their money to the province and to take a savings certificate in return therefor, with the guarantee of a specified rate of interest. As I recall it, the rate was four and a half per cent. As a result, a great deal of money had been lent by the people of Alberta to their provincial treasury, until, in 1934, their loans to the government totalled 812,000,000,- $12,000,000 of savings certificates which were, in effect, demand documents on the provincial government, just as though a person had money in a current account in the bank. Now it is quite clear that just as soon as people began to be uncertain about the stability of their government, or just as soon as they began to get into financial difficulties, there would be a heavy drain on that
812,000,000 and consequently a heavy drain on the government treasury.
In 1934 Alberta was off the money market of the world. I suppose the rumour has reached Ottawa that the Social Credit government destroyed the credit of Alberta. Never was a bigger lie created and foisted upon the people. The credit of Alberta had been des-

troyed in 1934, because in that year Alberta was already off the money markets of the world.
Again, there was a run on the savings certificates in the fall of 1934. In order that hon. members may be able to realize the import of that statement, let them call to mind that the Social Credit government was elected on August 22, 1935. There had been a run on the savings certificates in the fall of 1934. By 1935 the government then in power had redeemed $2,000,000 of these certificates in an endeavour to recover the financial stability of the province. But their cash was completely exhausted. As the Bank of Canada report points out, their liquid assets were gone. On July 28, 1935, the government suspended payment on the savings certificates. That meant immediately, of course, that the credit of the province was gone, if it could have been destroyed any further than it already was.
Those are not all the troubles. I am not complaining; all we want hon. members and the people of this country to realize is that when the new Social Credit administration of Alberta went into office it faced an exceedingly difficult task, and it set about to solve the problem confronting it with all the honour, the courage, the determination and industry that a group of men, honest and sincere, could command.
May I point out some other troubles which that group of men confronted when they assumed office on September 3, 1935. In the first place there was an overdraft at the bank against Alberta of $5,700,000. Let any hon. member of this committee imagine that he is the premier of a province taking office in a new administration; that he goes to the bank and finds an overdraft of $5,700,000 against him to start with. There were unpaid salaries of the civil servants amounting to nearly a million dollars. I notice that four or five hon. members have not begun to take this seriously at all, although others have.
Do not stop.

All right, I will go
ahead fast enough.

Pause once in a while;
then go ahead.

It is only a cough;
we will forgive it. I said that there were civil service salaries unpaid in the amount of a million dollars which had to be met; the money had to be got somewhere, and the administration had to get it with, already, an overdraft of $5,700,000 against them, with their province having been off the money market

for over a year, and with $10,000,000 of savings certificates in default against them throughout the province.
That was not all their trouble. In 1935 the United Farmers of Alberta government borrowed a quantity of money in addition to its budget and committed the province for those borrowings to the extent of $8,927,000. It is almost as though the bird knew that it was going to get off the nest, and decided to do everything in its power to foul the nest before it got off! Further there were in Alberta on the books of the tax collectors $17,000,000 of uncollected taxes.

They should be an asset
against a liability of $5,000,000.

All one needed to
do was to try to collect those taxes in 1935, and he would soon find that they were not much of an asset. Wait till you hear the facts. So much depends on the facts. You are getting them, and you will get them a lot faster if you will let me do the talking.

I am a bit dumb on social
credit.

This has nothing to
do with social credit. This is just the highly-lauded orthodox economics on which my hon. friend is such an authority.
Well, I am always suspicious that we will get a shot of social credit before we are through.

I would suppose that
1935 was one of the most disastrous years in the history of Alberta. We were burnt out in the south, frozen and flooded out in the centre; we had too much moisture away in the north, and there was a great deal of hail. Once in a while a great calamity like that occurs. It occurred in Alberta's history in 1935. I remember having met members of the caucus of the Social Credit government when !hey first came together to consider the tasks which had been placed upon them, and I recall one man in the caucus saying that there was not a constituency from the north of the province to the south that was not seeking agricultural relief in that particular year, 1935. In 1936 there was a repetition of the drought, and in 1937, believe it or not, there was another repetition of it.
May I call the attention of hon. members to the fact that the first debenture security to become due for the new Alberta government fell due on January 15, 1936, before the new government ever had a chance to draft a budget at all. and while it was still struggling to adjust itself and to make ends meet under the last budget of the United Farmers of 14873-2454
Alberta. That maturity was $1,577,000. I am not going to weary the committee by repeating the figures I have already given, but if hon. members will take the trouble to go over
them,	taking the financial commitments and obligations which faced the new administration, they will be astounded. The amazing thing was that the administration was able to get under way at all.
I will read now a statement from the provincial treasurer of Alberta which was given last year in the banking and commerce committee. I am not going to run the risk of misstating anything. I have had only a very short time to prepare this speech, as hon. members can see, because the last thing I expected was an attack upon Alberta to-day- the very last thing I I certainly was not prepared to deal with anything of the sort. I have had to rush around and get together some information that would help to put the case for Alberta. Let me read from page 68 of the proceedings of the standing committee on banking and commerce of last year, 1940. Mr. Low is speaking:
Immediately after this government came into power, you will remember the premier and a number of his advisers-I was not then a member of the government-came down to Ottawa; and on September 26, 1935, these are the amounts which they borrowed from Mr. Bennett's government. By the way, they asked Mr. Bennett for a lump sum of money which he said at the time he was not prepared to advance because of the imminence of a federal election. But he did say to the premier at the time, "If you will be content with this much, then after the election is over, if we are returned to office, come back and we will consider the remainder. Then you will get along all right."
As I remember, the leader of the opposition was in the administration of the man who made that statement. You can see quite clearly from that incident that the Prime Minister, Right Hon. R. B. Bennett as he was
then,	was quite in sympathy with the financial situation which existed in Alberta, because he knew it thoroughly.
These sums were then taken back or arranged for at the time of the premier's visit to Ottawa, in September, 1935, just after we took office: For unemployment relief, $330,000, for which commitments had already been made,-
The previous government had said that the money would be paid and they went out of office and left the new government to pay. -for agricultural relief, $1,200,000, for which commitments had already been made. We had to have that money to pay the amounts that had been committed. For re-loaning to the city of Calgary, another $200,000 which had been promised them by the previous administration. Calgary had been promised $450,000. They obtained $250,000 in June by loan from the federal government and another $200,000,

the balance of their request, in September. For completion of the trans-Canada-Jasper highway, a joint relief project of the dominion and the province, $300,000. The work had been done by September 26 and the contractors wanted their money; they came to us and asked us to pay it. We had to dig up the money somewhere. For public institutions, $25,000-for enlargement, by the way, of the mental institution at Ponoka; and for general purposes, including salaries of civil servants which were in arrears, $995,000. Those are the sums that were arranged for on September 26, 1935, on our first visit to Ottawa.
Mr. Donnelly: How much is that altogether?
The Witness: I have not the total here. I could figure it out for you if you just let me have a moment.
Further than that, in November of 1935, arrangements were made for further borrowings for unemployment relief of $1,000,000 for which no provision was made in the budget, but which we had to meet. These were absolutely uncontrollable.
January 15, 1936, is the date of the first debenture maturity after the Alberta government came into office. On that date $1,577,000 of bonds fell due, which amount had to be borrowed because no provision had been made in the budget; and for unemployment relief also in January of 1936, borrowings of $2,600,000.
May I point out once more to the members of the committee that the Social Credit government had not yet been able to draft a budget. They were still carrying on under the budget of the previous administration and had to meet commitments over which they had had no conceivable control.
They asked for it.

Just in the same way that my hon. friend will ask for control of this government in the next election.
There are one or two other matters that have a certain bearing on the question. Let me read now a statement or two from Right Hon. R. B. Bennett before he left this house- he is a viscount now. It is really too bad that the leader of the opposition of the present time was not a member of the house at the time his leader made these remarks; I think he would then have been sufficiently advised not to make the reckless statements which he has made. I am going to read from Hansard of April 9, 1937, at page 1410. I think we can pretty safely say that Right Hon. R. B. Bennett at that time was in an ideal position to pronounce definitely upon Alberta. He was himself the member for Calgary West; he knew Alberta as perhaps no other man in the dominion government at that time knew it; he had himself been in the Alberta legislature for a considerable time and understood the problems which were being considered; he had participated in the famous debate [Mr. Blackmore.l
in the Alberta legislature which destroyed one administration-the debate in connection with the Alberta and Great Waterways railway. Altogether he was in an admirable position to know whereof he spoke, and he was the man who was prime minister when Premier Aberhart first came and laid his cards upon the table and explained the situation. Mr. Bennett said:
When the minister said to the province of Alberta that he would not help them out of their difficulty by advancing them, through loans or otherwise, sufficient money to enable them to pay their maturing obligations, his statement was regarded as a policy. Many people scattered throughout the province in which I have long lived, as well as people residing in other parts of Canada, found themselves in straitened and difficult circumstances because their investments had been wholly in those securities the market value of which fell to a very low figure, and the interest upon which was reduced to half of what the coupons carried. If that policy is reversed, if it is not applied to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, obviously a situation is created in which the people of Alberta have just cause to say they have been discriminated against. Because if the minister will accept what I think he will, namely that the implication of his refusal to assist Alberta involved the thought that the same policy was to be applied to all the provinces-
Mr. Dunning: And it was.
Mr. Bennett: No, no.
Mr. Dunning:	I refused British Columbia
and Saskatchewan at the same time and on the same grounds, in connection with the same class of matter.
Mr. Bennett:	Yes, but the provinces of
Saskatchewan, Manitoba and British Columbia have not defaulted. The province of Alberta defaulted.
Mr. Dunning:	If the right hon. gentleman
will permit, on the maturity which was the occasion of the default, both British Columbia and Saskatchewan had maturities at the same time and received precisely the same answer.
Mr. Bennett: Yes, but I am pointing out that Alberta defaulted.
Mr. Dunning: Yes.
Mr. Bennett:	And the others did not.
Alberta defaulted because it was unable to secure money from the dominion government to prevent it from defaulting;-
Note those words:
Alberta defaulted because it was unable to secure money from the dominion government to prevent it from defaulting; that was regarded as an indication of a policy which I believe, rightly or wrongly, should not have been put in force at that particular time.
May I read another statement coming from the same right hon. gentleman after he had had another month or so to reflect and to read over the Bank of Canada report. The leader of the opposition will be impressed by the fact that Right Hon. R. B. Bennett read through the Bank of Canada report with great care, the report from which I have quoted,

and he estimated very accurately, I would say, the true situation with respect to Alberta. At page 2882 Mr. Bennett is reported as saying:
On a review of the report made with respect to that province-
That is, Alberta.
-I find that it has been treated entirely differently from the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. When Alberta first made application for a loan to enable it to meet its obligations, the application was refused. As a result of that refusal, and the statement made subsequently, they cut down their interest payments to half.
Now that is definite enough, surely!
As a result of that refusal, and the statement made subsequently, they cut down their interest payments to half.
Hon. members see where the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett placed the responsibility for the cut in the interest payments.
_ The report points out that if they had been in a position to discharge their obligations in that regard they would have been able, by securing money from the dominion, to be in exactly the same position as the other provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba. The report concludes in this way:
"Its position would be little worse than that of Manitoba, but distinctly better than that of Saskatchewan; and a claim for assistance would, no doubt, be considered in the light of these facts. It is the case, however, that Alberta's budgetary position differs materially from that of the other provinces, by reason of the fact that interest payments have been reduced by 50 per cent, or $3,400,000, and, other things being equal, its cash requirements have been reduced by the same amount. We can only deal with the situation as it is-not as it might have been in other circumstances. We find that Alberta can maintain its governmental services on as favourable a basis as Manitoba or Saskatchewan without receipt of additional assistance, and we therefore see no basis for recommending that temporary financial aid should be extended by the dominion government."
The Bank of Canada was taking it for granted that Alberta had cut its interest and was computing on that basis. Mr. Bennett continues:
Preceding that, the report states:
"Our recommendation of dominion government assistance in the cases of Manitoba and Saskatchewan was based on urgent needs of those provinces for cash during the time required for the examination which will be conducted by the royal commission. If Alberta were now paying full interest on its obligations the province in 1937-38 would presumably have to borrow its full share of unemployment relief from the dominion, and on the basis of budgetary estimates (not including debt retirement) would have had a cash shortage of about $600,000."
May I interject, before going on with Mr. Bennett's remarks, that the leader of the opposition made the statement that Alberta deliberately defaulted. Now I challenge the word "deliberately" as applied to the default,
except in this sense: men are faced with two very unpleasant and disagreeable paths, either of them is subject to many objections. They choose the one that they think is the less objectionable, the lesser of two evils. If the path they chose led to default, surely when the statement is made the qualifications and reservations should be included.
I read on from Mr. Bennett:
Then follows what I first read, and that condition exists because the government of this country declined to make an advance to that province which would have enabled it to meet its obligations. The minister may shake his head as much as he likes; it does not have any effect on my mind. I have read this report. Because of this refusal, because Alberta did not join the loan council, because it took the action it did, we find it treated differently from Saskatchewan, which was able to secure $3,000,000 from the Bank of Canada. Under the law that bank could no longer continue to loan that money, so it was compelled to purchase bonds of the Saskatchewan government, and to that extent it has made an investment in a bankrupt province, admitted by the bank to be such. Alberta has been unable to secure money from the bank or from the dominion; it has been denied any assistance, and as a result the bondholders have been compelled to take fifty cents on the dollar, while we are voting money to enable the other provinces to pay one hundred cents on the dollar in connection with their bonds.
May I interrupt here to express my admiration and my commendation of the Minister of Finance for the remarks he made in reply to the leader of the opposition. The spirit of fairness which he manifested in that speech will I believe redound to his credit for many a year. There was in it clearness of vision and willingness to be fair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words, not specifically in answer to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Blackmore) but in order to bring this debate back to where I think it ought to be. I would remind the committee that we are concerned with an item voting
845,000,000 to make good our offer to the provinces, and in discussion of that item the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) suggested that our offer, so far as Alberta is concerned, should be amended; that we should not offer to Alberta the two alternatives we offer to all the other provinces, but should modify that offer so that one option should be not on a basis of cash paid but on the basis of cash which would have been paid had the bond interest of Alberta been paid in full. Upon the speech of the leader of the opposition some discussion has developed, and unfortunately I think has now developed
Supply-Finance

into a debate as to whether the Social Credit government of Alberta was justified in taking the steps it did and whether dominion governments in the past have been fair in their treatment of Alberta.
I am not prepared to deal with those issues. I can hardly agree with the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, in his view as to the necessity of Alberta's default. I do not approve that default; I expressly disapprove it. I condemn it in no uncertain terms, and if the hon. gentleman had read some other parts of the report of the governor of the Bank of Canada he would have seen that the governor of the Bank of Canada took the same view. At page 39 of the report I find the following:
In our reports on the financial positions of the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, we expressed the opinion that the dominion government would be justified in extending temporary financial aid, pending the report of the commission referred to above.
As regards Alberta, we must note, in the first instance, that the decision of the government to pay only 50 per cent of the interest due on bond issues and savings certificates has had a major effect on the budgetary position and on the amount of the province's cash requirements. Yet we cannot report on the financial position of Alberta without expressing regret that this repudiation of interest liabilities should have taken place. There are legal and moral reasons for the fulfilment of contracts, but, leaving these entirely out of consideration (although we do not minimize their importance) we believe that self-interest alone should have induced Alberta to fulfil its contractual liabilities in respect of interest. Default produces a lack of confidence which is not confined to prospective buyers of government bonds. It has its repercussions on the investment of capital in enterprise, and hampers economic development. -In due course the government revenues are bound to be adversely affected by such a situation. If it were thought that Alberta was permanently on the down grade, that the era of expansion had ended, and that the government would have little or no occasion in future to provide the additional facilities which are needed by a growing and prosperous community, there are some who might claim that the loss of credit standing was of no great importance. We could not subscribe to any such pessimistic view of the future of Alberta. It is, therefore, our opinion that a situation which involves impairment or destruction of Alberta's credit standing also involves an indirect cost to the province far exceeding the immediate pecuniary advantage gained.
I want to point out that while the governor of the Bank of Canada thus somewhat decisively condemned the default of the province of Alberta, when he went on to make his recommendations, which appear at page 41, he did not suggest that the dominion should make a grant to Alberta on the basis of
[Mr. Ilsley.l
Alberta having paid or paying its bond interest in full. He said the situation would have to be taken as it existed. I want to quote from page 41:
With a scale of taxation no higher, and a scale of expenditure no lower than in Manitoba and Saskatchewan in 1937-38, Alberta expects to balance its budget on all accounts (ordinary, capital and relief) with the exception of debt retirement. Our recommendation of dominion government assistance in the cases of Manitoba and Saskatchewan was based on urgent needs of those provinces for cash during the time required for the examination which will be conducted by the royal commission. If Alberta were now paying full interest on its obligations, the province in 1937-38 would presumably have to borrow its full share of unemployment relief from the dominion, and on the basis of budgetary estimates (not including debt retirement) would have a cash shortage of about $600,000. Its position would be a little worse than that of Manitoba, but distinctly better than that of Saskatchewan; and a claim for assistance would, no doubt, be considered in the light of these facts. It is the case, however, that Alberta's budgetary position differs materially from that of the other provinces, by reason of the fact that interest payments have been reduced by 50 per cent, or $3,400,000, and, other things being equal, its cash requirements have been reduced by the same amount. We can only deal with the situation as it is-not as it might have been in other circumstances.
I want to call those words to the attention of this committee:
We can only deal 'with the situation as it is-not as it might have been in other circumstances. We find that Alberta can maintain its governmental services on as favourable a basis as Manitoba or Saskatchewan without receipt of additional assistance, and we therefore see no basis for recommending that temporary financial aid should be extended by the ' dominion government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am also answering or attempting to answer the leader of the opposition, who seemed to think that unless we deal with the province of Alberta as though there had been no default; that is, unless we pay them sums of money which perhaps we would have been prepared to pay if there had been no default, we are condoning that default. In 1937, when Mr. Towers made that report, it was never argued that we should pay the province of Alberta a large additional sum of money on condition that they pay it to the bondholders. Nor was it ever argued that this government condoned the action of Alberta because it did not take that step. I will come back a little later to the hon. member for Lethbridge, but the leader of the opposition argued strongly to-day that we were condoning or approving the action of Alberta by this step. My first point is that we are not doing so now, nor were we doing so in 1937 and 1938. We went upon the only possible basis, which is put very clearly in Mr. Tower's words; we can only deal with the situation as it is, not as it might have been in other circumstances.
The purpose of this offer to all these provinces is to make it possible for the dominion to collect the necessary tax revenues. The purpose of this offer is not to straighten up situations that may exist as between provinces and their creditors. Those situations might be various. We are now in a time of war, when we have to impose taxation efficiently and equitably, and the purpose of this offer to the provinces was to make a uniform offer which would be on the same basis for all and which would enable us to impose taxation efficiently and equitably. In making this offer it was important to have some regard to provincial sensibilities, shall I say, or at least certainly not to give the impression that we were wielding the big stick on the provinces. For that reason we made an exceedingly fair offer to the provinces, an offer which several times the leader of the opposition has said he thought was generous.
I think so yet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
When it became apparent that some provinces would) not want to leave the succession duty field, we made no attempt to get them to leave that field; we left them there and imposed moderate additional succession duties. It was pretty well known that some provinces wished to control their natural resources and to be left the right to tax those natural resources; so it was an express provision of this offer that the provinces would continue to tax their natural resources and that such taxation would not be
affected by this offer. In regard to the gasoline tax revenues it was not clear what the future would be with regard to the revenues which would be derived in that way; we therefore gave an undertaking to the provinces that we would see to it that their revenues from gasoline taxes were maintained at the 1940 level, provided that they did not alter the existing rates. We gave an undertaking that the arrangement would be entirely temporary, so that it could not be said1 that we were attempting to move into this field permanently, as we knew in all probability would be said. To ensure that it would be temporary we provided that any province could, at any time, withdraw from this arrangement.
The whole spirit of the offer was to give the provinces a chance to finance themselves and to raise their necessary revenues, and to give them all the necessary safeguards and guarantees. It would be inconsistent with the spirit of that arrangement if we went to one province and tied a condition on to the offer made to them. That is what is suggested-that we offer to pay Alberta a larger sum it is true than the amount mentioned in our actual offer, but that we attach to that a condition which in effect says to Alberta, "You, alone among the provinces, will get so much money, but you will get it only on the condition that we say what the destination of that money will be." That is contrary to the whole spirit of our offers to the provinces, which offers as I see them had a high regard for provincial autonomy, for provincial rights and for provincial sensibilities.
I cannot help saying again that I think the question is largely academic so far as Alberta is concerned. There is not the slightest indication that Alberta would want us to make an offer of the kind or would accept such an offer if we made it. They would be $800,000 worse off than they would be under the offer that is made, and I cannot help thinking that it would be just an idle gesture. It might muddy the waters, and it would place this province out of line with the others. It would be incorporating into these offers an element of domination by the dominion.
Before I conclude I should like to say something about the argument of the hon. member for Lethbridge which was, I think, that Alberta is not able or has not been able to pay its bond interest in full. That argument may have been quite good in 1936. I listened with interest to the facts which the hon. member has given but I should like to tell the committee that there has been a vast improvement in the financial showing of the province of Alberta since that time. I have Mr. Low's consolidated revenue and
Supply-Finance

deficit account. It shows that for the fiscal year 1935 revenues were 115,698,000 and in 1940, $24,410,000. In 1935 the expenditures were $17,436,000 and in 1940, $21,922,000. These expenditures include ordinary expenditures and unemployment relief but do not include agricultural relief or capital expenditures. It is hard for Alberta to maintain its position that it is unable to discharge its obligation. It may have been unable to do this in the past, but I do not think it is now.

The minister is giving a fine dissertation on the matter, but I think it is only fair to point out that Alberta is reducing her indebtedness. She has cleared off over $3,000,000 of these savings certificates that were causing her trouble, and she has made commitments to meet her debts just as rapidly as she can. The day will undoubtedly come when, if Alberta sees she can do it, she will pay off all the debts that it is possible to pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

Those are internal obligations; she is discriminating in favour of her own residents.
I conclude with a reference to the condonation which the leader of the opposition was pressing so hard this morning. He dealt with this matter before on May 26. It is most interesting to see the hon. gentleman's first reaction to this question of condonation, which I think was a sound one.
You think I am not sound to-day.

Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): Has consideration been given to what it is proposed to do under the circumstances? Is it proposed, by making a grant in that particular instance, to put the imprimatur of this dominion upon the default of one of the provinces?
Mr. Ilsley: I do not think it does that.
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): It may have that effect.

Mr. Hanson (York-Sunury): I would not put it in that way. It may have the effect- depending entirely upon the action to be taken after these negotiations have been completed- of condonation. I hope the minister will not put himself in that position.

Mr. Ilsley: The offer to Alberta is very clear. The offer is, the actual debt service assumed by the province, or the proceeds of the taxes-whichever the province likes-and since the amount collected in taxes for 1940 is higher than the actual debt service, undoubtedly the province will elect to take the amount collected in taxes.
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): If they do, that would eliminate the situation to which I have referred. There would not be in that event any condonation of the default of the particular province.
Mr. Ilsley: That is what I think, but-
Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury): At least, that would be my judgment. If, however, they should happen to accept the other alternative, the minister is faced squarely with this position: shall he, in consideration of their going out of the field, pay them a sum which would equal one-half of what, we shall say, they ought to pay if they keep their contract? Mr. Ilsley: I do not think it is. For example, we offer to Saskatchewan their debt service or their taxes, whichever is the greater; and Saskatchewan will undoubtedly elect to take their debt service.

I cannot see any great difference between the language just quoted by my hon. friend and the position I have taken to-day. It may be that I was approaching the matter with caution; I was inquiring as to what the minister's position was to be, and I was giving my first reaction to this subject matter. I am not going to debate the matter further. The minister seemed to be so definite before the luncheon recess that further argument would appear to be useless. I had not quite finished my argument, but I am not going to make a further argument at this time. I should like, however, to make one or two observations.
A few moments ago the minister made it abundantly clear that according to the data available, Alberta could pay as of this date. I am going to leave it on the basis of the minister's statement. The second thing I should like to say is this: the Rowell-Sirois report recommended the same treatment for Alberta as for the other provinces. My recollection is that it went even a little further and recommended the payment of back interest. I may be wrong about that, because it is a long time since I have read the report, but I think I am correct. Mr. Towers' report, part of which the minister read and part of which the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) conveniently omitted to read, I think makes it abundantly clear that they

Supply-Finance
could do the same thing now in the light of present-day figures. He recommended certain assistance in respect to both Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and said that he would make the same recommendation for Alberta had they been paying the full rate. Of course, it was apparent that they were not paying the full rate, but to-day they could. Therefore the same arrangement should be made with them. In the next place, at the conference it was proposed that Alberta should be treated on the same basis as the other provinces.
Just one word more and I am through with that subject. I think the minister should alter his second proposal to come to this position, that the amount paid to the province in each fiscal year during which the arrangement is to be in effect should be the amount of the total net debt service, provided that the amount so paid shall not in any year exceed the amount of interest due on the provincial indebtedness during the fiscal year ending nearest to December 31, 1940, not including contributions to the sinking fund, less the revenue obtained from succession duties during that period. That, I think, would put them exactly on a parity with the other provinces. The present wording of the estimate does not go that far.

We have no ministers
from the province of Ontario here this afternoon when this invasion is going on. What is the principle on which this vote in the supplementary estimates is based? The principle is this, that we shall revert to the old policy we had with respect to relief works, when the dominion, the provinces and the municipalities spent nearly a billion dollars on relief and relief works. At that time agreements had to be made between the governor in council here and the provinces, and that principle has now been extended to this particular vote, to provide compensation. We have had this compensation feature in our legislation for many years past, but Ontario has never got any compensation. Do not forget in connection with this principle that the loss of income tax and corporation taxes affects most seriously the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. When I entered the house in 1922, Mr. McCrea, the former government member for Sherbrooke, had a return brought down with respect to over-government and overtaxation in this country which showed that aside from the subsidies under the British North America Act the two central provinces, Ontario and Quebec, where we have so much real estate that is very heavily taxed, were paying 814 per cent of the cash taxes of the dominion. The taxes covered by this vote are cash taxes, and this proposal is going to
destroy our municipal institutions in this country. I know something about the burdens of our municipalities, as past-president of the Union of Canadian Municipalities, and I know that the municipalities in all the provinces have had a very hard time to live during the last thirty years. The city from which I come has a tax rate of 3i to 31 mills to carry purely federal burdens. The income tax was taken away from the municipalities in the first place and given by duplication to the dominion, and now it is to be taken away from the provinces and given to the dominion.
I know it is said that these agreements are to be made only for the duration of the war. This same game was played on the municipalities in 1917. I came to Ottawa with a delegation of municipalities at that time to protest against the invasion by the federal authorities of the income tax field. It was said that the invasion was only for the duration of the war and that after the war the income tax would be surrendered to the municipalities again, but we never got it back, and it will be the same with the corporation tax. Then some of the provinces invaded the income tax field and took it away from the municipalities.
Most of the income tax and corporation taxes are paid by the two central provinces. I have always believed in the principle, for all the provinces, of the old Cornish battle cry, " each for all and all for each," and that what should be for the benefit of one should be for the benefit of the other. But this big-stick proposal of the minister is going to make of Ontario a hewer of wood and a drawer of water for the rest of confederation and force a duplicate income tax on Ontario over the heads of the municipalities.
As to the Sirois report, I advised the government the day the report was on the table to forget it, and they did for six months. I advised them to commit it to the archives-earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust, in the sure and certain hope that it would never be resurrected so far as this government was concerned. It was only a half-baked scheme. If the Sirois report had been left alone you could have made a much better agreement with Ontario and other provinces for the duration of the war regarding income and other taxes, and coordination and cooperation, just as you made an agreement respecting the charitable fund. Business men from all the provinces agreed to give up certain features of their charitable war work so that all could get together and work together in unison under a harmonious system for the duration of the war. The same plan should have been followed with respect to income and corporation taxes. Where were the Ontario ministers
Supply-Finance

when this matter-was raised this morning and this afternoon? I believe that the federal government should at once meet Ontario in a spirit of good-will, and this matter could then be settled in half a day or a day and a new interprovincial conference held immediately. Why should Ontario be soaked duplicate taxes? Why should we be made the goat of the proposals of the finance department in the dying days of the session by big-stick methods? I protest against it. You may criticize Premier Hepburn as you like, but if Ontario had the representation in the cabinet we are entitled to, we would get fair play in taxation as the chief taxpayer of Canada. The Premier of Ontario wants to protect provincial and municipal institutions.
I believe that the people of our province are very much disappointed with this budget, and with the proposal to assess all these costs and burdens of taxation against that province by duplicate taxation. I was one of those who brought forward a motion eleven years ago for parliamentary, cabinet, law, taxation and constitutional reform in this country; I proposed amendments to and a reconstruction of sections 91 and 92 of the British North America Act, and after ten years' work that resulted in the appointment of a commission to investigate the whole economic basis of confederation and those five matters now referred to. I believe that the report of the Sirois commission is not accepted by a large majority of the people of Ontario so far as its municipal and educational features and other sections are concerned. Some of the principles proposed are not fair in principle to the two central provinces. It is a case of robbing Peter to pay Paul in taxation matters and leaves no adequate compensation, taking away something from one province and giving it to another. Some of the provinces are bankrupt, as we found out in connection with relief appropriations. I say that you should not interfere with the financial arrangements of the province of Ontario and of the municipalities of this country in the way it is proposed to do here, after they have passed their annual budgets and added so to their taxes. How are the municipalities going to live? It is all right to make an agreement with the provinces about income tax as to compensation, but the municipalities will not be listened to by the province who will grab the bulk of what this vote gives back. If a municipality gets a new source of revenue to-day, within a week or a month the province appropriates it to its own purposes. The municipalities of this country are getting a raw deal from federal and local authority. The city of Ottawa is well looked after through 
various votes in the estimates, but other municipalities are not. I do not know anybody who wants to own a foot of real estate to-day in our municipalities of Canada because of the heavy taxation upon real estate.
It is said that this proposal of the Minister of Finance is only for the duration of the war, but we know that once these taxes are given over to the federal government as in 1917 they will be kept by the federal government.
While I believe that the four parties in this house should get together for the war, I do not propose to sit here and see any political theories or doctrines that are not relevant in war time put over on the country as a war measure, when the country is not ready for them, and they should not be brought forward if you want to have unity in this country during the wrar. The battle of wits, by a correspondence course, between the Premier of Ontario and this government could be settled in a day in my opinion if the two parties would get together and forget a few things at a time like this, but it will never be settled by correspondence, telegrams and telephone calls. There should be a meeting; otherwise there will be no agreement. From a reply the Minister of National Revenue made the other day, I understand that no effort has been made to meet or confer with Ontario before these big-stick methods are to be used on that province in income tax, death duties and corporation tax. How are the municipalities to live? It is all very well for two or three officials here in Ottawa to propose these things. The minister has surrounded himself in two or three lines in his department with a great many officials in Ottawa, and we have learned a great many lessons from theorists in the Department of Finance who only call for help from Ontario and the municipalities when their own plans break down. That is the only time we ever hear from them as provincial and municipal revenues are taken away.
Although a brief of the mayors of the largest cities of Canada was left with the minister last year to deal with, not one of the terms of their proposals has ever been discussed and their ideas have been discarded. Why are they not here to oppose all this? The municipalities and the provinces are at the mercy of those who, by means of this big-stick policy, take their revenues and lay by duplicate taxes the whole burden on real estate and industry. That is what we are coming to. The minister is just making a scrap of paper out of the fundamental principle and doctrine of confederation, which was an agreement between the provinces. They came into

Supply-Finance
this union with an agreement that it should not be changed without their consent. The minister is upsetting the whole principle of taxation under confederation, and provincial governments might just as well be abolished, if all this big-stick taxation continues. It is true, as the report says, that we never should have had this overgovernment and overtaxation; indeed, we should never have had the province system in 1867; they were the creation of the fathers of confederation for political and not for economic reasons. There is no such system in Great Britain and we never should have had it here-a duplicate municipal system one within the other; for that is what it is, with both authorities fighting each other to grab each other's revenues and thus force taxes upon real estate, industry and labour.
I protest on behalf of the people of Ontario, who may be forced to pay duplicate taxes all along the line because the two sides will not- meet and settle it. They would have been compelled also to pay duplicate "sales taxes," under a bill introduced three years ago by this government, if the hon. gentlemen in the other part of the building had' not thrown it out so properly, and saved further duplicate taxes.

My observations with
regard to this resolution will be very brief, and I hope it will not be necessary to answer all the questions as to where, why and by what means the province of which I have the honour to be a citizen finds itself in the predicament in which it is to-day.
I suggest that if the minister would consider amending the resolution in one respect only, and with respect to one figure, Alberta would be placed in a position analogous to that of the other provinces.
The alternative contained in paragraph (b) of the resolution reads:
The net debt service paid by the province during the fiscal year ending nearest to December 31, 1940. . . .
I suggest that if the latter figure were changed to "1941", the minister would put Alberta in the position in which every other province of the dominion will find itself. From 1936 to the present time the government of Alberta has invariably said "We cannot pay our interest debt." Now, to all the other eight provinces the minister is saying, "We will put you in a position, if you vacate the income tax and corporation tax fields, where you can take care of your net debt service, in other words pay those people, wherever they may be, who bought your bonds, their full interest. You will be in that position by accepting (b) alternative, whereby every
province in this dominion will be able to carry out its contractual obligation to its bondholders."
The cut-off date here having been fixed as of December 31, 1940, Alberta is not put in that position. If the cut-off date were made December 31, 1941, then, without any dictation from this government or from any other body, Alberta would be put in a position similar to that of even' other province, whereby she could implement her contractual relations to her bondholders. Whether or not she would do it, she alone must take the responsibility; but at least it never could be said that this government in any way condoned or approved or attempted to take advantage of the situation in which the government of Alberta finds itself.
In round figures, the situation as I appreciate it is this. The net cost of carrying the debt of Alberta is approximately $6,000,000. The income in 1940 from the income tax and the corporation tax amounted roughly to 84,000,-
000.	Alberta will have paid for net debt service last year $3,000,000, by reason solely of the fact that she pays only half the interest on her bonded indebtedness. If she is put in a position analogous to that of the other provinces, she will receive out of the common pot $6,000,000, but perforce she must pay it all out in interest to those who hold her bonds, and she cannot get it unless she pays it out. All she will be able to get from the federal treasury is the amount she has paid to carry her debt.
This would put Alberta in the position of being treated on the same basis as all the other provinces. It means that the government of Alberta will be worse off by something less than one million dollars, which she will have to find from some other source. The only other source available to her is her own people, and from my knowledge of those people I feel quite satisfied that they will and can make up the difference.
I do urge upon the minister that the offer should be dated as of December 31, 1941. It is the only change which need be made in the resolution. If you put the responsibility where it belongs, you forever close the mouth of the government of Alberta with respect to the oft-repeated assertion that "we are not in a position to pay our bond interest." The fund is there available for that purpose; let her make her internal adjustments as she sees fit. I for one am, as I trust every Canadian is and should be, jealous of the credit not only of Canada but of the provinces-

Hear, hear.
Supply-Finance

-not of one province alone, but of all, and it is a matter of regret if one of the daughters of this fair dominion repudiates her obligations. Alberta does not say that she repudiates: in the evidence given by Mr. Low before the banking and commerce committee he side-tracked and side-stepped and refused to admit that there was repudiation. He simply said, "We cannot pay". Now the other provinces, or at any rate some of them, faced with the same situation, did get from the federal treasury in years gone by funds wherewith to meet their obligations. I do not think there is any doubt about that, and I believe the reports will show that the dominion is still carrying those obligations. Why not now, without giving any assurance to speculators in Alberta bonds that the principal will be redeemed or that bygone interest will be paid, say to Alberta: "If you will pay your bonded indebtedness from this time on, you will be treated on the same basis as the other provinces, but if you do not pay, then the federal treasury, perforce, does not assist you."
I am concerned with respect to another matter, and the fairness of this proposition, if I may say so, is reflected in this, that of the nine provinces to which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) referred .this morning, in making up his estimate of $45,000,000, five it would appear, or at least it is assumed, will resort to option (b), thereby indicating that the revenues from corporation taxes and income tax are not sufficient to pay their net debt charges. It is worthy of note that these provinces are the maritimes and the prairie provinces. It is a trite story in itself which we may not traverse this afternoon. I am suggesting to the minister that alternative (b) would be more advantageous and would undoubtedly be accepted by Alberta if it were made 1941; or if Alberta were in fact paying her interest charges, then undoubtedly alternative (b) would be the one.

My suggestion is that Alberta should be put in the same position as it is assumed Saskatchewan's position will be, because there is no question that that province met its bond interest in years gone by as the result of grants in aid from the federal treasury.
There is another aspect of this matter that is likely to be overlooked. After all, this money is interest. We are dealing only with interest, and a substantial portion of the money which will be paid out by Alberta will in turn be recaptured by the Minister of Finance under his income tax proposals, so that the amount involved is not as large as might appear at first blush. I do urge upon the minister that if December 31, 1941, were substituted for the year 1940 he would have removed, so far as this government and the house are concerned, any question of taking advantage of the default, so-called, of Alberta.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I should say a word in reply. I cannot see any good purpose, however, to be served by trying to cross this bridge before we come to it.

I do not see any particular item in the estimates under which I might ask a question in reference to the export of grain from Churchill.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. MacKINNON (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext: It will be quite all right under this item so far as I am concerned.

I wish to know what plans the department has put into operation recently-last year, if I may suggest it-or any plans that are proposed for this fall for the shipment of grain from Churchill, Manitoba. In view of the war and the necessity for convoy, it may not be practicable at the present time, but it was a year or two ago. When I visited there a year ago I learned from people at the elevator that for the past year

Supply-Trade and Commerce
2,500,000	bushels of wheat had been in storage To whom does that wheat belong? Did any loss occur while it was in storage? Who bears that loss, and has the department any plans for the shipment of wheat from that port?

I am glad to have the question asked under this item. With regard to the port of Churchill, there is stored in this elevator at the present time 2,617,000 bushels of wheat. The bulk of this quantity has been in the elevator since the fall of 1939. At that time charters were made for the movement of some of this wheat from Churchill, but immediately after the outbreak of war the British Minister of Shipping commandeered the boats intended to lift some of this wheat, and they were diverted to more urgent use. Since that time conversations have been carried on with the British Minister of Shipping, with a view to arranging for some boats for the Churchill movement; but owing to the difficulties of placing these boats in Churchill and then moving them to north Atlantic ports for convoy purposes, the British Ministry of Shipping consider that the boats cannot be spared for the additional period of movement, and the efforts to divert shipping to Churchill have not been successful. In view of the difficult shipping situation we feel that we should not press the ministry of shipping to do something which will affect their shipping programme.
Within the last week discussions took place with the agent of the British cereals committee in Canada with regard to the prospect of movements from Churchill, but his view was that the position was unchanged, and he could not hold out any hope for any movement from this port during the coming shipping season.
Mr. COLDWELL; Would the minister like us to ask questions now on this administration item, or would he prefer that we wait until the appropriate item comes up?
It would be quite all right now.

First I wish to draw the minister's attention to the freight car situation that arose on the prairies last year. I wrote to the minister and also to the wheat board about it. For many years there were railway car rights under the grain act for which the farmers had agitated over a period of years and ultimately secured. These rights were practically taken away from them during last season. There was set up under the Department of Trade and Commerce a committee known as the car allotment committee.
It decided that cars should be allocated between elevators not on the basis of the percentage of the grain they had handled during the preceding years but rather on the amount of elevator space, including the old annexes that had been built in former days. The temporary annexes, as the minister knows, were not included. In addition, cars of grain billed to Duluth, Portage la Prairie and Kenora, where some of the private firms had storage facilities, were not taken out of the car allotment. I believe it is now proposed that this shall be done during the coming year. The car order-book has not been maintained, a new car allotment committee taking the place of it.
This has affected adversely the farmer-owned and cooperative elevator companies in western Canada. These pool elevators to my knowledge-and I went over my own constituency, which was rather a strong pool constituency-were filled to the roof quite early in September of last year. I remember the situation was particularly acute at Beechy. There, if I may digress for a moment, one of the line companies still had, I think it was nine cars, to be filled-I speak from memory- and so long as they did not fill them, no further allotment of cars could be made to the pool elevator.
This situation caused a great deal of misgiving on the part of the farmers who were cooperatively minded. They were forced to market their grain through line elevator companies with which they had done no business for a number of years, and there was a serious amount of discontent, particularly among the keen and ardent pool members. The result was that over the province of Saskatchewan last year the pools did not maintain their percentage of crop receipts. I believe they dropped about 6 per cent, which is a considerable drop in percentage from around 45 or 46 per cent. This system undoubtedly played into the hands of the line elevator companies. Consequently there is at the present time a feeling of resentment on the prairies about .this whole system.
It has been suggested to me that since the wheat board has been handling the wheat, it might be well if the distribution of cars were placed entirely under the wheat board. At present the distribution is supervised by the car allotment committee, which I believe consists of nine persons, three representing the three western pools, two representing the two railway companies, three from the line elevator companies, and I am not sure how the remaining one is appointed. If that could be done it would assist materially in satisfying the farmers. But if the space is to be considered,
Supply-Trade and Commerce

then it seems to me the space in the new annexes should be considered as well as that in the old annexes. I can, however, assure the minister that last autumn as I moved around my constituency there was serious dissatisfaction with the condition. As I say, I took the matter up last September with the proper people and received prompt attention.
Further, why should the farmer not declare, when he applies for his permit, the elevator at which he wishes to deliver his crop, as well as the point to which he wishes to deliver it? That is, restore to the individual the right to decide through what facilities his crop shall be handled.
I place that suggestion before the minister because I believe that before the new crop moves, this matter should be given consideration, and at least this should be done, that the cars should be allotted not on the basis of space but on the basis of the percentage of the business of the elevator companies, during years that the minister thinks it right and proper to take, say 1937-38-39, the average of these years. Of course he would not take years when there was serious congestion as there was in 1940. On that basis I think there would be much more satisfaction with the local wheat-handling situation than there was last autumn.
At one point I was told that out of forty pool members only fourteen were able to deliver their wheat to their own cooperative elevator. The others had to find accommodation elsewhere with companies with which they had not been dealing in former years. That, of course, was bound to develop a good deal of dissatisfaction.

I shall be glad to take note of the hon. member's suggestion that distribution of cars be placed entirely under the control of the wheat board. During the past season I had complaints about the alleged unfair distribution of cars; in each case they were investigated by me through the wheat board, and so far as I remember, reasonable explanations appeared to be given.
I think attempts were made to minimize the difficulties. We appreciated what the department and the wheat board did.
I appreciate the hon. gentleman's remarks. His suggestions will be given careful consideration.
May I ask who owns the elevator at Churchill?

The Canadian government.
[Mr. Coldwell.l
Who owns the wheat in the elevator?
The wheat board.	[DOT]

I understand that at the present time this elevator contains approximately 2,600,000 bushels of wheat. This would be the equivalent of five or six boatloads, which would be, sufficient to make up a convoy. It occurs to me that this wheat should be moved out, which would leave that space available for use this fall and perhaps eliminate the necessity for the construction of extra storage capacity on the prairies. Has the department considered this point?

I am afraid the hon. gentleman did not quite follow what I said a moment ago. We have made attempts to have that wheat shipped out, but the difficulty is purely one of shipping accommodation. It would take eight or nine ships to move this wheat, and under ordinary circumstances the ships would have to go to Halifax or some other eastern port in order to join a convoy.

When we were discussing this item a few days ago and the question of the shipment of wheat to Japan came up, I asked the minister if he had any information as to whether lumber from British Columbia was being shipped to Japan at the same time. The minister said he would look into the matter and give a reply later.

As a matter of fact I have not been able to make inquiries. I do know that no permits have been issued for the shipment of lumber or any other materials to Japan except in connection with orders which were placed before the permit system came into operation.
I will make, however, the inquiries to which the hon. gentleman has referred.

At the time the British
Columbia members were advised that this wheat was being shipped to Japan the question of certain shipments of hemlock lumber was also discussed. Do I understand that there have been no permits for shipments of lumber other than those? When the minister has answered that question perhaps he would say whether these permits are continuous, or whether they apply only to a particular quantity of lumber.

No shipping permits have been asked for or granted in connection with any orders not placed prior to the inauguration of the permit system. I know nothing about the logs

Supply-Trade and Commerce
referred to, but in connection with wheat I understand there are separate permits for each boatload that is shipped.
Perhaps before the house closes, or before I leave Ottawa, the minister could obtain the information I have requested in regard to lumber.

I
should be very glad to do so.

I should' like to add a
suggestion to the one advanced by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, which I thought was thoroughly sound. If the government cannot see its way clear to allocate cars on the basis of demand by farmers instead of on the basis of space, then the space in the annexes which are not connected with the elevators by an auger also should be taken into consideration. As I understand it at the present time, if an annex is not connected by an>
auger the space in that annex is not taken into consideration. At the point where I live the pool elevator, which is a large one, is not so connected and therefore the annex is not taken into consideration in this way.
I am informed that this is being done.

Has the department given any consideration to the question of the freight rate to Churchill? On the line from Prince Albert to Hudson Bay junction the freight rate to Churchill is three cents less than the freight rate to Fort William; but if the grain grown by farmers on that line goes to Churchill they have to pay the Fort William rate, which makes a difference of about two cents a bushel on that grain. These farmers feel that they should have the advantage of the Churchill freight rate, since farmers living in Alberta have the advantage of the freight rate to Vancouver even though most of their grain goes to Fort William. I should like to know also whether the department intends to make an advance on grain stored in granaries on the farms this fall.

The question of the rates to Churchill does not come under this department; it is under the Department of Transport.
Did I understand the hon. gentleman to ask whether it was the intention of the government to pay storage on farm-stored wheat?
No; whether there would be a cash advance on farm-stored wheat.

That matter has been given a great deal of consideration, not only by the government but also by the bodies advising the government in connection with wheat. No decision has been arrived at as yet, and no decision can well be arrived at until we see what will be the nature of the crop now growing.

When this item was under discussion a couple of days ago some hon. members brought up the question of section 17, and I was wondering whether anything has been done in this connection. I feel quite sure the minister realizes that farmers have certain costs to pay. In a great many cases they have no other way of paying those costs except by delivering their quotas, and if others are allowed to horn in on these quotas under this section the farmers may have difficulty in threshing their grain. The minister understands, I am sure, that at present in the various provinces threshing bills are a first charge on the grain, and in many cases farmers are compelled to obtain credit for twine, binder repairs and other things as well as groceries. I am sure the minister also realizes that the farmer is responsible for the wages of the threshing gang while they are on his farm; that is the rule in Alberta, and I believe in the other provinces as well.

Section 4 of order in council,

4. No person unless he is duly authorized by the board so to do, shall during the crop year commencing on August first, nineteen hundred and forty-one, buy, take delivery of, or mill wheat and no person during such crop year shall sell, deliver, or otherwise dispose of any wheat to or have it milled by any person not so authorized by the board.

There seems to be a mistaken idea with regard to coarse grains being taken by the wheat board. The only authority the wheat board

has under this order in council is in connection with the acceptance of coarse grains at the elevator, in order to give them the power to accept wheat quotas as arranged.

The other evening the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Ross) was explaining the operations of the grain exchange under war conditions, but I did not follow him as closely as perhaps I should have done. I certainly did not gather the informationi I wanted. We have been told that the cereals controller of Great Britain wishes the grain exchange kept open. During the last few days I have seen the hon. member for Moose Jaw around my office in earnest conversation with the officials of the wheat board. I do not know of anyone in the House of Commons better qualified to give this information than the hon. member, and I believe he is ready to do so.

The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has asked me to explain the movement of wheat from the country elevator to export, and I shall endeavour to do that. When the wheat business was operating in the ordinary way on the open market, before we had a wheat board or even afterwards, grain was taken into the elevator, was purchased by the elevator company from the farmer and then was hedged on the Winnipeg market by the sale of futures. This was often done by wheat boards which acted prior to this one, I believe. It was done for the purpose of protecting the later sale of the wheat by the elevator company, but it is unnecessary now because the wheat board guarantees the price to the elevator of the wheat delivered to it for their account. Therefore, there being no necessity for futures trading in connection with that wheat purchased at the country elevator for the board, there is no futures trading in connection with wheat bought at the country elevator and delivered to the wheat board at Winnipeg.
The wheat is purchased for the board and comes to Fort William-Port Arthur. The board take actual possession of the wheat there and it becomes cash wheat in their hands. They pay the elevator companies under their contract with the wheat board for the handling of that wheat east to Fort William. The British cereals import board does not want to set up machinery in this country for the purchase of wheat. They have intimated that they would rather purchase wheat through the ordinary exporters in this country and that they would be willing to pay them a commission on the deal.
They have already agreed to buy the wheat from the wheat board Where does the exporter come in?

I got a little
ahead of myself. The wheat board this year have made a contract with the British cereals import board for the purchase by that board of 120 million bushels at a figure. I do not know what that figure is. Nobody knows it except the wheat board and the British cereals import board. That is not a trade through the grain exchange. It is a contract to deliver to the British cereals import board 120 million bushels of wheat over a period of time at a price. In order that the ordinary exporter in the trade can get that wheat into position
at our ports to be delivered when required, the wheat board then sells for cash to the Canadian exporter. A commission of one-sixteenth of a cent a bushel is paid to the cash broker who sells that cash wheat for the board to the Canadian exporter. The Canadian exporter moves that wheat down, but at the same time that he makes his cash deal when buying the wheat he sells back to the wheat board a delivery option in a future month.
What for?
In order to protect himself, at the time he buys the cash wheat on the market he sells a future option to the wheat board.
What is the commission on that?

It is one-fortieth of a cent a bushel. That trade is .made, and the wheat board, by buying that option, agrees to take delivery of that wheat, if necessary, at the end of the option. The wheat is moved down to the port. When the British cereals import board wish to take delivery of part of that wheat they get in touch with the different exporters in Canada who have that wheat in position, and these exporters make offers of their wheat. These offers are made on the basis of so many cents over a July future, or over an October future, or whenever they are selling. They have so many cents over for handling charges, insurance, freight, storage, brokerage or commission.

What
would that amount to?
In all, the charges would be around eleven cents.
But what would be the brokerage on that last transaction?

That brokerage is fixed by the British cereals import board. They know exactly what the exporter bought the wheat at; when he offers the wheat he knows exactly what he has paid in brokerage, and they make their deal in competition with other exporters in this country who have wheat in position.
What is the brokerage on that transaction?

I do not know exactly, but I would not think it would be over one-quarter to three-eighths of a cent a bushel. The British cereals import board then buy cash wheat from the Canadian exporter, and when they buy that wheat they buy it
Supply-Trade and Commerce

at so many cents over the option. Then they ask the Canadian wheat board to take in to their account that short option or to give a long against the short and close out the trade, which is closed through the clearing house at Winnipeg. There is a charge of one-fortieth of a cent a bushel on that trade on the Winnipeg grain exchange, and, as I understand the situation, the exporter pays one side of the trade and the wheat board pays the other side.
I said the other night that nobody could tell what the price was at which the wheat was sold. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle, who is not in the chamber at the moment, thought that perhaps that could be learned, but the reason why nobody can tell is this. No matter what that wheat is supposed to be sold at by the exporter at the port of shipment, that is not the price at which it is sold. That is the price at which the wheat was bought, plus freight, handling charges, insurance, storage and commission up to that point. They take back in the option; then an adjustment is made between the wheat board and the British cereals import board for the balance of the price whatever it may be, and nobody knows that except the wheat board and the British cereals import board.
Perhaps the minister-I am addressing myself to the hon. member for Moose Jaw who seems to be the minister at present-would tell us what the commission is and what the handling charges are.
I was asked that question before by an hon. gentleman opposite, and I said that I did not know exactly but that it was probably one-quarter or three-eighths of a cent a bushel.
There are five brokerage transactions in the handling of that wheat?

The cash brokerage sale at Winnipeg carries a charge of one-sixteenth of a cent.. Then there is the exporter's brokerage which is paid by the British cereals import board, not by the wheat board, and it is paid by them because they would rather pay it than set up in this country the necessary machinery and offices to handle that part of the business. That is done at their request.

The brokerage which the British cereals import board pay is a direct charge against our wheat. When the British cereals import board and the wheat board settle up, that brokerage is taken into consideration, and therefore we should know what 
that brokerage is because it enters into the price when the import board make their final settlement with the wheat board.
The cereals import board pay that commission to the exporter, and it is not deducted from the price realized by the wheat board. It is an additional price for handling that wheat.
If I got correctly the figures of the hon. member for Moose Jaw, there would be a total of nearly half a cent a bushel on these different transactions. Would that be about correct?

There is one-sixteenth of a cent, cash wheat brokerage at Winnipeg; there is one-twentieth of a cent which covers two transactions-one each way -on the futures trade; that is all. In fact, that is more than all that comes out of the wheat board. There is only one-fortieth of a cent provided by the wheat board on the option trade and one-sixteenth of a cent on the cash wheat brokerage. The other brokerage spoken of, of the exporter, is over and above the price of the Canadian wheat and is paid by the British cereals import board direct to the exporter.
I believe that all three brokerages amount to a little less than half a cent.

We now have a much clearer picture than we had before. I was born in the old country; and when I hear about this extremely complicated way of handling a direct trade, I wonder how Great Britain has managed to wiggle through her wars and worries in the past.

I followed very closely the remarks of the hon. member for Moose Jaw. He has explained how we dispose of $600,000 in connection with one transaction, and for the life of me I cannot see why the cereals import board want to spend $600,000 in that particular way. I could think of a dozen other ways in which the British people might spend $600,000 and which would do them much more good. I think we should have a little more information.

A year ago, when it was decided to take the national registration, the then newly appointed Minister of National War Services (Mr. Gardiner) appealed to all hon. members to give their
