whole-hearted support to the completion of this project. Although the then Minister of National War Services has never been supported in the west by this group, I am sure all members of the house gave him complete cooperation. In my own case I did what might seem an unusual thing, I named two Liberals to occupy the hey positions in my constituency of registrar and deputy registrar-
The hon. member was not playing polities, was he?

I did this because these two men had recently completed the work of returning officer and clerk, and their services were, on the whole satisfactory; they knew the constituency, and I thought that experience should warrant their appointment for this responsible position. The people throughout the constituency carried out the work in the same spirit. They thought that with the war on, we should forget partisan politics.
I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce made a start on those lines in connection with the census.
I have here a return showing the correspondence that went out from the minister's office. I am sorry that he did not carry through. I find that a letter went out from the dominion statistician-there is no date on it-mentioning that he was sending out this letter on the request of the minister. The letter reads:
In this connection I am now writing on the instruction of the minister to bespeak your special care in selecting enumerators who are in every respect suitable for their duties and who will be acceptable to the general public. . . .
I am instructed also to direct that you make a fair distribution of the appointments from amongst the political parties represented in your district and to this end that you confer with both the sitting member and the defeated candidates for your constituency.
Hon. members on this side complain, about those instructions not being carried out. In my own constituency the instructions were carried out to the extent of consulting me, and I spent two or three hours in going over my constituency lists carefully. To fill one hundred positions I suggested some thirty names, giving special consideration to the requirements outlined in another letter which went out from the bureau of statistics, and which I have here. This other letter set out the special qualifications for the enumerators, and laid special emphasis on the fact that the enumerators should have certain qualifications. First, there should be a preference to men who served overseas; second, crop correspondents of the dominion bureau of statistics 
should be considered; third, officers and leading workers in farmers' organizations, live stock associations, et cetera, progressive farmers and their sons and daughters, and especialy young men and women who have attended agricultural colleges or universities. Then school teachers when available, and it was further suggested that in certain sections women would make excellent appointees, owing to the fact that in many instances the information must be obtained from the female head of the house. It said that in the last census several women had done excellent work as enumerators.
The next paragraph of course gave the commissioners a way out:
At the same time we want you to clearly understand that the appointment of enumerators rests solely with you and that you are responsible for the efficiency and accuracy of the census of your electoral district.
What is the date of that letter?

There is no date on
any of these letters.

I
may be wrong, but I think the hon. gentleman must be quoting from notices or forms that went out on some other work, because I do not remember those forms going out on the census work.

Perhaps I should have pointed out that I am quoting from sessional paper No. 290A, "copy of all letters, telegrams, recommendations and other documents in the possession of the department relative to the appointment of the census commissioner for the constituency of Mackenzie, Saskatchewan."
This last letter is No. 4, prepared by the Department of Trade and Commerce, R. H. Coats, Dominion Statistician, on "appointment of enumerators, eighth census of Canada, 1941."
I might mention that in the future I think these letters should be dated. There is a whole series here. There is no indication to whom the letter was sent, but I presume the policy was of writing to the defeated candidate.
These were the general letters that went out first. I thought the hon. member was referring to communications direct with the census commissioners.

I explained that I was reading the general instructions given in order that the enumeration might be carried on impartially with a view to having the information so collected that the people would feel

Supply-Trade and Commerce
that this money was being spent to get information which would be of use instead of appointments being made of friends of the party in power. Naturally I thought that these recommendations were going to apply to my riding.
As I said, I spent considerable time in going carefully over my lists, giving special consideration to returned soldiers and the other qualifications mentioned. I was given to understand from the commissioner that these recommendations would be taken into consideration. Out of one hundred to be appointed, I suggested thirty, if I remember correctly, but I have a list here of the hundred later appointed, and not a single name that I recommended appears on this list.
The hon. member has not enough pull.

I know that the commissioner has his way out, seeing he takes final responsibility. I am not saying that these people are not qualified. I am not suggesting that; I know many of these people will carry on their work efficiently; but so far as I can see, these appointments have been made on a strictly partisan basis, and that is not good enough.
He would not accept any of the Liberals recommended by the hon. member.

As a matter of fact
I did recommend two Liberals last year to the Department of National War Services, in order to indicate that for my part I was not going to play politics in this emergency. In carrying out this census the minister might have gone as far as the Minister of National War Services went last year, in order to see that all the people of the country were asked for their whole-hearted cooperation. I know it is too late now to do anything about the matter, but in future an important service such as this should be taken away from petty ward heelers, who seem to be doing most of the work this year. In every community throughout the country there are people who have a special flair for this sort of work. In my constituency I have people who for thirty-five years have been voluntarily sending information to the bureau of statistics because they are interested in compiling and studying statistics. I believe this department should have tried to locate people in the various communities across the country who will supply the department with a constant stream of valuable information every month and every year. After looking over this list, I think I am safe in saying that 90 per cent of these people will feel that they have no
further responsibility after they receive their pay cheques, and their interest in this work will end. This is one field where, as part of a permanent policy, we should get away from narrow partisan politics and see that appointments are made on the basis of merit.
I cannot let this item pass without a protest over the failure of the minister to carry out this census according to the outline he gave the house originally.	[DOT]

I should like to endorse what has been said by the hon. member for Mackenzie. I was not even approached with regard to my constituency; not that I particularly wanted to be, because I think these matters should be handled altogether apart from any member or any defeated candidate. In my constituency, however, there is a good deal of feeling that since many of the people volunteered their services in connection with the registration last year, and have been busy this year with the salvage campaign, the sale of war savings certificates and now the victory loan campaign, this census should have been handled altogether apart from local politics. As I say, I was never approached in my own constituency. I have sometimes said that I was suspicious that some so-called Social Credit candidates who were brought into Saskatchewan in 1935 became Social Credit candidates just in order to split the vote and elect the Liberal candidate. In my own constituency the gentleman who has been appointed commissioner was the Social Credit candidate in 1935, having transferred his allegiance from the Liberal party to the Social Credit party a few weeks before the election. When I was in my constituency at Easter I found that the people had been told they would have to approach not only the defeated federal Liberal candidate but the sitting Liberal members or defeated Liberal candidate for the provincial legislature. Apparently the recommendations were being received through the local provincial politicians for parts of my constituency which is a bad situation.
We have nothing to do with that.

I know the minister had nothing to do with that, but I am pointing out that the local political game is going to destroy any unity we may have in connection with our war effort. I should like to add that so far as this group is concerned, we have leaned over backwards in trying to play the game fairly with the government. There have been times when we might have been more embarrassing but refrained from doing so because we did not wish to do anything that would undermine confidence in Canada's
Supply-Trade and Commerce

war effort. We expect that in all constituencies there will be a measure of nonpartisanship exercised in government expenditures in war time. I want to protest most emphatically against what has been done. I quite agree that this practice has not been followed everywhere; that in many constituencies the sitting -Liberal member has tried to carry on this work more or less on a proper basis. But there have been constituencies, and mine is one of them, where the sitting member was never asked for a recommendation. I would not wish to be approached, because I do not believe in any form of political patronage. At the same time, however, I object to having what I may call- and I do not use this term disrespectfully but because I know of no other-local ward politicians making recommendations for remunerative government employment, when a great deal of voluntary service is being rendered by all the people of the constituency, irrespective of their political persuasion.

I find myself pretty much in agreement with the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar, particularly with regard to the question of political patronage. As I understand it, one of the fundamental principles of our organization is that political patronage is one of the first things we would eliminate if we were in a position to do so.
I find fault with the Minister of Trade and Commerce specifically with respect to this matter. I view the minister of any department exactly as I view the commander of a battalion or regiment in the army. He should be and is responsible for the discipline and direction of his department, and any violation of orders issued by the department is the direct responsibility of the minister. As the hon. member for Mackenzie pointed out, the minister did issue specific instructions to those selected as census commissioners across Canada, that with respect to appointments the commissioners were to get in touch with the defeated candidates and also the sitting members. I was in my constituency, in the very town where the commissioner for the constituency lives, for some weeks after the appointment was made, but I never saw or heard from this gentleman, whom I know very well. On May 7 I wrote the minister pointing out that I had not been consulted in any way, shape or form by the man to whom had been delegated the authority to appoint enumerators for the constituency. The minister replied on May 8 stating that he was suggesting to his permanent officials that they check up on this particular case, but to date I have heard no more about it.
[Mr Coldwell.]
I have nothing at all against the man who
has been appointed in my constituency. He is a local merchant; he is very well off, and I know many men better qualified and more in need of the work than this gentleman. I can say that without reservation. In my constituency it has always been the practice-I hope it still is, although I cannot say-in matters of this kind to make the fullest possible use of the ex-service men's organizations. They have always been given preference. This gentleman of whom I speak is not a returned man, nor do I expect him to become a returned soldier in this war, although I believe he is not too old to make his contribution. What I am finding fault with is this. I do not care whom the Minister of Trade and Commerce appoints; that is his responsibility, but when he sends out specific instructions to small-town politicians throughout the country, I expect him to see that those instructions are obeyed and followed out.
The registration campaign was conducted on a voluntary basis. I travelled throughout my constituency and checked every registration booth. A good job was done there. I am reasonably sure that the people who carried on that work will receive absolutely no consideration in this connection. I am adding my protest to those of other hon. members. When orders are issued by the government to -people on the outside, those orders should be carried out.

Mr. Chairman, I can
agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar so far as the present census taking is concerned, but' if it were not for the war I would disagree because, in the past, census appointments have always been made by the party in power. Personally I take no exception to that method except in war time when we should all be united in our war effort. During the war I do not think these appointments should be made in a political manner, and to that extent I agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
I have no fault to find, so far as my own riding is concerned. When the registration was taken last year, the minister of the department sent out regulations that the sitting members should name both the chief registrar and the deputy registrar, and likewise the enumerators. When I received my instructions I at once got in touch with the Liberal candidate who had opposed me at the last election, and I said to him, "You name one-half of the appointments from top to bottom, and I will name one-half from top to bottom." Then I-and when I say "I", I mean my association-named the registrar, and the Liberal association named the deputy registrar. My association named 131 enumerators, and the Liberal association named 131 enumerators. In that way we eliminated politics in Davenport riding; the registration was taken efficiently, and everything was harmonious throughout.	,
When it came to taking the present census, the instructions sent out by the minister or by the department were quite clear to me, and, I am glad to say, quite clear to the commissioner who had been named by the department for my riding. He w'as a Liberal.
He got in touch with me, and when I was home on Saturday last I got in touch with Mr. T. W. Meriam, the president of my association, and asked him how the census preparations were going in my riding. He said, "Fine. The commissioner has been fair, and1 I have no cause for complaint. In fact, he was quite willing to give me more than I was entitled to." Therefore, so far as Davenport riding is concerned I have no fault to find, and I am convinced that if fault has been found elsewhere it has probably been on account of partisanship in the appointments. I have seen no evidence of that in Davenport, but here and there one will find a Liberal candidate or a Liberal member, perhaps as a Conservative candidate did in other times-

I have in my hand an editorial from the Huron Expositor, of Seaforth, of May 16, 1941. That is in the riding represented by the hon. member for Huron-Perth (Mr. Golding), who is not in his seat at the moment. He is the Liberal member for that riding, and this editorial shows that he deserves credit for what he did. I may say that ever since I have known him in this house I have always found him fair, and the way this newspaper represents him to be convinces me that he is fair. The editorial is headed "The Wrong Presumption" and reads:
Speaking of the forthcoming census, the Globe and Mail said in a recent editorial:
"On June 2nd seventeen thousand census enumerators, presumably all good Liberals, will sally forth with armfuls of nine different kinds of forms for the decennial stock-taking of the Canadian people."
As far as this riding is concerned, the Globe and Mail's presumption as to "all good Liberals" is very wide of the truth. In this riding of Huron and Perth, and, we understand, in a good many other ridings, the census enumerator appointments are made on a fifty-fifty basis-* half Liberal and half Conservative.
The hon. member for Huron-Perth told me that as soon as he received notice that the census was to be taken, he got in touch with his commissioner and instructed him to split the appointments from top to bottom. There is no trouble in Huron-Perth.
I would close by saying that had all the commissioners interpreted the regulations sent out by the department as they were interpreted in Huron-Perth and in Davenport,

I understood from what the minister has told us that the census commissioner in each constituency would get in touch with the sitting member. In my case I have not heard from the commissioner. I wish to say that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has been very considerate in all dealings with me, and I wish to make it plain that the reflection is not upon him 'but upon the political machine which is 'being set up and which is disrupting the unity of this country. Let me illustrate what I mean. I hold in my hand

a letter written to a gentleman in my riding 'by the commissioner of the federal constituency of Vegreville. It is as follows:
Eighth Census of Canada,
Commissioner's Office
Vegreville, Alberta, May 17,1941.
Mr. D. Prokop,
R.R. 1, Andrew,
Alberta.
Dear Sir:
With reference to your recent letter, I regret I was unable to have your appointment^ made as enumerator, as there was some objection by the committee on the grounds that you were connected with the Social Credit work in the last election. However, if any enumerator fails to take his appointment, I will endeavour to put you in without having to resort to the committee.
Yours truly,
John Decore per JD
I should like to know what "committee" that was. Was it not a political committee, the Liberal committee in the constituency? Of course it was. Because of incidents of this kind I must lay at the door of this government some responsibility for the result of certain national efforts in which I have been asked to cooperate. I have here a telegram sent to me from my constituency, telling me that the victory loan campaign is going on very slowly in the riding for the simple reason that the people of the district are disgusted with politics. I should like to know why, in time of war, when we are confronted with the gravest responsibilities, we see fit to behave like school children. I should like to know what possesses grown-up men, in times like these, to make appointments upon a political basis. To be a true Canadian and a loyal citizen does not necessarily mean that one has to be a Liberal. I respect men who have Liberal views, but we want the Liberals to respect our views as well. That is why we have a democracy.

speechtext:
As member for one of
the western constituencies, I was asked to assist the government in the matter of national registration. I did my best, and with the cooperation I received from every group and from all parties the thing went over wonderfully. Next we were asked to help in the

Supply-Trade and Commerce
salvage campaign. I sent out a circular and invited the people in my constituency to help, and everything was done that could be done. Next, we were asked to help in the war savings certificates campaign. We enjoyed very general cooperation in that effort. I received a letter a week or two ago from the Minister of National Defence requesting help in the recruiting campaign. I have tried and am trying to do as much as I can along that line. Then came the victory loan campaign, and, of course, there are the Red Cross and other appeals which require our support. I wish now to make it clear that I am not going to stand for any party politics in connection with our national problems. I will go on. the platforms and just tear politics to pieces if anyone tries to introduce partisan politics in my constituency in times like these.

subsubtopic: CORRESPONDENCE WITH PROVINCES AS TO THEIR WITHDRAWAL FROM THESE FIELDS FOR DURATION OF WAR
speechtext: Including the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation?

subsubtopic: CORRESPONDENCE WITH PROVINCES AS TO THEIR WITHDRAWAL FROM THESE FIELDS FOR DURATION OF WAR
speechtext:
Anybody at all; I do not care who it is. In one district of my riding named Podola, where the people have not had. a good crop for ten years, they contributed to the Red Cross fund $100 last year, $100 this year, and have pledged themselves to contribute $100 every year until the end of the war. In that district the people, who are mostly Social Crediters, are really poor; yet that is what they have done. Now, when it comes to census enumeration, this chap writes and tells Mr. Prokop he cannot accept him because he is a Social Crediter. Is that not a shame? It is enough to break one's heart. I must confess that after coming to this house I soon became disillusioned. I do not wish to reflect unfairly upon any horn, members, some of whom are very good men, but I must admit to having been disappointed ait the petty attitude which is so. often shown at a time when we should cooperate, when we should try to understand the other fellow's point of view. Instead of doing so-, we play party politics; we do petty things which one would not expect of high-school kids. I have already given the .committee an example of what I mean.
The people of my riding are of varied racial origins. Let me tell you, Mr. Chairman, that it is quite a job to bring them together, to speak to them in, probably, two or three languages, to organize and to put anything over. Yet I have tried to do it, and I have had wonderful success. Then there comes along the Liberal political machine and spoils the whole effort.
To some this may be a laughing matter, but I say that in time of war we cannot stand this sort of thing. I do not wish to

say much more about this, but I insist that the people of Canada are sick and tired of party patronage; they are not in the mood for petty politics. As I have already said, I believe the minister is trying to do his best, and I do not wish to reflect unfairly upon him. But we in Canada must rid ourselves of these political machines which are being built up and which interfere seriously with our war effort.
I happen to be the only member in this House of Commons of Ukrainian extraction. I travel from one end of the country to the other trying to explain to our people the problems that face Canada. It is not an easy matter, and when I get letters and telegrams from my riding indicating that politics are carried on, it breaks my heart. It makes it hard for me to do much in other parts of Canada. I shall leave the matter at that. If there develops in my constituency anything that will interfere with the victory loan campaign-because there have already started some mass meetings which are being held protesting against politics of this sort-and if we are not able to get as good a result as we might otherwise obtain in all these campaigns, do not blame me, place the responsibility on the government.

Surely we are living in a new decade and a new generation, and the people are quite aware of what is taking place. I do not complain too much, but at the same time I do protest a little, and I say 'that in time of war this expenditure of $3,000,000 odd, going through the mill of the political machine, does not help Canada at this juncture. I question whether it will have any bearing on the victory loan. Lot us subscribe our victory loan to the full, and those who would use this as an excuse for not subscribing to the loan, those who would use it as an excuse for not encouraging recruiting, are not real Canadians. This is a small, piffling political matter, and we cannot do anything about it. The minister is unable to do anything about it. It is part of the system. At the same time, however, let us not forget that this system, which in a time of war is almost iniquitous, is something which the minister, when he has to make decisions with regard to complaints that come from individual constituencies, should disregard, taking, instead, a broad and generous view. He should not base his decisions on any considerations arising out of the system. Let him not think of his place in a political party; instead, let him consider the difficult situation in which we find ourselves to-day and ask himself what would be best in the interests of Canada.

I do not think the minister's remarks concerning the hon. member for Vegreville going into Edmonton East a few weeks ago are well taken. Perhaps I may have some right to say this because I also was one of the Social Credit members who went into Edmonton East then. I might say for the minister's information, if he is not yet aware of it, that the stand of the Social Credit forces in the Camrose provincial

Supply-Trade and Commerce
by-election was that in time of war the sitting member should have an acclamation. That was our stand in connection with the Edmonton East by-election. There would have been no Social Credit or New Democracy candidate in Edmonton East had not a certain gentleman from Toronto invaded that constituency and forced those people to a vote, which would have forced our own supporters either not to vote at all or to vote Liberal or to vote for that other gentleman. When the present hon. member for Edmonton East took her seat here yesterday, I w'as one of the first to go over and welcome her. 1 confessed to her that I did my best to keep her in Edmonton, but since the hon. lady is here and the people in Edmonton East have spoken, this group welcomes her to this house.
Some observations made by other hon. members speaking to this item in the estimates have revealed that appointments of enumerators have indeed been political. The fact that the hon. member for Mackenzie recommended thirty names not one of whom was appointed is evidence of that fact. The fact that a letter was sent out by the chief statistician to all chief enumerators suggesting to them that they communicate and confer with the sitting members; the fact that there are some chief enumerators who never did so -the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar says he was not informed; I was not consulted in a single case; the hon. member for Bow River says he was not, and I suppose other hon. members could say the same thing-and the fact that the hon. member for Vegreville places on the record a letter which declares that one name was not considered for the particular reason that he was an active Social Creditor in the last election, certainly savour of politics. I would suggest that if the gentleman mentioned in that letter had been active in Liberal politics in the last election he would never have received a letter of that kind.
These conditions, together with the fact that we are now asked to vote nearly $3,000,000 in order to take the census in time of war, put the question to us whether or not we are justified in voting this huge expenditure. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Bow River:	[DOT]

speechtext:
This is a subsidy that has been granted for a number of years.
With regard to the shipment of wheat to south Africa, the difficulty in the way of meeting the wishes of south Africa and the desires of Canada is the question of shipping space. Very large shipments of war supplies from Canada to south Africa have made it almost impossible to secure space for the shipment of wheat. In addition, south Africa has been in the habit of buying a certain quantity of our hard wheat to mix with its own wheat. This year, on account of difficulties with regard to foreign exchange as well as lack of shipping space, south Africa is relying on its own wheat and also on the use of rye and soya beans. We are very anxious to sell wheat to south Africa or any other part of the empire, but the main difficulty at the present time is in connection with shipping space.

subsubtopic: CORRESPONDENCE WITH PROVINCES AS TO THEIR WITHDRAWAL FROM THESE FIELDS FOR DURATION OF WAR
speechtext:
The special committee on aeronautical, electrical and hydraulic research facilities, comprising representatives of the departments of national defence, public works and transport, and of the national research council, under which the project has been developed, held its first meeting April 12, 1939. The design of buildings and equipment is being carried out by the council staff. Contracts are let and construction supervised by the Department of Public Works. Expropriation proceedings were initiated in April, 1939, and active design of buildings and services commenced that month.
The new laboratories are located on a site of some 130 acres, adjacent to the Royal Canadian Air Force, Rockeliffe air station, at the corner of the Montreal and Skead roads, about four miles east of Ottawa. The original project comprised some fourteen separate laboratories and buildings. Subsequently, following the outbreak of war, the construction of four laboratories, not of direct war importance, was postponed. The present
Supply-Trade and Commerce

project includes ten of the original buildings and an explosives laboratory, a total of eleven structures.
Construction on the first building commenced October 17, 1939. The present position is as follows. Settlement of all expropriation claims has been affected. A water supply and distribution system has been installed; sewers laid, and construction of a system of roads is well advanced. The Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario has constructed a transmission line to the site and a transformer station on the property. The corner-stone of the aerodynamics building was laid on July 23, 1910. Construction of the following buildings is nearing completion and they are now occupied wholly or partly:
Aerodynamics building (wind tunnels and aircraft instrument laboratory).
Central heating plant.
Instrument and model shops.
Storage building.
Aircraft structures laboratory.
Gate house.
The following buildings are in various stages of construction and all should be completed by September 30:
Aircraft engine laboratory.
Model testing basin (floats and hulls).
Gasoline and oil laboratory.
Flammable storage building.
The design of the explosives laboratory is practically finished, and tenders are about to be called.

speechtext: Before we leave the estimates of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I should like to ask a question with respect to the Hecker H-0 company in my riding. I was unavoidably absent this afternoon when the minister's estimates came up. Could the minister make a statement now as to whether there has been any change in the situation with regard to this company getting permits to export to Great Britain?

subsubtopic: CORRESPONDENCE WITH PROVINCES AS TO THEIR WITHDRAWAL FROM THESE FIELDS FOR DURATION OF WAR
speechtext:
The hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) has spoken to me about this particular company and its shipments to the United Kingdom markets, and since it is a typical case, I think I should make a brief statement respecting the negotiations between this company and my department.
On the outbreak of war in September, 1939, the United Kingdom prohibited importation of many commodities and subjected others to import licence. From time to time new commodities were prohibited or restricted by licence control. Cereal breakfast foods, including "Force" manufactured by the Hecker H-0 company, were subjected to import licence as from March 21, 1940.
The Department of Trade and Commerce on March 21, 1940, instructed the Canadian trade commissioner in London to give every assistance possible to the representatives of the Hecker H.-O company in the matter of obtaining import licences for "Force". The trade commissioner replied on April 9 that the representatives of this company had received licence to import 8,700 hundredweights of "Force" during the ensuing three months.
In July, the Hecker H.-O company informed the department of further difficulty in obtaining licences for "Force". The Canadian trade commissioner was again asked to assist. He reported on July 18 that the matter had been discussed with the dominions office of the British government and also that a subcommittee of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, comprising London representatives of different Canadian breakfast cereal companies, had been formed for the purpose of negotiating with the ministry of food over import licences.
Writing further on September 11, the trade commissioner stated that owing to the urgent necessity of concentrating overseas exchange resources and shipping and port facilities upon essential services, the rr inistry of food had decided that they could not issue licences for

Supply-State-Civil Service Commission
importation of breakfast foods. The general and economic situation had become even more critical than earlier in the year. The trade commissioner was of opinion that in view of the attitude of the authorities toward various staple food products, no useful purpose would be served by pressing the matter with the ministry. For example, about this time licence was refused for importation of packaged rolled oats.
A further effort was made to assist the Hecker H-0 company by furnishing a statement of their case to the Canadian delegation, headed by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), which went to England in September, 1940. On their return, the delegation reported that discussions with the ministry of food definitely indicated that there was no prospect of any reversal of the position taken by the ministry regarding breakfast foods at this time. The whole matter is one of shipping space.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Will the minister explain the attitude of the government with regard to that portion of the annual report of the civil service commission for the year 1940 which is to be found at page 5 and deals with salaries of employees in the lower grades who have been brought into the service since the war started? The passage reads:
The commission accordingly recommended that the salary of these employees should be increased on satisfactory service to $65 per month after six months' service, $70 after one year's service and $75 after two years' service. This recommendation was not approved by the treasury board, although an increase to $65 after six months' service was allowed, and a new class carrying a salary of $75 per month was set up for duties of a higher nature, to apply to certain employees giving exceptional service and having served for at least two years.
The commission goes on to use these significant words:
While this step affords some alleviation, the commission is still of the opinion that the form of increase originally proposed by it is' best suited to meet the situation, and that it is in the public interest that it should be applied.
Will the minister explain to the committee the attitude of the government with regard to that recommendation?

speakeroldname: Hon. P. F. CASGRAIN (Secretary of State):
subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
That is a matter to be dealt with especially by the treasury board. At the present time there is before the government a petition from the Civil Service Association with regard to that matter, and that, is under consideration as well as other representations 14873-247
received more recently from the Amalgamated Civil Servants. This will be considered, I think, at the same time as the other matter is being adjusted.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
What about the next paragraph of the recommendations of the commission found at the top of page 6, which has to do with the present limitation on the number of permanent positions in a department? The report reads as follows:
Difficulty has also continued during the year with reference to the granting of permanent status to employees who are performing work that is permanent in nature. This does not apply to war employees, but the reestablishment of the quota regulations limiting the number of permanent positions in any department to a definite proportion as set by the treasury board has renewed difficulties which it was hoped had disappeared when the original quota order was rescinded by order in council in 1939. The commission is of the opinion that permanency in tenure should depend not upon an arbitrary figure but upon the permanency of the work involved, and 111 at if the work is permanent, the employee, if giving satisfactory service, should also be permanent.
I think that is the belief of many members of this house as well as being the belief of the civil service commission, and I would ask the minister to explain why the government continues to insist on a certain percentage of employees in any one department not being allowed to become permanent.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I am given to understand that there is always a certain percentage of permanent employees in a department, 80 per cent, and that the rest are what are called "temporaries" by the nature of their service. It has been thought from time to time that certain temporary employees should be permitted a permanency. For instance, the other day, as the hon. member will recall, certain readjustments were recommended by the civil service commission with respect to the servants of this house, and the commission's report was adopted by the house whereby certain temporary employees on the house staff were made permanent. I have in mind to bring this matter up anew with a view to seeing that action such as my hon. friend has suggested be further considered.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I should like to support what the hon. member for Vancouver South has just said. Until 1936, I think it was, the proportion of temporaries to the permanent staff fluctuated from time to time according to the needs of the departments. There was no arbitrary figure or fixed percentage of temporaries to permanents. The civil service committee which met in 1938 and again, I think, in 1939 reported on that question, and the passage just quoted from the commission's

3906	COMMONS
Supply-State-Civil Service Commission
report is, I believe, in accordance with the findings of the civil service committee of those years. That is a matter which should be taken into consideration at once by the minister, because it is not right that persons employed in work which is of a permanent nature should be continued year after year as temporary employees and thus debarred from participating in the advantages which come to the permanent staff.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I might say that this rule which I have mentioned, whereby 80 per cent of the employees are permanent and the remainder are temporary, is a rule of the treasury board. As to many of these cases, the hon. member should bear in mind that although there is a minister in charge of the operation of the civil service commission, all these matters which have to do with increases in salary that are recommened by various committees of the house which have sat from year to year, as well as changes in the personnel, have to be dealt with by the treasury board. They become, therefore, matters for the finance department. For that reason I am not in a position to say that all these recommendations will be carried out, because even though the minister made them, they would have to be scrutinized and passed by the treasury board.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: If the operation of the civil service commission comes under the Department of Finance, why is this item not in the Department of Finance estimates? How can we discuss estimates of a department unless the minister under whose jurisdiction that department comes is in the house so that he may be in a position to answer questions which are asked?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I wish I were able to give my hon. friend the answer he desires. At the present time the functions are distributed in this manner. The civil service commission is a public body created by parliament, and it so happens that its minister in the house is the Secretary of State. But when there is a question of adjustment of salaries, the civil service commission investigates them. When a body of employees of the civil service makes representations to the civil service commission that certain positions be made permanent, or with regard to other matters such as we have discussed this evening, they are referred to the civil service commission for attention. Then the commission makes its report, which is dealt with by the treasury board, and finally the government assumes the responsibility of either adopting or amending the recommendations.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
On June 10, upon motion of the Prime Minister, a report of the civil service commission classifying certain positions to which employees on the temporary staff of the House of Commons are to be appointed on a permanent basis, laid on the table of the house on March 5, 1941, was approved, whereby it was provided that the six constables transferred to the messengers and cleaning branches in the reorganization of the house services be made permanent by the civil service commission at the same salaries as they are now receiving.
The last clause reads:
It is recommended that appointments of temporary employees with five years of service be authorized at their present salary rate, or, if there is no rate in the range equal to their present salary then at the next higher rate, but not exceeding, however, the maximum rate of the class.
I should like to inquire of the minister, regarding some of the sessional employees, such as messengers and the like, who have been here for a period of five years or more, not continuously, but just from session to session, whether they would come within the purview of this section which provides that "appointments of temporary employees with five years of service be authorized at their present salary rate." I speak particularly of these men, some of whom have been here for more than five consecutive sessions, some as many as ten, and I put in a plea on their behalf and ask the minister if he is able to bring them within the purview of that section, or, in any event, to enable their appointments to be made permanent.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that if the messengers and other employees of whom he has just made mention are among the classes of employees mentioned in the resolution adopted by the house, they would come under the recommendation and would be made permanent. If not, it would be for the internal economy commission of the house to make a recommendation to the civil service commission; the civil service commission would deal with it; another motion would be made such as was made on June 10, and then they would be made permanent. subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I have before me a copy of an advertisement of a civil service examination. I should like to ask a few questions, not exactly with regard to this particular position, but with regard to positions of a similar nature. This is an advertisement for a caretaker for an armoury in Winnipeg. The rate set is $60 a month, and the question to my mind is, who sets such a salary? While this has reference to a particular appointment, I have no doubt that it is typical of many positions.
The advertisement goes on to state that $15 additional will be allowed in lieu of quarters. It appears that as a rule, in positions of this sort, a man is employed at a certain rate and quarters are provided, but in this particular case quarters are not to be supplied, and that is the situation now in quite a number of such positions. I should like to know how the figure of $15 came to be set, because I should say at once that a salary of $60 for a man who has to be a mature person-in all probability the sort of man who would take this kind of position would be a married man with a family-is an entirely inadequate remuneration. I do not think it is a fair wage to offer any person for this sort of work.
In the second place, I cannot imagine who ever thought any person could rent a house in a city in Canada for $15 a month. I wish to know who is responsible for fixing so small 14873-2471
an allowance in lieu of quarters. I suppose that if I were to rent a tent here in Ottawa to camp out on the banks of the river and enjoy the view-and accommodation is so difficult to obtain that it might be necessary to get a tent and live that way-and if I were to put it up myself, it would probably cost me $7.50 a month. One cannot get quarters in any city in this country for $15 a month, and it seems absurd to me for some organization to have fixed such a figure.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: The salaries are generally fixed by the treasury board, and the reclassification is recommended by the civil service commission. I will look into the case which the hon. member has mentioned and see what can be done.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: In the Department of Pensions there are returned men, married and with families, who although they are permanent are receiving only $60 a month, and yet in some instances they are training temporary men who sometimes receive as much as $125 a month. That situation is absolutely unfair, and there should be a change. I do not see how the government can expect any married man to carry on with a salary of $60 a month. In some instances people in charge of war veterans' allowance investigation receive that small a salary. In one of our largest cities such a man is getting a very small salary, and while I suppose it is nob the fault of the Minister of Pensions, who is bound by the salaries that are fixed, it is a disgrace to Canada. Something should be done about it. These men are actually training other men who come in as temporaries and who are getting nearly twice the salary.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I fully appreciate what the hon. member has said, and I may tell him that a few years ago I was prompted to make changes so that some temporary employees would not get as much as old permanent civil servants in similar situations. I do not know the facts of this case, but I will look into the matter myself to see if we cannot remedy it.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: It is a question, not of the temporary employee getting too much but of the permanent civil servant getting too little. In the cases I have mentioned I should have said that the salary is $60 plus $5 bonus.

speechtext:
If the treasury board is
responsible for such salaries as are paid to non-permanent employees, the government or whatever minister directs non-permanent employees should bring one circumstance to the attention of the board. Here is a young lady, an artist. She is an exceptionally capable

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: Will the minister make a brief statement of policy with regard to naturalization?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext: I cannot do much more ' than repeat what I said in March last when a certain question was debated in the house, and supplement the remarks I made on July 15 last, when I first presented my estimates. At the present time the naturalization proceedings follow their usual course as set out in the statute, but when reports of any judge come up, the case is subject to review by the minister. He has discretionary power under section 4 of the act to grant or to refuse a certificate. In practice we have a conference with the officials of the department. We have decided that persons who are of enemy origin or extraction, such as Germans or Italians, shall not be naturalized and we do not naturalize them. We do not issue certificates of naturalization to enemy aliens. subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
I have found in western Canada that British subjects and Canadians may be called up for military service, while on the other hand foreigners who have resided in this country for a long time are exempt. It is high time we said that when foreigners come to this country and have resided here for five years, if they do not think this country is good enough to become citizens of it they should be deported, unless they can show good reason for not having taken out their papers. I do not wish it to be inferred that I am suggesting that all foreigners who have not taken out papers should be deported, because I know that many apply and are refused.
I have in mind two or three cases with which I am familiar. I sat in at the court hearing when they made application. Apparently at that time it was not considered advisable to grant those men naturalization papers, and therefore they were asked a series of questions that I believe the majority of our Canadians could not answer. For example, they were given a geography test that the majority of Canadians could not answer and were asked many questions of that kind, obviously with the intention of making it impossible for them to obtain papers. Consequently, when I say that all foreigners who have not taken out papers should be deported, I am not referring to those who have tried but who through no fault of their own, have been refused citizenship. It is, however, causing a great deal of resentment at present throughout the country when there are two or three families of British origin and two or three of foreign origin who have not taken out papers, and the sons of the British families are called up for military service, while the-sons of the foreign families can jump in and take their jobs. That will not help recruiting. It is time we took a different attitude on this whole question of naturalization.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Montreal and Toronto vie-with each other for the financial leadership of Canada. By reason thereof, a large number of our national corporations have their head offices in those cities, or in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. Most, if not all, of these corporations have their shares listed on the stock exchanges in Toronto or Montreal or from time to time offer their securities through brokers to the people of Canada. Response is made to that appeal from people all over Canada, and it is well that it should be so, that investments should be made in our national corporations from all parts of Canada. When this investment is made and something happens the holder of the security
Supply-Secretary oj State

and it becomes necessary to probate his estate, whether that estate be in Nova Scotia or British Columbia or on the prairies, it is necessary that letters of probate be taken out in the province in which the head office of that company is situated, and a permit must be obtained from the succession duties branch of that province before the securities can be disposed of. In a great many instances there are only a few shares of stock or a few bonds held. But the executors of the estate must go to the trouble and expense of obtaining letters probate and paying the succession duty, if any; yes, in some instances, double succession duties. Mr. Chairman, I presume I am in order in making a few observations on a matter which was mentioned in the house last fall by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis), dealing with gold mining and silicosis in my section of the

Supply-Labour
country. I shall deal with the matter, not in a critical way but rather in a constructive and national way. Since that time I have had the pleasure of meeting the hon. member for Cape Breton South personally, and no one can doubt his sincerity of purpose, also his. profound knowledge of the workers' problems and trade union interests throughout Canada.
Last fall he made mention-it was not an accusation-of silicosis in northern Ontario. A few weeks ago he made another trip to the gold mining section of northern Ontario. Only last Monday, the 9th of this month, the hon. member stated, and rightly so, that he knew conditions in the coal mining industry in his own constituency because he represented a coal mining riding. The same remark should apply to myself with reference to gold mining, for I represent a gold mining section, and it is my duty to correct a misapprehension that the hon. member may have left on the minds of the Canadian people by his remarks on silicosis.
I do not think on his last trip the hon. gentleman visited the Porcupine section. He was at Kirkland Lake, and he was quoted by the Northern News of May 27 as having made the statement with reference to the silicosis situation, "You have to stir up trouble to get anything done." Of course the word "trouble" may be interpreted in several ways. I do not want to tell any member of parliament or any labour leader who visits my section of the country or anybody else what their line of behaviour should be, but it would be fine if some of the so-called labour leaders, because some are real and some are not, would see the management of Canada's nationally known mines. They will find them alert and progressive. I have in mind a labour leader whose name is well known in every section of Canada who made it a point to see the management of some of our mines in this country during his last visit, and I believe the interviews and conversations he had were beneficial both to the labour leader and to the mine management.
I am going to read to the committee a letter that was issued by the Ontario Mining Association in February, 1941. If my information is correct, this letter was sent to every member of parliament. It deals with the problem of silicosis, and I believe it is worth while putting this letter on Hansard. I have wanted to speak on this matter before, but I had to wait for the department to get in, and always it seemed I waited a little too long. I repeat, however, I believe it is my duty for the welfare of the workers, for the
good of labour unionism and of the gold mining industry itself that I should bring this matter before the committee in an absolutely unbiased way. I impute no motives to anyone, and certainly none to the hon. member for Cape Breton South. The letter dated February 15, 1941, reads:
Dear Sir:
In the House of Commons Debates, as published for November 18, 1940, Mr. Clarence Gillis (Cape Breton South) is recorded on pages 180 and 181 thereof as having made certain remarks relative to-

I rise to a point of order. Is it permissible for the hon. member to read into the records of this house a letter with reference to statements made by a member of the house? I observed your ruling last night, Mr. Chairman, when the hon. member for Mackenzie was speaking, and that is why I raise my point of order now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is not in order for an hon. member to read from a letter a criticism of any statement that has been made by a member of the house. A brief reference to such letter may be made, or a member may assume as his own a statement that has been made by others. Paragraph 306 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms states.
It is not in order to read articles in newspapers, letters or communications emanating from persons outside the house and referring to, or commenting on, or denying anything said by a member or expressing any opinion reflecting on proceedings within the house.

I certainly wish to abide by the ruling, but I am astonished to hear it. I have not spoken much during the present session, but I yet have to be accused of reading speeches. I have never done it, over a period of sixteen years. I wish to place on record-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order was, not that the hon. member was reading his speech, but, if I understood rightly, that he was reading from a private letter, written by somebody outside the house, commenting upon and criticizing a statement made by an hon. member. That is out of order.

Then I shall read a
brief dealing with the facts as far as silicosis is concerned, and dealing with the gold-mining industry of northern Ontario, without making any comment upon the statement made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I hope that in this I shall be in order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
will understand that my ruling does not prevent him from commenting, on his own
Supply-Labour

responsibility, upon a statement made by any other hon. member. But it is not permissible to read a comment or a criticism made, by somebody outside the house.

I am going now to give the facts, answering some of the arguments made by the hon. member last fall. I believe I shall be in order in making these statements on my own responsibility, as a citizen of northern Ontario who has lived in that goldmining section for the last thirty-four years, I know something about the gold-mining activities dealing with the problem of silicosis.
The Workmen's Compensation Act of Ontario was amended on April 8, 1926, to include silicosis as a compensatable disease.
Since that time, the Ontario mining industry has paid, solely in connection with silicosis, the following amounts to the workmen's compensation. board:
