To the end of 1939, 462 claims for silicosis were allowed by the workmen's compensation board. The sums paid into the silicosis fund as outlined above indicate the extent to which benefits have been provided for the mine workers and their dependents on account of silicosis.
No industry could face such a staggering burden without making a complete study of the situation with a view to all possible improvements. The Ontario mining industry has taken the following steps:
The Ontario Mining association has a very active silicosis committee which has been constantly studying the problem and which has actively joined in research work conducted under other auspices. This committee employs two engineers who investigate conditions at the mines and who make recommendations to the managers for improvements in mining practice to effect the lowering of silicosis incidence. This has cost the mining industry
858,000.
The McIntyre Porcupine mine, at Porcupine, has been exceedingly active in research work in connection with silicosis. Their investigators, the late J. J. Denny and Doctor W. D. Robson, made important discoveries indicating the preventive effect and possible curative effect, of aluminum dust on silicosis. They have actively carried on this work for many [The Chairman.]
years and for a great part of this time in conjunction wdth the Banting institute. This company has not published the cost of this work, but it cannot have been less than
870.000.
Three years ago I had the great honour of meeting the late Sir Frederick Banting, who was spending some time in the Porcupine section and also in the Kirkland section in order to study silicosis right on the ground, and make reports. Even at that time the mining industry believed they had found an aluminum dust which would prevent silicosis to a very large extent. I am sorry, however, to have to state that it was not found to be applicable; it was not a remedy for that disease but laboratory work is still going on.
To enable the Banting institute to study general silicosis problems and to cooperate with the McIntyre mine in the study of the effects of aluminum dust on silicosis, the Ontario Mining association has supplied them with funds each year as requested. These investigations were made by members of the staff of the Banting institute, particularly Doctor D. A. Irwin, under the personal direction of Sir Frederick Banting. Contributions to the Banting institute up to date have amounted to $61,000.
In 1939, the mines of Porcupine supplied funds for the setting up of a clinic in Timmins for experimental treatment of men who had contracted silicosis. The matter was handled by the Ontario department of health and the workmen's compensation board. The work is being conducted under the direction of doctors from the Queen Alexandra sanatorium, London, Ontario. While more funds will be supplied as needed, the first cost to the Porcupine mines was $25,000.
In 1940, the silicosis committee suggested a still further investigation of one aspect of the effect of aluminum dust on a non-occupational disease, by the doctors of the Queen Alexandra sanatorium, London, Ontario, and the Ontario Mining association granted for this purpose the sum of 84,000.
It was early recognized that lessening the dust content of mine air would automatically lessen the incidence of silicosis. Studies for the furtherance of this object have been carried on by many mines and by the silicosis committee. The underground practice in ventilation, drilling, blasting, et cetera, has been improved immeasurably since 1926, and constant further improvements are being sought. This has been the major effort of the industry, and while figures cannot be presented for this, we know that these improvements have cost the industry many hundreds of thousands of dollars.

Supply-Labour
I also know personally, Mr. Chairman, that at the present time the mine managements are trying to diamond-drill every one of their holes, every one of their shafts, hoping that by that means they will do away with the hard-rock dust which is responsible for silicosis.
I have seen some of these experiments, and there are great hopes in all the hard-rock sections of this country that something will come out of these activities in helping the fight against that terrible disease.
The workmen's compensation board of Ontario maintains four X-ray examination stations in the principal mining centres. These are staffed by doctors and mechanicians who have become real experts in this work. Well over 25.000 X-ray examinations are made every year in these stations. All the X-ray films are studied carefully and filed for record, each workman's films being kept in a separate file.
When the films disclose a disabling silicotic condition, the workman in question is advised by the examining doctor to file a claim for compensation. A very large proportion of the claims are made in this way. Shortly after the claim is made, this man appears before a referee board-of three doctors-which gives him a thorough physical examination and examines his X-ray films and the records of same which have been kept for this purpose. The workmen's compensation board either grants or disallows the claim depending upon the finding of this referee board. Should a claim be disallowed, it is subject to review from time to time as the case may warrant.
The referee board is composed of three doctors from the Ontario department of health. The members of this referee board are all specialists on lung diseases. They have been functioning since 1927 and have acquired great skill in interpretation of the X-ray films in correlation to the physical condition of the man himself.
Workmen are examined at the X-ray stations before being permitted to work in dust-hazard occupations. Only men free of lung and chest disorders can get work cards. Thereafter they are examined yearly, and should they begin to show signs of silicosis they are examined every six months, or oftener, as the examining doctor may decide. Each man's accumulated X-ray films and the records of same are available to the referee board when a claim for silicosis compensation is made on his behalf.
Every device known to >be useful for the purpose has been employed on this work. The members of the referee board and the examining doctors have maintained constant
contact with known authorities on lung diseases. Nowhere on this continent have more complete facilities been set up for this purpose than in Ontario. This is evidenced by the stream of inquiries received from all over the world.
Comparisons on a question of such importance are always odious. However, I listened attentively to the arguments of the hon. member for Cape Breton South wherein he stated, and no doubt sincerely, that Nova Scotia is more advanced in the treatment of silicosis than we are in Ontario. If that is so, it is the duty of the department of health of Ontario and of the mining interests , as well to study the problem as it affects Nova Scotia. I would go further. We are coming to the stage where we are going to have more and more hard-rock mining, and I think some credit should be given the hon. member for bringing up the question, because it is undoubtedly becoming increasingly a national problem. There is hard-rock mining in all Canada to-day with the exception of Prince Edward Island-in eight of the provinces-and wherever you have hard-rock mining you are bound to have silicosis which, as hon. members know, is practically incurable.
We have made wonderful strides with tuberculosis in the last twenty-five years, and although we have done something in grappling with silicosis we have been unable to find any permanent cure. The problem is becoming so grave that the time is not far distant when the federal authorities, through the Department of National Health, will have to undertake the study of it as a national matter. They have the necessary machinery in the national research council, and they could cooperate with the different provinces in which miners are occupied in hard-rock mining. I leave that thought with the government, and I urge upon them the importance of trying to find some means of dealing with this question.
The hon. member mentioned an individual case. I know of a few that are very sad indeed. There are times when these men, although they are properly taken care of, although they are given hospitalization by the management and financial help through the compensation board, tend to get impatient. They believe that sufficient progress is not being made in the treatment of their cases. There may have been some acceleration. I do not want the committee to be under the impression that Ontario particularly and the gold-mining industry as well have not been doing their utmost to solve the problem. The solution of the problem would be welcomed
Supply-Labour

by the workers, and also certainly by the mine managements. I make this statement in no spirit of antagonism.
I know it is hardly proper at this late hour to make any long speeches, but I have not inflicted myself upon the house to any extent this session, and I wish to say a few words on the question of labour organization and unionism.
I have always been in favour of the proper organization of labour. I have always advocated the greatest cooperation between capital and labour, and I believe that so far as our section of the country is concerned, there has been cooperation between capital and labour to an admirable extent. But even in our own section of the country-and I say this in all sincerity-men who would like to belong to labour unions are baffled. They do not know where to go. We have some wonderful labour leaders, such as the Moshers, the Drapers, the Charpentiers, the Meikles, and others who have had at heart the welfare of the workers, but in. my opinion what labour unionism stands in need of to-day is house-cleaning. In my own section we have the spectacle, in one mine, of three or four different kinds of unions trying to establish leadership, and there is rivalry among them. I want labour to have its full share of the comforts of life; but, I repeat, our workers are baffled. They do not know whether it is for membership fees that they are approached or because one particular section desires to get the upper hand over the rest so as to hold the whip-hand over the other sections. I appeal to all labour leaders in Canada; it is not sufficient to talk of union; you must unite in your own ranks.
Speaking of labour leadership, I have never been in favour of class representation. I represent tens of thousands of gold miners, but I wish to see the problem studied from all its angles-management, administration, labour, farmers, bushmen, professional men, and everything else. The same applies to the sulphite and newsprint industry in my constituency.
As regards most of the miners and workers in northern Ontario, the section of the country I know best, I can say that they are not socialists, and the moment any labour organization or any labour leader tries to tie up the principles of socialism with unionism, there is a profound reaction among the workers. They want to know why an attempt is being made to tie them up with socialism. The labour leaders will experience the same antagonistic reaction if they advocated their belonging to the Liberal party, or the Conservative party, or the Social Credit group, or the Cooperative

Commonwealth Federation? Labour unionism has a right to be represented in this house or any legislature in Canada, but I make this statement on behalf of real labour organization, that it should be divorced from any outside "ism". It is heavy enough and important enough to stand by itself. There are terrific conflicts going on at the present time within the labour leadership, and to prove the truth of this statement I should like to quote a few passages from an article that appeared in the Canadian Unionist in February, 1941- and no one can doubt the national spirit of that publication. This is what it says:
Canadian labour is far from being ready to take advantage of the opportunities which to-morrow is almost certain to bring. It is just as well to face the situation frankly now while there is time to do something about it, for in a year or two we are either going to drift before the historic forces now bearing down upon us or we are going to use those forces to direct society toward a way of life which will be worthy of human beings.
Labour is taking a leading part in Great Britain in giving direction to this better way of life. In Canada, however, labour is by no means ready for the task which this involves.
This article goes on to say there is no unity within the ranks of labour. But the author of the article, Mr. Lee McIntyre, makes the same mistake as do most of the labour unions, namely, that he relies on socialism as a panacea for all the workers' problems. I have no quarrel with socialism, although personally I feel that it borders on utopianism, or with the representatives of that philosophy in Canada; but I do say emphatically that when it comes to applying that principle to our section of the country, it is absolutely repugnant not only to the mine owners but to the workers themselves, because these workers know that there are different blueprints of socialism, and there is no agreement, and absolute disunity in the manner of its application. Moreover, most of our miners become property owners. They own their own homes in many instances. The housing commission will bear me out in that statement. The business of gold-mining in our country could never have been developed to the stage it has reached to-day had it been carried on under a socialistic system or governmental regimentation.
I believe in governmental regulations, but I suggest that in many cases of strikes the trouble is not so much dissatisfaction with the management of certain industries as dissatisfaction among the workers with leadership which is given by so-called labour leaders. I wish to pay this compliment to many speeches I have heard on labour, that they were constructive, logical and practical; but the same

Supply-Labour
cannot be said of the views of some so-called labour leaders we have in our section of the country. Some are out-and-out communists, who set out to destroy the work of the Moshers, the Drapers and others. They do not want a solution of the problem, and it is up to our national labour leaders to see that Canadian workers are properly led. We have also the sad spectacle of agitators endeavouring to destroy Canadian unionism, and I speak on this question as a working man; for I spent my youth in connection *with railway construction, farming and lumbering work. In my day the trouble was not as pronounced as it is at the present time, but I have seen a good deal of it in the Porcupine area and in northern Quebec. I have seen people who have never had at heart the solution of the workers' problems keeping up this sort of agitation. In my opinion, there is need of house-cleaning so far as labour unionism is concerned, and the practical sense of the workers realizes and feels strongly about that situation.
That is all I wish to say at the moment. I could enlarge greatly on that problem. I want to thank the committee for giving me this opportunity of stating to a limited extent the problem we have in our section of the country. I could cite case after case of big mines which have done everything possible for their workers-life insurance, bonuses at Christmas, improvement of working conditions. The' situation is not perfect yet, and it is the duty of the workers themselves to do all they can to work with the management for further improvement.
The other day I had the good fortune to visit the Sault Ste. Marie section and was speaking with some labour leaders of the Algoma Steel corporation, and I found there that collective bargaining was working to perfection. I found a union-management cooperation committee and one of the managers told me, "This thing has not only been good for the workers; it has been a wonderful institution for the management"; showing that in that big steel industry proper leadership and organization will do wonders to help labour and industry to work together to their mutual benefit. Labour has passed the diaper stage; it has taken on heavier responsibilities the same as industry has. We have some Bourbons among industrialists, and we certainly have a few of them among labour leaders also. This is not a time to play into the hands of any subversive or mushroom organization, anything that would be a bar to the efforts of our loyal workers in this country,
and the closest cooperation possible between capital and labour, and this for the welfare and progress of Canada.

I am sorry I had to object to the hon. member's reading of that letter. I did so because that letter was circulated by the Ontario Mining association to every hon. member of this house; they were familiar with the statements in that letter, and we on this side of the house are religiously held to that rule. I have no objection to the hon. member making his own argument, but I did not think he could bring in the analysis of the mining association. I did not intend to raise this matter at this time, although I did intend to speak of it on the estimates of the Minister of Pensions and National Health.
I am very much impressed by the fair and reasonable way that the hon. member made bis presentation. That leads me to believe he is interested in the question, and the fact that he has raised it here is, I think, a vindication of my statement that if the working people of this country are to obtain redress of their problems, they must of necessity bring them to the notice of those who can deal with them. That is what I meant when I told the workers in northern Ontario that until they became vocal and could bring their needs, desires and. aspirations in an intelligent way through an organization to the people in authority, no attention would be paid to those problems.
The only comment I have to make with reference to that letter is this:	I accept it
from the mining association because it is the kind of letter I would expect them to write. I am not discounting the activities of the government of Ontario with respect to finding a solution for the problem of silicosis. I have a fair conception of the medical difficulties surrounding that question. They are perhaps doing the best they can with the machinery they have. I am not discounting the work done by the Banting institute. But I would say this in reference to the figures presented by the mining association. They say, "We, the Ontario Mining Association, have paid this amount of money." I say that the Ontario Miming Association did not pay any money. The man who goes under the ground and gets the ore that creates the wealth of those who live on that wealth within the structure of that organization that functions above ground paid the bill 100 per cent.
That applies to all industry.

Exactly. The first charge on any industry when you are negotiating a wage agreement is compensation, and the miners
Supply-Labour

of Ontario will find that out when they begin to sign collective agreements with that association, which I am reasonably sure they will be doing in the near future. In the final analysis the men pay the bill, but the mining association takes the credit.
There is one statement they make here which I am not going to say is wrong; for we have no access to the facts and figures, and we must accept the statement they make. They say that in the settlement of silicosis claims they have paid out the sum of $3,843,198.80, and then in the next paragraph they say:
To the end of 1939, 462 claims for silicosis were allowed by the workmen's compensation board. The sums paid into the silicosis fund as outlined above indicate the extent to which benefits have been .provided for the mine workers and their dependents on account of silicosis.
If 462 claims cost the mining association or the workmen's compensation board $3,843,000, that would work out at about $81,000 a claim, and I cannot see any individual claim settled by the compensation board costing $81,000.
The hon. member could easily get all the statistics he wants from the workmen's compensation board as to the money paid in individual cases. It certainly never meant $80,000 to each individual case.

Exactly. I say the statement can be questioned on the face of it. That letter in my opinion did not refute anything I said. I brought this matter to the attention of the government for that section of the country on account of the fact that at a convention of unions in Toronto about a year ago I met one of the gold-miners from Kirkland Lake who brought to my attention the fact that I pointed out here. He handed me a copjr of the last will and testament of a man employed for a considerable time in the mines of that section who developed silicosis, and had considerable difficulty in the establishment of his claim. They ruled that he did not have silicosis, and in order to protect his family after his death he willed his body to his friend in order that an autopsy might be performed and his family protected in the event of silicosis being diagnosed. I thought that was a peculiar situation. Our situation in Nova Scotia is much better than that because we do not have to pass away to establish our claim. That man has since died; an autopsy was performed some three months ago, but to date there is not any report as to the cause of death. That is the information I got two weeks ago in Kirkland Lake.
I recognize silicosis as a national problem. When I find in the Department of Pensions 
and National Health an appropriation being made for industrial hygiene I think that includes research work into industrial diseases, and the minister agrees. Therefore I bring the matter up here.
I had the pleasure of an invitation to a miners' union that was in process of formation at that time. They asked me, not as a politician but as a unionist with considerable experience in the legitimate trades union movement, to give them the benefit of my experience in laying out a proper organization, free from the subversive elements described by my hon. friend. I made it clear that I was not there representing any political party. I firmly believe, and instructed them so, that in order to get anywhere politically in the labour movement you must first ground yourself in your economic organization and set up your trade unions. Then they will judge for themselves where they are going politically.
One of the first and fundamental things they have to do is to form a collective bargaining organization. I discussed these matters with the men themselves. They have no organization that is functioning; they have no contract with their employers, no understanding and no recognition; they have not the necessary machinery to deal with compensation boards and provincial governments. They told me their stories individually, and with all due respect to the efforts of the people of Ontario, that story was disturbing. For example, when they are X-rayed and silicosis is diagnosed, even in the incipient stages, they are taken above ground and given work, and then X-rayed every four, five or six months. They may be kept working above ground for a year, two years or five years, but in the latter stages silicosis becomes tuberculosis. If, after five or six years of service, a tubercular condition develops, it is said that they are suffering from tuberculosis, regardless of the fact that it was caused by silicosis, and when they die, their families receive no compensation.
I think my hon. friend will agree that round these mines there are many men who have been brought above ground. They are not paid compensation; they are given work above ground in order that the condition may have a chance to clear up. It is, however, something that does not clear up very easily. When that silicate gets into the lungs it rots them; in the end the diagnosis is tuberculosis, and many cases are ruled out in that way. I also met many men in that section who, after working in the mines for perhaps twenty years and reaching the age of forty, when they began to go down hill, were laid off, not because they were unable to work, but

because they had reached the point where they might be more susceptible to this disease. I am sure my hon. friend will agree with that.
On the contrary, I know some men over seventy years of age who are still working underground. They certainly were not let out at the age of forty.

I do not deny that, but I am only dealing with those I met. These men of seventy years of age did not come to see me, and I have no knowledge of them. I did meet many men of forty or forty-two years of age who had no work, who apparently were considered unemployable.
Were they dead?
No; they were not dead.
But they received some compensation.

No; the hon. gentleman
misunderstands what I am saying. For the moment I am referring, not to silicosis but to men who have been laid off because they have reached the age of forty or so. In that section of the country a man cannot get a job if he is forty years of age.
Not if he just applies for one; but if he has been working, he is not laid off then.

After they pass the age of forty, many of them are let out. I met many men in Timmins and Kirkland Lake who told me that story. I think if you check in any of these mining sections you will find perhaps two or three hundred men working in and around these mines who have been diagnosed as suffering from silicosis but who have not reached the point where they have to be laid off. Their fear is that when the silicosis reaches a certain stage and tuber-closis develops, they will not be eligible for compensation. That is the story which was told to me, and that is why I bring it up here. That is why I asked the Minister of Pensions and National Health to use the machinery at his disposal in order to look into this question, to augment the work already being done. If I am wrong in what I say, someone should prove me wrong; if the men in that section are wrong, they should be given that assurance, but if the system at present followed in that section of the country is continued-

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Did I not send my hon. friend a thorough report on this whole question last year?

Yes; I was coming to that. I wish to pay tribute to the Minister of Pensions and National Health, because, after
the matter was raised in this house, I received enough information from him to give me a pretty fair education in it.
The hon. gentleman could very easily have obtained that information from me, because in that part of the country we have been living with this problem of silicosis for many years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I have allowed this discussion to continue because I thought it had to do with industrial disputes, which come under the Department of Labour. I have had serious doubts, however, as' to the propriety of this debate under these items. Now that the hon. gentleman has spoken at this length, I would not wish to curtail his remarks unduly, but I do not think I should permit this discussion to continue very much longer.
I never would have raised the question if I had not been brought into it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I appreciate that.

I have no intention of continuing the discussion. I should, however, like to pay tribute to the Minister of Pensions and National Health, because he did not let the matter drop after it was raised here. He got in touch with many experts in Ontario and sent me copies of all the reports he received from them, and as a result I obtained a fair education with regard to this question. I am now quite satisfied to let the matter rest, because it is receiving some attention, and I believe we shall get somewhere with it. I am glad that the hon. member for Cochrane has become interested in this question, since he lives in that section of the country.
The hon. member must realize that I have been interested in it for a long time.
But the hon. member never raised it in this house.
Perhaps I am just as conversant with this problem as anyone else in this house.

While I am on my feet, there are one or two matters I should like to bring to the attention of the minister. I wish to support what has been said with respect to the question of organization in that section of the country. I know that for a number of years the miners in the gold-mining districts have been endeavouring to build up an organization, and have met with considerable opposition on the part of the operators. That organization made some progress within the last few years, but I believe the wrong elements got into it and did much to discredit it. Last
Supply-Labour

November, however, I had the pleasure of visiting that part of the country; I was there also two weeks ago, and to-day in northern Ontario they have a legitimate organization, sensibly and intelligently led, with ninety-nine per cent of the men heading the organization employed in the gold-mining industry and living in that area. They have made a great deal of progress during the last few months. I believe the minister would be well advised if he got in touch with some of these men who are making an effort to establish legitimate unions there. With respect to strikes, sabotage, and the wrong kind of people leading these unions, just so long as the operators remain unaware of their own interests and those of the country and continue their opposition to signing agreements, establishing satisfactory working conditions and cooperating with committees of their employees, then just so long will the door be left wide open to every subversive element to play upon the fact that in this country we have no industrial democracy; and just so long shall we continue to pave the way for the trouble we are experiencing in many sections of industry to-day.
That is all I have to say on this point. I believe the minister is fully aware of these matters, and I hope that within the near future he will utilize his department in an effort to bring about the results I have suggested.
I should like to bring to his attention a matter that came to me in a brief from Sydney, htova Scotia; possibly the minister has received a copy of the brief as well. It is from the Sydney organization of carpenters and joiners, and I should like to read one paragraph:
We have been employed in the construction of huts in this district for the Department of National Defence, to accommodate the troops stationed here, in some instances 50 per cent of those employed were men in uniform, while a large number of local mechanics including carpenters, painters and labourers could not secure employment.
They go on to give more specific information. I wish to know if the labour end of this national defence work, especially with respect to wages, is under the Department of Labour. Apparently this was a unionized project, and these men object to men in uniform receiving $1.30 a day being used on construction work.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This discussion would properly come under item 102. Shall we take that item with this one?

We shall probably confuse matters if we take too many items at once. I would sooner clean them up as we go along.

Perhaps the hon. member would be willing to let his remarks stand until we reach that item.
I am quite satisfied.
How many men engaged in the mining industry in Canada were killed, injured or disabled by disease during 1940?
I am sure we would not have that information in the Department of Labour.
Where would it be?

In the Department of
Pensions and National Health. I know that the question of silicosis would be under that department. It is possible that we have those statistics, but I should be surprised.

I was reading an article dealing with the diseases which affect miners, and this quoted figures given out by the British ministry of labour. The number of killed, injured or disabled by disease between 1928 and 1937 is given as 1,602,497, and the comment in it is that it is a startling figure. I was wondering whether we had comparable figures so that we might be able to see how we were progressing in meeting the diseases referred to by the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Bradette) and others.
I imagine that the only way we could obtain those figures would be from the workmen's compensation boards of the various provinces.

We shall take it up
with the Minister of Pensions and National Health a little later.

Perhaps this would be
the time to have a statement from the minister on the general labour situation. During the last few days the labour situation has received a great deal of publicity. That eminently respectable and utterly reactionary organization, the Canadian Manufacturers' association, has been holding a convention in the congenial atmosphere of the Seigniory club at Lucerne, Quebec. They appear to be greatly disturbed over the activities of less fortunate people who are not able to hold conventions at the Seigniory club and enjoy its many pleasant and comfortable facilities. The press tells us that their three-day convention was largely taken up with labour questions, not with the ordinary business of the Canadian Manufacturers' association; not in discussing ways and means of improving production and the efficiency of their industries. They ended the convention by sending a long telegram, a most amazing telegram, to the Prime Minister. They asked the government to intern

everybody who might, interfere with the Canadian Manufacturers' association doing as they jolly well pleased. Those are not the words I should like to use, but parliamentary procedure compels me to use them. There are certain words in this telegram which all trade unionists should enlarge and frame, for they compose the best illustration of unmitigated gall that I have seen in the last twenty-five years.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: I understand there is consent that we sit until twelve o'clock, and therefore a formal motion will not be necessary.

This telegram is printed
in the Ottawa Journal of to-day, and it reads in part:
Second, that you immediately make these laws effective by the internment, not only of those who are guilty of inciting to illegal strikes and generally doing their utmost to create discontent and unrest, but also the disseminators of subversive propaganda, written or oral, whose object is to obtain control so as to degrade decent unionism, sabotage the efforts of industry and play into the hands of our enemies to the end that our war effort may fail.
I refer particularly to the words "to degrade decent unionism." How long since has the Canadian Manufacturers' association come to the conclusion that there was any such thing as decent unionism? If unionism is decent, why have they opposed unionism of every kind right up to this very minute?

Oh, no; do not make it
so all-inclusive. I was in business myself.
Let us be quite clear on this.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I fail to see how the
opinion of the Canadian Manufacturers' association on unionism would come under this item. The opinions of the Canadian Manufacturers' association certainly would not come within the ambit of the administration of the department, and therefore I cannot see that this debate is in order.

The opinion of the Canadian Manufacturers' association is of the utmost importance in dealing with the labour question because, when the opinions of that organization clash with the opinions of the workers who are attempting to organize or who are organized, trouble is created, and the Department of Labour is called in to solve the difficulty in one way or another. Consequently the opinion of such a body as the Canadian Manufacturers' association or any labour organization, is of importance in a discussion of this item, the administration of the Department of Labour.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Except that this is not a public forum in the meaning generally given to that phrase. This discussion might be in order when the house was discussing labour legislation, when it was discussing underlying principles which should be laid down. But when we are confronted with estimates or the administration of the Department of Labour,
I would say that it is not in order to discuss all kinds of labour questions and opinions.

I think, Mr. Chairman, you are trying to inject something entirely new into the discussions in this house. If this house is not a forum for the discussion and airing of those problems which confront us from day to day, we ought to close the house and go home, for there is nothing here for us to do.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am relying on standing order 58, subsection 2, which I have quoted time and again and which says that in committee the discussion must be strictly relevant to the item under consideration. The hon. gentleman is discussing general labour policies. General labour policies may be in order when discussing legislation but are not in order on a specific item of administration expenditures in committee of supply.

But, Mr. Chairman, this is not a specific item; it is a general item of departmental administration expenditures, and if we cannot discuss on this general item the whole work of the department which it covers, where in the world and on what item can we discuss it?
- The CHAIRMAN: I have mentioned twice that general labour conditions and general labour problems or policies may be discussed when legislation is before the house, and otherwise perhaps, but certainly not on a specific item of the estimates. The discussion on a specific item of the estimates must be relevant to that particular item, and I must rule that the hon. member is out of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
With the utmost respect for the Chair I would submit that on an item for departmental administration in any department it is absolutely in order to discuss questions of general policy affecting that department. I think it has always been the practice on items of general administration, whether concerning the labour department or the health department or any other department, to have a general discussion on questions of policy respecting the department under review, and I think for the sake of progress in getting along with the business of the house it would be far better to allow hon. members to have a full and free discussion on this particular item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have always seen a general discussion on an administrative item of a department take place by unanimous consent. I must say with all due respect for the minister's opinion that it is not done without unanimous consent, and by standing order 58 it would be out of order to discuss general policies on the item that is before the committee, except by unanimous consent.

With all deference to yourself, Mr. Chairman, I think the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) is quite in order, and I submit that it is also in the interests of progress that he should be allowed to continue his discussion.
I do not believe, Mr. Chairman, that there would be the slightest difficulty in obtaining the unanimous consent of this committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of this committee that the hon. member shall have unanimous consent to proceed with his remarks?

I was going to suggest respectfully to you, sir, that we do not require unanimous consent. As the Minister of Pensions has just stated, under the general administration item all matters concerning the department which come under the supervision of the minister should be open for discussion, and we should not create any precedent here and now by giving unanimous consent, because we do not require it. There is one place and one place only in this parliament where private members are supreme, namely, in supply when discussing the estimates. This is his majesty's purse, and the age-old right of members of parliament is to decide to what extent his majesty's purse shall be filled. That is what we are doing now, and I certainly wish to protest against any precedent being established that would curtail the right of this parliament to discuss any matters in connection with the administration of the minister's department, the minister's salary, or any question of general policy.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The house itself has established rules of procedure, and standing order 58, subsection 2, says that discussion in committee must be strictly relevant to the item under discussion, and the word "strictly" is there in all its letters. The item of administration for any department is not capable of covering any kind of discussion of any opinion such as the one to which the hon. member referred of the Canadian Manufacturers' association. It has been my experience that when a minister in charge of the estimates of a department has desired to open

discussion freely, it has always been done, in order to sustain standing order 58, with the unanimous consent of the committee.

Speaking to the point of order, Mr. Chairman, I think hon. members will recall that throughout the whole of the session when discussion has arisen on certain bills, members of the house have been told that when the estimates come up they will have the privilege of discussing all these matters. On two or three occasions I recall that the leader of the opposition raised that point, and if that be so, surely the Chairman ought to see that that leeway is given to all members.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If there is the unanimous consent of the committee, to sustain the rule.
I am objecting, Mr. Chairman, to that limitation of our privileges as members of the house.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: Let us agree to proceed.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I take it that the hon. gentleman has the unanimous consent of the committee to proceed?

I protest against you putting it that way, Mr. Chairman. I maintain that we do not need unanimous consent to discuss general matters on an item involving the expenditure of money for general administration and supervision.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Let us proceed. Everybody is unanimous.

I have been in the house, Mr. Chairman, for the past ten or eleven years, and this is the first time I have found even an attempt being made to limit general discussion on the item in a department's estimates for departmental administration. Certainly these questions I have been discussing come under the Department of Labour, and certainly the Minister of Labour and his department have to deal with them because they affect people outside this house. Otherwise we should 'have no opportunity to speak on their behalf. ' The Chairman may not like my opinions, but that is no reason why I should not state them to this committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The ruling of the chair is not debatable. The hon. gentleman will proceed with his argument.
Mr, MacINNIS: The reason why I raise this matter at this time is that within a day or so we hope we shall have finished our business here for the present, parliament will adjourn and the members will leave for their homes. What I am fearful about is that pressure such

Supply-Labour
as was indicated by the telegram to which I referred and part of which I read may be brought to bear upon the government and action be taken which will not make for industrial peace in this country. If industrial unrest has come to the stage that the Canadian Manufacturers' association maintain it has, then, as was told them at one of their convention meetings by Mr. Ralph Bell, director of aircraft production, the fault is largely their own. If we are going to have orderly and harmonious labour relations in this country, we can have them only by encouragement and recognition of labour organization.
We can leave it to the workers themselves, when they have established decent working conditions and decent wages, to take care of subversive activities within the organization. But when we resist, as employers in this country have resisted, trade union organization, there comes a stage when only desperate men will be heard, and the ordinary, orderly trade union official has no chance at all. Any hon. member who has had experience in the trade union movement knows that is correct. I could give any number of authorities to prove the point. The late Hon. Norman Rogers, in addressing labour on New Year's eve, 1938, stated that most of the labour disputes during the previous year had been caused by the refusal of employers to recognize the trade union organizations of their employees.
Therefore I earnestly plead with the Minister of Labour, who, I know, is just as anxious in this matter as I am, not to let himself be stampeded by pressure of a kind which I know is even now being used, to take action which would not only be harmful to our war effort, but would embitter labour for many years to come.
I am not going further into this question at the moment, but as we get into other items there are other specific points I wish to raise. I wish, however, to refer to one statement made by the hon. member for Cochrane. He referred to the necessity of keeping politics out of trades union movements.

Isms.
Mr. MaoINNIS: You will have the isms anyway.
We look to-day with high regard and with hope to the labour movement in Great Britain. Possibly nothing which has happened in the last year gave us more hope than the entrance of labour's representatives into the Churchill cabinet last May. I met Sir Walter Citrine when he was in Canada last winter. Walter Citrine had no apologies to make for labour being in politics. As a matter of fact, he
said, they found it necessary to create their own political party. When he spoke in Vancouver as a guest of the trades and labour council I had the honour of a seat on the platform with him. Sir Walter Citrine was not a bit ashamed of saying that he was a socialist-

Certainly a mild
socialist.

-and said that there would have to be a great many changes such as he and the labour movement in the old country were demanding, before there would be any hope of a better world organization. I am not, however, going into that; the Chairman could very well have brought me to order for referring to it.

I understand that these estimates are to be discontinued at half-past eleven, and I should like to make a more lengthy reply to the hon. member for Vancouver East. I will say at this time, however, that in the matter of collective bargaining this government has gone about as far as any government can go. We passed section 502A of the criminal code, making it an offence to discharge a man for the sole reason that he is a member of a trade union. In our order in council No. 2685 we recommend, as one of the principles on which better labour relations can be established, the freedom of any man or group of men to engage in collective bargaining.
Will you take into consideration interning employers who won't carry it out?

I have nothing to do with internment, nor am I a great advocate of internment unless necessary evidence is there on either side. But I consider it would be undesirable to make compulsory that provision in order in council 2685. When you enter the field of compulsion, the principle works both ways and, I believe, inevitably gets you into trouble.
That is what we are fighting in Europe.
Exactly. If you compel one side you have to compel the other, and eventually it leads to a form of government such as we are fighting in Europe.

Conciliation is much
better.

Much better. The hon. member referred to Sir Walter Citrine's visit. I wish we had in this country the happy situation they have over there, in that they have one large trade union congress, the only one
Supply-Labour

body with which it is necessary to deal. In this country we have a number of bodies, and it increases the difficulty where a unanimous opinion cannot be obtained on a number of questions.
In addition to this, the hon. member referred to the conference of employers held at Lucerne. I must say that I received the telegram only yesterday afternoon. The same telegram was received by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice, and so far I have not replied. But I would point this out, that the telegram is largely directed toward subversive activities. The Department of Labour cannot deal with subversive activities. I have prepared a short statement which I wish to make in this connection.
In another place it was suggested that when difficulties arise, the Department of Labour washes its hands of the problem and turns it over to the Department of Justice.
It has also been suggested that the Department of Labour should not tolerate any subversive action.
Might I make this perfectly clear, that the Department of Labour has never been and cannot be the appropriate department to deal with breaches of the law, or any subversive activities. It has no police force, nor has it any machinery to conduct prosecutions.
It is quite true that subversive activities may make the work of conciliation much more difficult, but it was never intended that the Department of Labour should become a department for carrying out any provisions for the enforcement of law and order, or for the punishment of subversive activities.
In fact, so far as the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act is concerned, the department is definitely precluded from doing so.
The only possible course of action which the Department of Labour can take in the event of an illegal strike is to report the matter to the law officers of the crown, and they take such action as may be necessary to enforce the penalty provisions of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act.
The Department of Labour is not the department to enforce the law, whether the subversive activities refer to a labour dispute or to any other acts of a subversive nature.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, the impression seems to be abroad that the Department of Labour should clamp down on labour; that it should apply the law in a rigorous way to the activities of labour. That is not my conception of the duties of this department. We are there to provide for fair wages, to provide conciliation, to furnish facilities for

settling a dispute once it arises. But it is not and cannot ever be the function of this department to act as a police force.
I do not know that there is anything more I would care to say to-night on that particular point. I thank the hon. member for Vancouver East for according me an opportunity of making that statement.

182. Normal services. Cadet services, $171,500.

I wish to make a statement on the militia department set-up and on training in this country. About a year ago the department was completely reorganized. A new minister was appointed, a new chief of general staff, a new adjutant general, a new quarter-master general, a new master-general of ordnance. Those of us who have been serving in the forces had) great hopes that there would be a decided improvement in the efficiency with which the department was run.
The third and fourth Canadian divisions have been mobilized now for over a year. During that year the basis on which we have been trained does not in my opinion compare with the intensive training which the men received in 1914 and 1915, when I was a private in the 21st battalion, whereas in my opinion the training should be based on the type of war to be met in 1945 and 1950, because, certainly we should have on the general staff men who can think of the possibilities of the future and the type of fighting we may have to come up against. During the year in which those divisions have been mobilized we have had, so far as the fourth Canadian division is concerned-
