speechtext:
We are on item 182,
cadet services.

If I understood the
minister correctly, he said that we might discuss any subject.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Not on cadet services.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext: I did not notice the number of the item called. I suggested that anything could be discussed on the salary item, but I am quite satisfied for the hon. member to proceed on the item of cadet services. I said that there would be an opportunity to discuss general subjects and I suggested the item of minister's salary, which is statutory. If, however, my hon. friend desires to discuss the subject now, I have no objection.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The minister moves
that the discussion be general on item 182.

Supply-National Defence

I do not move it. I
intimate that I am satisfied if the committee is agreeable that that be done.

So far as the fourth
division is concerned, we were organized as from June 8, 1940. We had our artillery organized, and the other technical units. Early this year, after the announcement that the fourth armoured division was to be formed, these troops were transferred over to that division and as a result we of the fourth Canadian division

and I think I can speak for the third too-have had no training in cooperation with other arms of the service.
After thirteen months of active sendee, surely the department should be in a position to bring about the combined training of all arms of the service. After all, if we go on active service we must have that training before we can possibly be fit to go into action. We have had no brigade or divisional training, and nothing that would fit us for active service if we had to meet that situation to-morrow.
Again, the fourth division has been organized for a year but we are still without a divisional commander, and without a divisional staff. I cannot see any business man taking on his workmen first without having a management to carry on the business. I suppose the government have not yet decided to whom they wish to give that political plum; but there is no question about it that, as a division, we are entitled to know who is to command us if we go on active service.
Reverting to the fourth division we were regarded as an overseas division. The men of that division gave up their civilian employment on the word of the minister that we were an active service unit. In all the speeches made by the minister during the last few months no suggestion has ever been made that the fourth division will go overseas as a division, and the minister owes it to those men who took his word they were enlisting for active service, to make a statement to them and so hold out some hope that the division will go overseas as a unit and not be broken up like the fifth division in the last war.
The minister knows as well as I do that the third and fourth divisions are still under strength, the fourth division especially so, on account of the transfer of certain services to the armoured division. In forming the armoured division, the militia department did not take the units which had completed their basic training. They mobilized completely new units, and as yet they are not up to strength. Had we had an efficient militia department, they would have taken complete units out of the fourth division or some of
the unbrigaded units and transferred those units to the armoured division, so that the armoured division would have the benefit of completely trained units. What will happen is that the manner in which new units have been taken on will retard the progress of that armoured division.
Speaking of the armoured division, the Minister of Munitions and Supply said the other - day that after a short period tanks would be produced at the rate of three a day. If I know my figures correctly, it will take at least six months to supply the tanks necessary for that division. Then again, let us take the equipment for artillery units. There is no up-to-date artillery in this country, and I am surprised that the department has not improvised such equipment. I understand that on the coast they are still using 18-pounders from the last war and 75-pounders they got from the French, whereas the arm of the artillery is the 25-pound field howitzer.
We come now to the question of vocational training. Last December it was decided by the Minister of Labour, together with the Minister of National Defence, that tradesmen in the various units would be sent to school. The unit with which I am connected sent something like forty-eight men to trade schools in Hamilton and Brantford. After three months, those men came back to us, and we did not know what to do with them. They stayed with us for about a week, and they were sent away on another course. The consequence is that the men do not know what is going to happen to them. Within the last few days, before the unit moved from Toronto, they were struck off the strength, and they do not know what fate is going to overtake them.
Regarding the medical boards, I think the minister will agree with me, that when he served during the last war, once a man was in the army he was in the army and he did not get out. But it seems that we in Canada have demobilized well over a division of men. In other words, half of the 32.000 recruits which the department is looking for to-day have been demobilized on account of the medical boards. There is something wrong there. Surely when a man gets in the army, although his category may be changed, there is something he can be given to do to keep him busy.
Then we come to the question of national defence headquarters, district headquarters, and various headquarters of the army service corps, ordnance corps and other branches of the service. It seems to me that with the minister conducting a great recruiting campaign at this time, he should comb out those departments,
Supply

National Defence

and men who are A-l should wear their uniform in the front line or the field of action, not in the headquarters in Ottawa and other places. I do not think there is any job in national defence headquarters, and district headquarters that cannot be filled by a man who saw service during the last war, who has the capability to do it and who would not be willing to fill the job. The minister should make a clean-up of that situation. I could give him names of officers who served in the militia in peace time, who are here doing senior staff jobs and who never saw active service. That condition is definitely wrong. I think everyone will agree that those of us who wore the uniform in peace time should fight in the front line.
Then we come to the recruiting. If the Minister of National Defence had organized his recruiting campaign as the victory loan campaign has been organized, he might not have been faced with the difficulty he appears to be facing with regard to recruiting to-day.
I was very much surprised to hear that certain suggestions or guidance to speakers had been sent out. In this there is one paragraph to which I take great exception. This paragraph states:
While the empire theme has naturally many attractions for the public speaker it should not be stressed too frequently. Rather for recruiting purposes Canadians should be taught to think of this war in terms of the battle of Canada.
That does not seem to me the right way to get recruits, at any rate not in the province from which I come. We believe that we are fighting for Canada and fighting for the British empire. Whoever was responsible for sending that out should be disciplined.
Last July the Department of National Defence organized what they call to-day the reserve army. There have been so many changes in the designation of the active force and the reserve army in the last six months that I doubt whether anyone in the reserve army or in the active army knows definitely what initials are supposed to come after the name of a regiment, whether it is Canadian Army active, or what have you. It seems to me they must have someone in the Department of National Defence who must be playing alphabet instead of doing a job with maximum efficiency. I am positive that the men who are serving in the army to-day have not the confidence in the Department of National Defence that they had six months ago. Orders are made, and no sooner do you get them than they are changed. It is like the old habit, when men were marching, they would yell, "Lost again." I think there are many officers in the Department of National (Mr. Cockeram.)
Defence who are lost again. As one who served in the last war and in the militia for a period of years, and one who is serving to-day, I am not satisfied with the direction of the militia. If we have to defend this country, we must have faith in those who are going to be in charge of the defence of the country. This country does not lend itself very well to defence; we have too many roads; supposing the Bismarck had been able to land her extra thousand men somewhere along our coastline with the necessary equipment, and the Prim Eugen had a similar number of men, I am sure that with the equipment our men have for the coastal defence we would be licked; they could do anything with us.
Let me give an illustration of what I mean as to lack of equipment. I believe the minister stated in this house on March 31 that equipment would be coming along; I think the third division was to be completely equipped at this time and those of us of the fourth division would be getting equipped. Since that date the regiment to which I belong has not received one additional piece of what we call technical equipment. We are on our way to the east coast, presumably to defend this country. Our establishment of Bren guns for instance is fifty; we have twelve. We have some obsolete Lewis guns,
I think twelve of them. We are supposed to have ten carriers; we have none. We are supposed to have two 3-inch trench mortars; we have one. In that connection the department waits until we get trench mortars before teaching the men how to operate them, instead of giving them a prior course so that when we receive the equipment they would know how to operate them. We are supposed to have twelve 2-inch mortars; we have none. We are supposed to have six anti-tank rifles; we have one. That is the condition in which the regiment to which I belong is going to defend the east coast of this country. What would happen if we were attacked? Surely it is time that the Department of National Defence came to life and that some system of training should be conceived and that bottle-neck removed. I ask the minister to see if he cannot have a clean-up in that department. Let those of us who are serving in the army know that we have guidance that we can trust, because we do not have it now. We have no faith in the officers directing the destiny of this country.
Possibly every member of this house and the people of Canada are responsible for that, because over the period of years we have had a militia, a great deal of it carried on by voluntary effort, with the result that those members of the service who were permanent became nothing but senior civil

Supply-National Defence
servants. They had nothing to work with, and any imagination that they may have had and anything they may have learned during the last war have definitely disappeared. I am of opinion that there should be drastic changes. When General Crerar was appointed chief of the general staff, although I had been in the militia for many years I had never heard his name until he was appointed commandant of the Royal Military College. He was sent over to England with General McNaughton, and I had high hopes that when he came back he would be able to put into that department the pep that is necessary if we are to have a well trained army. I would hate to think of the third division leaving here and being sent to the island of Crete, for example, with the amount of training it has had to date. I appeal to the minister to do something, to give us some dynamic system of training that will put renewed vigour into our men, because he must know that with the system of training which prevails to-day, the morale of our men is going down. I think the minister has the ability to do this; he has been a soldier for some years, but for some reason or another we are getting nowhere. With these remarks I shall resume my seat.

Mr. Chairman, I think my hon. friend forgets just what the situation is and has been in Canada with regard to the training of large formations. What my hon. friend is suggesting is, I think, that there should be training of divisional formations, or training of brigades. My hon. friend knows, or should remember, that in the last war we never had a division formed in Canada. In the last war the first 33,000 men went overseas and the division was formed. After that, all the divisions were formed in England, and were trained there. Here we are endeavouring to form the divisions in Canada and to complete, so far as we can, the individual, platoon, company and battalion training here. So far the units which have gone overseas have not had sufficient time to do formation training; and if my hon. friend will remember, there is at present in Canada only one formation which is concentrated. That is the armoured division, which is concentrated at Borden; but even that division is not completely concentrated there, because both the artillery and engineers are at Petawawa, where the facilities exist for their training.
My hon. friend should realize that we must walk before we can run in connection with training, and I wish to say to him that the training which is being done here is basic training, and that is required before the
higher formation training can be attempted. Let me read to him what the chief of the general staff of the United States, General Marshall, said only a short time ago:
Our training programme is building a seasonal body of men who have the basic knowledge and skill to handle any job we may give them. We are making soldiers and leaders.
. . . The fact is that each individual soldier must receive the basic training of an infantryman no matter in what branch he will ultimately serve.
Later, speaking of the soldier, he says:
He has spent his time learning the things that make a man efficient in combat, that make him act intelligently in an emergency and that toughen him physically to withstand the rigours of modern warfare.
Let me say to my hon. friend that contrary to the idea he seems to have, I have received- and I am not complacent or contented about it-not from Canadian officers but from British officers who are at present at Borden, the highest testimony with regard to the quality of the men we have at Borden at the present time, and the training that is being given them.
With regard to the third division, the hon. gentleman will remember that this division was organized, that is to say mobilization was ordered, in July; but as a soldier my hon. friend knows that mobilization is only the first step-that you cannot have effective mobilization, and training cannot begin, until the officers themselves have received training, and until there is a trained cadre formed. In the old days we would mobilize a battalion of officers and men, who would go into camp together. The officers would have had no special training, with the result that we never had the concentrated and intensive training which is being given to-day. At the present time the method of mobilization is to warn the units so that they may have their men enlist; but in the meantime, before you actually call them up and before unit training commences, the senior and junior officers train so that they may be able to take care of the men when they actually come into the unit. That takes time; .and let me tell my hon. friend that although the third division, was actually ordered up for mobilization, I think in June or July, two brigades of that division were concentrated at Debert, I believe as late as November, if I am not mistaken. Even at that, I believe one brigade was two battalions short, and those two battalions did not arrive until some time later. As a matter of fact one battalion did not go into camp until early this spring.
There has been no opportunity, as yet, for brigade training. There has been less opportunity, of course, for divisional training,
Supply-National Defence

because even when the two brigades were there at Debert there was still a brigade over at Sussex. We did not plan to accommodate them down there. These men were placed as a mobile force, and at the same time to do all the training possible. The general officer commanding the third division was appointed; he came over here, and he has been conducting an intensive system of training during every waking hour. He is not a man who was given some political plum, to use the words of my hon. friend. He is a seasoned soldier, a man who gave fine service in the last war, a man who has devoted his life to soldiering and who was recommended in the highest terms by General McNaughton himself.

To whom is the
minister referring?
Major-General Sansom.
I agree with the minister there, but it was another gentleman to whom I was referring.

There was no political plum in what my hon. friend was talking about. Those are the facts with regard to the third division, which is carrying on its unit, platoon and company training every day. I believe, when that division leaves Canada, it will go in as high a state of efficiency as any formation that has ever left this country, and I think that is saying something.
Let me now say a word with regard to the fourth division. As my hon. friend knows, the fourth division was mobilized later and was not concentrated. The fourth division was in different camps throughout the country during the winter. Training is difficult in winter; nevertheless training was carried on intensively. Then, when we came back from England, and the decision was made to send over an armoured division, my hon. friend is quite right when he says that we did take the artillery and the technical units from the fourth division and put them iqto the armoured division, and probably they were very glad to get into that formation. What we are doing now, as I have said-I have made no secret of it whatever-is recruiting men to fill up the technical units of the fourth division.
1 say to my hon. friend that I feel he is a little impatient about this. I do not pretend to be an expert in training, but I believe that in the chief of the general staff, General Crerar, we have a man who does understand training and who has put into effect a system of training which, I believe, will show excellent results.
[Mr. Ralston.}
My hon. friend has said that he never heal'd of General Crerar before. That is unfortunate, but at the same time I do not think it is anything against General Crerar. Let me say to the hon. gentleman that when I wanted a chief of tilie general staff I did not appoint him myself; I did not ask my colleagues with regard to the matter; I did not select someone to be given a political plum. I asked General McNaughton to recommend to me the best man he had over there, the man he would recommend as chief of the general staff. General McNaughton himself had been vicechief and chief of the general staff and knew what was required. He had served under General MacBrien, and had acted as chief of the general staff himself. He recommended General Crerar to me in no uncertain terms, the gentleman to whom my hon. friend has referred. General Crerar has been on the job constantly ever since. The changes which have been made from time to time-I admit they are many, and I make no apology whatever for them-have been due to no small extent to the recommendations which General Crerar has made.
Let me to say to my hon. friend that if I could take up the time of the committee I could go over the training syllabus, go over the schools which have been established in order to train men in every branch and every arm of the service. There is the question of training men in their units with their officers or training them in training centres. I had a recommendation the other night from an officer commanding an active unit. The question was whether or not a second battalion would be formed in order to reinforce that unit. This officer, like my hon. friend, had been an officer in the last war. He had spent three or four months at a training centre, and he said th" t he would prefer to have reinforcements from a training centre than reinforcements from the second battalion, mobilized in the ordinary way. The testimony from United States officers who have been in England, and the testimony from British officers, is unanimous that the training centre system which has been adopted during the last year is the only system which can be adopted in order to give results.
I say to my hon. friend that nobody is satisfied with the training, and he should not think that General Crerar is satisfied with the training. The officers at headquarters are doing everything they can to improve it. What are they doing? We sent the director of military training to England, and I believe he spent two months with the different units in England, with General McNaughton and his staff, finding out what the necessities of training were. He came back here and put

Supply-National Defence
these suggestions into effect. We are doing more than that. We are sending officers and non-commissioned officers to England in order to get training in their special arms of the service. We are bringing officers from England to take charge of training and to deal with the special problems which have arisen in connection with this war.
Does this change the original policy of having men rise from the ranks rather than through the, training centres?
My hon. friend has misunderstood me. The. men in the training centres are men in the ranks. .
I understood the minister to say that the men from the training centres were highly trained officers.

There are officers' training centres, and there are other ranks' training centres. I am speaking of the other ranks' training centres. I was saying that the training centre system is the system which has proved itself to the British and to the United States authorities, and I believe it will prove itself to the people of Canada when they see the results.
Only to-day I was called upon by a gentleman who had been most critical last July. He is a man who knows a great deal about training, and he called upon me with regard to that matter. He has been watching this training quite closely, being in charge of an officers' training centre. He said that in his opinion the present training far exceeds anything that has been done before. I am not puffed up about that, I only wish to say to my hon. friend that there are some people who do not agree with him in connection with this matter of training. This training has been done on the advice of officers in whom I have the greatest confidence, and it is producing results.
My hon. friend" spoke of demobilization on account of medical boards. I dealt with that matter as frankly as I could not very long ago. I told the house that I considered the 10,000 that had been discharged as excessive, and I said that steps were being taken to correct this matter. Yesterday I had a talk with the director general of medical services. He had made a personal tour of all parts of Canada and, in addition, has sent medical officers to the different centres in order to see that the medical boards are doing their duty. The complaints I am receiving is that the medical examination is too strict. It is that way because we do not want to have these medical discharges if they can be avoided.

How many men have been
discharged from the active army since the war began?

Since September, 1939,
14,000.

Not only those by medical
boards, but also those discharged on other grounds?
I have not those figures.
We were told in the special committee on pensions that they are being discharged at the rate of 1,800 a month, even yet.
I do not know that.
Could the minister get those figures?
Yes.
Does that cover only those who have been sent back from overseas?

No; all who have been
discharged anywhere, in Canada too.

Could the minister
give the proportion of those sent back from overseas?

I cannot give that tonight. My hon. friend referred to front line officers and suggested, to use his own words, that I clean out national defence headquarters. We have sent quite a number of national defence headquarters officers overseas, and we shall be sending more from time to time. We are also bringing officers back from overseas.

I am talking about
A1 men who should be utilized for active service, men who did not see service during the last war.

I heard what my hon.
friend said. I thought he was talking about officers.
Officers and men.

Every endeavour is being made, not only in connection with this recruiting campaign, but at all times, to see that, wherever possible, civilian employees are used. Without wanting to reflect upon my colleagues, I think national defence, army services will show a favourable record compared with the other service departments, with regard to the number of civilian employees compared with military clerks. When I was overseas I found a demand for military staff clerks in the units which is very difficult to supply. We have to keep and train a certain number of military staff clerks in order to supply that demand. A number of military staff clerks went down on the Nerissa. They were being sent overseas partly to fill the demand. I say to my hon. friend that I have in mind what he has in mind, and I assure him that men who can be spared,

Supply-National Dejence

will be replaced by men who are not physically fit, or by women. We are glad to do that at National Defence and will see that it is done.
My hon. friend referred to his own unit, which is in the fourth division. He knows that our present commitments are for an army tank brigade, for a third division and for an armoured division. Those are the commitments we made for this year, and our endeavour naturally is to see to it that these units are supplied with equipment just as rapidly as possible. I cannot get equipment for these units any faster than Canadian industry turns it out. I can assure him that every step is being taken so far as my department is concerned to see that the equipment is turned out as rapidly as possible. At times I have felt I have almost gone too far in butting into matters which are for my colleague, the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). I have frequently visited plants and interviewed executives of plants which were engaged in the production of this equipment, and endeavoured to impress upon them the seriousness and urgency of equipping our forces.
Just a few days ago I interviewed a man who was most anxious for me to see his plant. He was getting together components to prepare for production. I told him I appreciated what he had shown me but that I should like to take him down to some of the camps; since he had shown me what he had to show, I should like to show him men who needed equipment. He said, "There is no use in your taking me down there; I know what the situation is, and I assure you that I am working just as hard as you are in trying to get this equipment out; it will be in your hands just as rapidly as possible." One of the jobs of the vice-chief of the general staff is to keep up tables, from month to month, of equipment supplied and forecasts of deliveries. He endeavours to see to it that industry, through the Department of Munitions and Supply, lives up to the forecasts which are made. I assure the committee that the equipment position is improving. I could name over a dozen items in respect of which there has been marked improvement, even since I spoke in March last. It is true that there are some items which it will be difficult to get for some time to come. There still is a serious shortage in equipment, but that shortage is being made up just as rapidly as Canadian industry can do it. I took the trouble to go yesterday to the meeting of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association to say a few words about that very matter.
With regard to the fourth division, I say to my hon. friend that his Bren guns will come

along before his unit is called upon to meet any operational situation, and that the other items of equipment, in so far as they are procurable, will come along too. When he says that he has no confidence in the officers at national defence headquarters, let me say to him that I do not share his views. Judging from the results which I have seen since they took the situation in hand, I believe they know their business. Some changes may have to be made, and I do not propose to hesitate to make them. As a matter of fact, I am not making any reflection on other officers, but I have felt that round pegs should go in round holes and square pegs in square holes. I was not in the defence department veiy long when, as my hon. friend suggests, I did make a number of changes in the senior positions. He will find that there is not a district officer in this dominion to-day who was occupying the position of district officer commanding in the same district a year ago. Those are the changes we endeavoured to make, and a number of them have been new appointments entirely. My hon. friend will not find any political plums among them. At all events my political friends do not think so, judging from what I hear. These appointments are being made on account of merit and on the recommendation of a board of officers in whom I have confidence, and who know the qualifications of these officers. I have no complaint whatever against my hon. friend for bringing this matter up. I am not complacent; I am not contented; I am not satisfied about the matter; but I assure him that if hard work and industry, if concentration, if faithfulness to a job and determination to do it count, he will find that national defence headquarters will fulfil his expectations.
Item stands.
Progress reported.	.
